recipes.title: Tofu Zensai - Before The Meal
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 2 hours, plus
9-20 hours soaking time
Cooking time: I hour 25 minutes
Makes:
2 (5½ x 4 x
2-inch/
14 x IO x 5 cm) blocks
r% cups
(ro½ oz/300 g)
dried soybeans
½ fl oz (12. 5 mi) liquid
nigari,
diluted in 1½ fl oz (45 mi) water
TOFU
Japanese tofu is like a creamy custard
with a gentle flavor of soybeans.
Making your own may seem like an
undertaking, but you will be well
rewarded. Look for organic soybeans
and the best water, since the flavor
hinges on the beans and water. You
will need tofu forms.
Soak the soybeans in 5 cups
(40 fl oz/I. 2 liters)
cold water for
8 hours in warm weather, 15 hours
in cool weather , and 20 hours in
cold weather. (If your house is
air - conditioned or heated, use your
best judgement.)
Scoop a third of the beans and
a third of the soaking liquid into
a blender and process on high speed
for 2 minutes. Pour into a large
bowl. Repeat with the remaining
beans and liquid in 2 batches.
In
a pot large enough to hold the
water and the blended soybeans,
bring 5 ½ cups (44 fl
oz/ I. 3 liters)
water to a boil. Add the soybean
mixture to the pot and stir con­
stantly to avoid scorching the
bottom (a flame tamer/simmer ring
is useful here). Bring the contents
of the pot back to a near boil , then
remove the pot from the heat and
set aside for 15 minutes , until the
foam subsides.
Meanwhile, set a large wire - mesh
strainer over a medium bowl and
line it with the muslin bag provided
with the tofu forms (alternatively,
use a large piece of cheesecloth).
Set the pot over low heat for
IO minutes. Pour the hot soybean
mixture through the cloth and let
the liquid drip into the bowl. Once
cool enough to handle, twist up the
muslin bag (or cheesecloth) and
squeeze to remove as much of the
liquid as possible. (The solids left
in the muslin bag are called okara
[soybean pulp] and the liquid in the
bowl is soy milk. Use the okara for
stir-fries; if not using right away,
freeze for up to 3 months.)
Pour
the soy milk into a heavy­
bottomed medium pot and heat
over low heat (on a flame tamer,
if you have one) until the mixture
reaches 175°F (8o°C), about I hour.
Meanwhile, prepare a large bowl
and a long wooden spoon. Set
the diluted nigari next to the bowl.
Once the soy milk reaches the
desired temperature, pour it into
the bowl and stir vigorously in wide
revolutions to create a vortex into
which you will pour the nigari ( while
stirring). Make 2 more
revolutions
and come to a full stop in the
middle of the bowl. Remove the
wooden spoon and let the curds sit
undisturbed for 15 minutes.
Meanwhile, place two 6½ x 43/• x
3
½-inch (16.5 x 12.5 x 9 cm)
wooden tofu forms in a pan
with sides to catch the drips, and
line with the muslin cloths
that
came with the forms (or with
cheesecloth); the cloth should drape
over the sides of the forms.
After 15 minutes, gently ladle the
curds into the forms. Fold the
overhang on top and set the flat
wooden insert (provided with the
forms) over it. (Alternatively,
jury-rig a flat surface the same size
as the form to evenly distribute
weight over the tofu .) Set a r-1¾ lb
(500-800 g) weight in each form
and press down gently but firmly.
Leave for 30 minutes to set.
Remove the weights and slip the
cloth-enclosed blocks of tofu into
a lidded rectangular container filled
halfway with
cold water. Refrigerate
for 30 minutes. If not eating right
away, remove the cloth and store
the tofu in a covered water-filled
container for up to 4 days.
[
variation]
For soft tofu: In a double boiler,
heat 3 cups (24 fl oz/750 mi) soy
milk
until just shy of 185°F (85°C) .
Vigorously stir the soy milk to make
a vortex as described above, add
2 teaspoons nigari, and stir twice . .-bet ­
sit
for 15 minutes before serving.

Preparation time: 35 minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Serves: 6, as a small bite
4-inch (ro cm) piece daikon , scrubbed
I½ oz (45 g) fuki no to [butterbur buds)
• 1/4 teaspoon fine sea salt
4 tablespoons rice vinegar
• 2 tablespoons
mirin
SPINACH AND CHRYSANTHEMUM
PETALS IN SOY DASHI
The bright yellow chrysanthemum
flowers add color and a lovely bitter
note to the mineral- rich , sweet
spinach.
Tear the maitake lengthwi se into
attractive pieces easily eaten with
chopsticks. In a dry frying pan ,
roast over medium-low heat until
fragrant and golden in spots. Toss
with the citrus juice.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil
over high heat. Lower the spinach
stem ends into the water (do not let
go) for a co unt of 20 , then sub­
merge
the sp inach in the boiling
water and cook another 20 seconds,
depending
on the toughness of
the leave s.
Plunge into a bowl of cold water
and run more co ld water into the
bowl until the spinach is cool.
Drain well. Align the stem ends
and squeeze down the length of the
spinach, from the ends to the tips
to remove excess water.
Cut the spinach crosswise into
¾-I inch (2 - 3 cm) pieces.
Bring
a medium pot of water to
a rapid boil and add the vinegar.
Drop in the chrysanthemum petals
and cook until the petals are shiny,
20-30 seconds.
Plunge into a bowl
of cold water and run more cold
water to coo l. Drain well .
Mix the dashi and soy sauce together
and toss with the spinach and
chrys ant hemum petals. Spoon into
a bowl and lay the
maitake pieces on
top in one clump, so the tops rest
against the middle of the spinach .
Serve.
BUTTERBUR BUDS
WITH GRATED DAIKON
Bitter is the taste of spring in
Japan and fuki no to (page 430)
are the buds of the quintessential
mountain vegetable-butterbur­
that peek out from th e snow once
spring is around the corner. The
buds are often served as tempura or
sauteed with miso.
Grate the daikon on an oroshigane
Uapanese grating plate). Set a wire­
mesh sieve over a bowl and scrape
the daikon into the sieve to drain
for IO minutes. Squeeze the grated
daikon and drop into a small serving
bowl, but reserve the drained and
squeezed juices.
Bring a small saucepan of salted
water to a boil. Pare off any
discolored portions from the fuki
no to and blanch for 2 minutes in
the boiling water. Scoop out with a
wire- mesh sieve, cool. squeeze, and
chop roughly. Toss with the drained
daikon juices, place an otoshibuta
[drop lid) or plate on top , and wait
for IO minutes.
Stir the salt into the vinegar and
mirin. Squeeze the fuki no to and fold
into drained grated daikon. Drizzle
with the dressing and serve. It is
best on the first day, as fuki no to
tends to lose its vibrant color and
grated daikon develops a slightly
funky nose.
61 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Flowering Greens In Sake-Soy Dashi-Drenched
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 15 minutes
Cooking
time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6
· % lb (300 g) nanohana (page 436)
or broccoli rabe (rapini)
· 2 tablespoons soy
sauce
• 2 tablespoons sake
l large handful freshly shaved
katsuobushi or hanakatsuo
Preparation time: IO minutes, plus
overnight soaking
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Serves, 6
3 1/2 oz (100 g) fiddlehead ferns,
bottoms trimmed
l tablespoon baking soda (bicarbonate
of soda)
Boiling water
· 1¼ cups (ro fl oz/300 ml)
Katsuobushi
Dashi (page 156)
• I teaspoon soy sauce
· I teaspoon mirin
¼ teaspoon flaky sea salt
l large handful freshly shaved
katsuobushi or hanakatsuo
FLOWERING GREENS
IN SAKE-SOY
In the spring, the fields all over
Japan are covered with bolting
brassicas with small yellow flowers.
The season is short-lived, so take
advantage when it arrives.
Bring a medium pot of salted water
to a boil. Lower the nanohana stem
ends into the water, but do not
let go. Cook for 30 seconds, then
drop the nanohanae into the boiling
water and submerge with a wooden
spoon. Cook until the nanohana is
pliable but hasn't lost its structural
integrity, 2-3 minutes more,
depending on thickness. Drain and
refresh under cold running water.
Drain well and pat dry. Align from
the stem ends and squeeze down
the l engt h of the
nanohana to remove
excess water.
Stir the soy sauce and sake together.
Lay the nanohana in a rectangular
pan and pour the sake-soy mixture
over it, rolling the pan to coat the
greens evenly. Lifting them by the
stem ends, remove the greens from
the pan , shake excess liquids back
into the pan, and cut crosswise
into ¾-inch (2 cm) pieces. Align
thos e pieces attractively in a shallow
bowl, keeping the cut clumps
together. Swirl the sake-soy mixture
from the pan over the greens and
garnish with the katsuobushi. Serve
immediately .
DASHI-DRENCHED
FIDDLEHEAD FERNS
Fiddlehead ferns are a harbinger of
spring and one of the few Japanese
mountain vegetables (page 430)
easily sourced outside of Japan.
Because of the delicate nature of
the fiddleheads, the dashi should be
lightly seasoned.
Place the fiddlehead ferns in a large
bowl. Sprinkle with the baking
soda (bicarbondate of soda) and
pour boiling water over them. Lay
an otoshibuta [drop lid] or a plate
on top and leave overnight. Drain
and rinse in several changes of
cold water to remove the naturally
occurring toxins in some varieties
of fiddlehead ferns.
In a sma ll saucepan, bring the
dashi, soy sauce, mirin, and salt to a
simmer, then immediately remove
from the heat and cool.
In a medium saucepan of rapidly
boiling water, blanch the fiddle­
head s until slightly softened but
still crunchy, about 30 seconds.
Scoop the fiddleheads out of the
water, blot dry, and slip into the
dashi to cool.
If too long to eat comfortably
with chopsticks, cut the fiddleheads
into 1'/•-inch (3
cm) lengths , stack
in a bowl, and pour the dashi over.
Strew with katsuobushi and serve.
The fiddleheads keep well for
several days, if stored refrigerated
in the dashi.
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Ginger-Infused Greens And Vegetables Carrot With Smashed
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Serves, 6
5 1/, oz (150 g) shungiku [edible
chrysanthemum greens]
· 5¼ oz (150 g) bok choy
5 'I• oz (150 g) komatsuna U apanese
mustard greens] or mustard greens
• 5'/• oz (150 g) spinach
• 2% oz
(75 g) mitsuba
4¾ oz (135
g) Japanese eggplants
(aubergines), peeled at intervals for
a striped effect
• 3 tablespoons
soy sauce
• r½ tablespoons
mirin
3 tablespoons grated fresh ginger
5 'I• oz (150 g) daikon (or other root
vegetable such as turnip), scrubbed and
cut into thin julienne
Preparation time, 45 minutes
Serves, 6
l (ro½ oz/300 g) momendofu or
Japanese-style soft block tofu
½ lb (225 g)
carrots, scrubbed and
finely julienned
1/s teaspoon flaky sea salt
2 tablespoons white sesame seeds
• ½ tablespoon mirin
½ tablespoon usukuchi shoyu
%, sheet nori, snipped into fine strips
I½ inches (4 cm) long
GINGER-INFUSED GREENS
AND VEGETABLES
This medley of simmered, steamed,
and crunchy raw vegetables is
brought together by the ginger­
infused dressing. Leftovers
are good for several days, if
refrigerated.
Fill a large pot halfway with water
and bring to a boil. Hold the
greens with a large pair of tongs
and dip the stems into the boiling
water to cook for 30 seconds. Drop
the greens into the water, push
down, and cook for an additional
30 seconds. Drain and refresh in
a colander under cold, running
water until cool. Squeeze the greens
of excess liquid, chop coarsely, and
squeeze again.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil. Arrange the
eggplant (aubergine) in the steamer
basket, cover, and steam until soft,
about 15 minutes . Tear or cut
lengthwise into strips and halve
crosswise.
In a medium bowl, combine the soy
sauce and mirin. Squeeze the grated
ginger to express the juice into the
bowl. Toss the greens, eggplant,
and
daikon in the dressing and serve
in a rustic pottery bowl.
CARROT WITH SMASHED
TOFU AND SESAME
This version of shira-ae [smashed
tofu dish] omits miso, but includes
a generous helping of white sesame
seeds, which pair particularly well
with carrots.
Set the tofu on a cutting board and
prop a small plate underneath it
to angle the board into the kitchen
sink (to catch drips). Lay another
cutting board on top of the tofu
to press out moisture for 20
minutes . Massage the carrot with
the flaky salt and let sit for at least
IO minutes while you prepare the
other ingredients.
In a small, dry frying pan, warm
the sesame seeds by shaking the pan
over medium-high heat until the
natural aroma wafts off of the pan.
Slide into a suribachi [grinding bowl]
or spice/nut grinder and process
until powdery. Squeeze the tofu by
handfuls and drop into the
suribachi
with the mirin and usukuchi sh'!Y"·
Smash with the surikogi [grinding
pestle] until creamy and well
emulsified.
Strew the carrots across a clean tea
towel, roll up to remove moisture,
and fold into the tofu mixture.
Scrape down the sides to clean up
the presentation, sprinkle with the
nori, and serve in the suribachi.
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Stamina Salad Sauteed Onions With Natto 66 Aemono - Dressed
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 35 minutes
Cooking time : 5 minutes
Serves, 4
•
3 ½ oz (100 g) moyashi [mung bean
sprouts]
• Boiling water
4 tablespoons
white sesame seeds
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
I small red onion, thinly sliced
8 oz (225 g) daikon, scrubbed and
julienned
4 1/2 oz (125 g) carrot , scrubbed and
julienned
5 1/+ oz (150 g) Japanese cucumber ,
julienned
2 large
or 3 medium
egg yolks, at room
temperature
I large handful freshly shaved
katsuobushi or hanakatsuo
• 2 tablespoons
rice vinegar
• 2 tablespoons
soy sauce
I tablespoon fresh lemon juice
Preparation time : IO minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Serves: 2-4
½
tablespoon canola (rapeseed) oil
• I small onion (3½ oz/Ioo g), halved
and sliced into half - moons 1/+- inch
(6 mm) thick
• 2 teaspoons slivered fresh ginger
I package (3 oz / 85 g) natto, well aerated
· (see
Note, page 46)
1/+ teaspoon
flaky sea salt
STAMINA SALAD
This vegetable-packed salad gets
its name because Buddhist priests
eat it from the rainy season in
June, to the height of summer
during Obon . Obon is a three-day
Buddhist celebration in mid­
August , when people burn straw to
shepherd the ancestors back from
the spirit world through the smoke.
This is the busiest time of the
year for priests, so they need extra
energy.
Drop the
m'!Yashi into a sieve and
pour boiling water over them for
IO seconds . Blot dry on a clean tea
towel. In a small , dry frying pan,
toast the sesame seeds over medium
heat until fragrant, shaking the pan
and lifting it off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Smash the seeds
in a suribachi [grinding bowl] to
partially break down.
Massage 1/+ teaspoon of the salt into
the sliced onion and let sit for
IO minutes. In a medium bowl, toss
together the julienned daikon and
carrot and massage in ½ teaspoon
of the salt. Let sit for IO minutes
as well.
Squeeze the onion, daikon, and
carrot gently by small handfuls and
drop onto a clean tea towel for
blotting dry.
Toss the onion, daikon, carrot,
and cucumber with the m'!Yashi
and mound attractively in a large
shallow serving bowl or deep
platter. Make a hole in the center
of the vegetables and slip the egg
yolks into the hole . Sprinkle the
salad with the smashed sesame seeds
and the hanakatsuo. Break the egg
yolks with a pair of saibashi [cooking
chopsticks] or salad servers and
toss well to distribute all of the
ingredients. In a small bowl , whisk
together the vinegar, soy sauce,
lemon juice, and remaining
1/+ teaspoon salt. Drizzle over the
salad right before serving.
SAUTEED ONIONS WITH NATTO
Natto can be an acquired taste
and here the sweet sauteed onion
mellows the natto's bold flavor . If
possible , use never-frozen, locally
made natto (page 436). This small
bite is good as is, or spooned onto
Japanese rice (page 291).
In a large frying pan, heat the
oil over medium heat. Add the
onions and ginger and cook until
no longer raw but not completely
wilted, about 2 minutes.
Scrape
into a medium bowl. Fold the natto
into the cooked onions, season with
the salt, and serve as a condiment
with other Japanese dishes.
66 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Spinach With Walnuts Nameko Mushrooms With Grated Daikon
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes, plus
IO minutes for cooling
Cooking time: IO minutes
Serves: 6
I small carrot , scrubbed and cut into
fine julienne, 2 inches (5 cm) long
· 7 oz
(200 g) spinach
• 5 oz (150 g) shirataki noodles
• 2 dried shiitake, soaked in I cup
(8 fl oz/250 mi) boiling
water for
30 minutes
· 2 tablespoons soy sauce
· 1½ tablespoons mirin
½ cup (2 oz/60 g) walnuts
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Serves: 4, as a small bite
22h oz (75 g) nameko mushrooms,
bottoms trimmed
¼ teaspoon grated fresh wasabi
• 2 tablespoons rice vinegar
• I tablespoon mirin
I tablespoon Katsuobushi Dashi
(page 156)
½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
¾ cup (7 oz / 200 g) drained
grated daikon
½ sheet nori , toasted and snipped into
fine threads
SPINACH WITH WALNUTS
In Japanese cuisine, spinach is
often paired with walnuts in the
form of a walnut dressing. Here,
the spinach is enlivened by crunchy
carrots and umami-rich dried
shiitake, and tossed with shirataki­
transluscent noodles made from
konjac-for an unexpected twist.
Bring a pot of water to a boil over
high heat. Drop the carrot into a
wire-mesh sieve and dip the sieve
in and out of the boiling water to
barely cook the carrot. Shake off
the sieve and spread the carrot on
a clean tea towel to blot dry. Drop
the spinach into the boiling water
and immediately scoop out with a
wire-mesh sieve. Run cold water
over the spinach to stop the cooking
process. Squeeze down the length
of the greens and cut crosswise into
1¼-inch (3 cm) pieces. Cut the
shirataki noodles into 1¼-inch
(3 cm) pieces, place in a wire-mesh
strainer and dunk in and out of the
boiling water to blanch. Set in the
kitchen sink to drain.
Drain the
shiitake over a small
saucepan, reserving the soaking
liquid. Remove the stems,
discard, and and thinly slice the
reconstituted shiitake caps. Reserve
the shiitake separately , but add
I tablespoon each of the soy sauce
and mirin to the soaking liquid and
bring to a simmer over medium
heat. Drop in the shirataki and once
the liquid returns to a simmer,
adjust the heat to maintain a gentle
simmer for 5 minutes.
Roast the walnuts in a small dry
frying pan over low heat until
fragrant and grind in a
suribachi
[grinding bowl] or spice/nut
grinder until powdery but not
paste-like. Mash the remaining
I tablespoon soy sauce and ½
tablespoon mirin into the ground
walnuts.
Drain the shirataki (discard the
simmering liquid) and slide into
the grinding bowl with the walnut
mixture . Separate the squeezed
spinach with your fingers, and
drop into the walnut mixture along
with the shiitake and carrot. Toss
with your fingers until the walnut
dressing is well incorporated into
the spinach and other ingredients.
Scrape down the bowl, or mound
in a ceramic serving bowl , and serve
with any Japanese meal.
NAMEKO MUSHROOMS
WITH GRATED DAIKON
Although nameko mushrooms are
often found floating in a bowl of
dark miso soup, here they are served
on a bed of grated daikon and aro­
matics, taking on a livelier profile .
This dish is best freshly made.
Bring a pot of water to a boil. Place
the nameko in a wire-mesh sieve and
dip in and out of the boiling water.
Blot dry on a clean tea towel, then
remove immediately because they
tend to stick. In a small bowl, stir
together the vinegar , mirin, dashi,
and salt and mix into the daikon and
wasabi until well incorporated. Fold
in the mushrooms and sprinkle
with the nori. Give the mixture one
light stir, and serve immediately .
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Sweet Potato With Lemon Dressing Summer Salad With Dumplings
recipes.transcription:

2 hours chilling time

For the dressing,
I small onion (3 1/2 oz/roo g)

· 4 tablespoons rice vinegar
½ cup (4 fl oz/r25 ml) neutral oil such
as canola (rapeseed) , sunflower ,
or peanut

For the salad ,

and

(kaiware daikon) , sponge base cut off and

SWEET POTATO
WITH LEMON DRESSING
Lemon and sweet potato are a
natural pairing , because ~e citrus
plays well with the sweet, dense
flesh. Served in butter lettuce or
crispy iceberg lettuce ''cups, " this
salad makes for a brilliant summer
luncheon :fi.rst course.
Bring two medium pots of water to
a simmer over medium-high heat.
Drop the potatoes into one pot
and the carrot into the other
and cook at a lively simmer for
2-3 minutes,
until the pieces are
cooked in the center, but still
hold their shape . Drain.
Massage the cucumbers gently with
¼ teaspoon of the salt, let sit for
IO minutes , then drain in a sieve set
over a bowl to catch the drips. Place
the cabbage in a wire-mesh sieve
and pour a steady stream of boiling
water over it in a circular motion
for 30 seconds. Cool and squeeze.
In a small bowl , stir together the
lemon juice , remaining I teaspoon
salt , soy sauce , and pepper. Whisk
in the olive oil to emulsify.
In a large bowl , toss together the
sweet potatoes , carrot, cabbage ,
cucumber, walnuts, and lemon
dressing. Chill for 2 hours.
Set
out 6 small plates and lay
I iceberg lettuce leaf or 2 butter
lettuce
leaves on each one. Spoon
an attractive mound of salad on
the lettuce leaves and serve . This
salad holds up for I-2 days,
if
refrigerated , though should be
stored separately from the lettuce.
@ p .69
SUMMER SALAD WITH DUMPLINGS
The carrot dressing not only gives
the greens a luxurious coating , but
also contrasts nicely with the hittsumi
[dumplings].
Make the dressing, Grate the onion
and carrot on an oroshigane ijapanese
grating plate] using a circular
motion. Transfer to a blender and
add the vinegar , oil, salt , pepper,
soy sauce , and mustard. Whirl to
form a thick, pourable dressing .
Make the salad, Lay the drained
hittsume across a large platter .
Julienne the cucumber and strew
over the dumplings with th e kaiware
daikon. Fluff the shiso chiffonade and
sprinkle over the salad . Distribute
the tomatoes around the perimeter
of the salad .
Drizzle the carrot dressing across
the surfac e of the salad and serve.
68 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.transcription:

r½
lb (650 g) small turnips with

UME-FLAVORED
Umeboshi [salted sour plum] pair well
with white root vegetables such as
turnip , daikon, and radishes . Serve
as a pickle-like side dish for rich
dishes like grilled meats .
Lop off the turnips' stems at the
base, wash the leaves , and set aside.
Scrub the turnips with a vegetable
brush , but do not peel. Pare off
any brown discolored spots and
blot dry on a clean tea towel. Halve
the turnips lengthwise , then lay the
turnips cut side down on a cutting
board and cut into slices 1/s inch
(3
mm) thick . In a medium bowl,
massage the turnips and ito konbu
with the salt.
Line the turnips stems up on a
cutting board and slice crosswise
at %-inch (r
cm) intervals. Put in
a wire-mesh sieve and pour a steady
TURNIPS
stream of boiling water over them
for 30 seconds. Shake off the hot
water and squeeze the leaves to
remove excess liquid.
Grind the sesame seeds coarsely in
a suribachi [grinding bowl] or spice
grinder. Mash in the umeboshi to
form a paste. Dribble in the mirin
to thin the consistency and to
adjust the sweet-sour balance.
Rinse the turnips and konbu and
squeeze. Drop into a medium bowl
and toss with the turnip leaves and
sesame-umeboshi paste. It keeps in
the refrigerator for several days,
but the flavor will lose some of its
brightness, as the vegetables exude
liquid and dilute the
umeboshi flavor .
[Qj p .71
EGG YOLK-DRESSED CRAB
AND CUCUMBER
Kimizu is an egg yolk-based sauce
similar to a silky mayonnaise and is
particularly good on seafood and
vegetable salads. Artisanally crafted
kamaboko [crab-flavored fish cake]
can
be amazing. Substitute freshly
picked crabmeat if the only choice
for kamaboko is one containing MSG
and preservatives.
Tear the crab-flavored kamaboko
into pieces 2 inches (5 cm) long
to resemble strips of crab leg.
In a bowl , combine the konbu,
cucumbers , fine sea salt, and
1% cups (14 fl oz / 400 mi) cold
water
and soak for IO minutes.
Drain and pat dry in a tea towel.
In a small stainless steel bowl set
over a pan of simmering water
(make sure the bottom of the bowl
does not touch the water), whisk
together the vinegar , mirin, egg
yolks , flaky salt, and I tablespoon
water and cook over low heat,
whisking constantly , until warmed
and slightly thickened , r½-
2 minutes . Whisk in the potato
starch mixture and cook for another
I minute to make a creamy sauce­
if the bowl is too hot, lift slightly
above the pan of simmering water a s
you stir. Press through a wire-mesh
sieve into a small bowl and cool.
Mound the cucumber mixture in a
serving bowl and strew attractively
with the kamaboko or crab. Drizzle
the dressing over it and serve . It
holds up to the following day, when
refrigerated, though there will be
some seepage from the cucumbers .
70 AEMONO - DRESSED

Cooking time, IO minutes

I medium stalk celery, julienned
• ¾ teaspoon flaky sea salt

unpeeled, julienned
3 egg

rice vinegar

mirin

tablespoons potato starch

I2 oz
(340 g) boneless, skinless chicken
breast , cut into ½-inch (I2 mm)
cubes

tomatoes, halved through the stem end

SUMMER CHICKEN SALAD
Make this summer salad once the
celery, tomatoes , and cucumbers
are available from your garden or
farmers market.
Massage the celery gently with
¼ teaspoon of the flaky salt and
the cucumbers with the remaining
½ teaspoon of the flaky sea salt.
Bring a medium pot of water to a
boil over high heat. In a metal bowl
(that will fit snugly over the pot of
water), whisk together the egg yolks,
vinegar , mirin, and½ tablespoon
of the potato starch until smooth.
Stir in % cup (5 fl oz/I50 ml) cold
water and set the bowl over the pot
of boiling water over medium-low
heat. Continue whisking and cook
until the mixture has thickened and
forms thick ribbons , 2-3 minutes .
Remove the bowl from the pot (but
keep the water at a boil) and stir in
the
wasabi. Scrape the kimizu dressing
into a small bowl, cover , and chill .
Toss the chicken pieces with the
fine salt,
then with the remaining
2 tablespoons
potato starch and
blanch in the boiling water until no
longer pink in the centers, about
2 minutes.
Spread out on a baking
sheet and chill for 15 minutes .
Strew a platter or large serving plate
with the celery and cucumbers ,
followed by the chicken, and then
the tomatoes. Drizzle with the kimizu
dressing and serve immediately as
a refreshing luncheon dish.
SWEET MISO-DRESSED NEGI
WITH CLAMS
Silky steamed negi dres sed with
sweet miso sauce is irresistible when
combined with briny clams. If you
like a more pronounced miso flavor,
use more inaka miso (country-style
miso, page 432), than white miso.
Rub the clam shells with the salt.
Scrub and rinse in several changes
of cold water to encourage the
clams to expel their sand. Place in a
small saucepan with the sake , cover,
and bring to a boil over high heat.
Adjust the heat so the liquid does
not bubble over and cook until all
(or almost all) of the shells have
opened , 3-5 minutes, depending
on the size of the clams . Discard
the unopened clams and strain the
simmering liquid. Remove the meat
from the shells. Leave small clams
intact, cut larger clams into ½-inch
(12 mm) pieces.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil. Arrange the negi
whites in the steamer basket, cover ,
and steam for 4 minutes. Add the
negi green pieces and steam for
4 more minutes. Uncover , remove
the steamer basket. and let the
negi cool.
In a bowl , whisk the mirin and
vinegar into the miso and drizzle
in I or 2 tablespoons of the
strained clam steaming liquid to
lighten the miso consistency to a
creamy paste. Fold the steamed negi,
clams , and dressing together. Serve
at room temperature or cold the
following day.
72 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Greens And Chrysanthemum Petals With Sesame New Potatoes With
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Serves: 4-6
I tablespoon rice vinegar
• r¾ oz (50 g) fresh edible
chrysanthemum flowers, about I2
• 7 oz (200 g) spinach
· 3½ oz (roo g) kikuna [edible
chrysanthemum greens]
3 tablespoons white sesame seeds,
warmed in a small, dry frying pan
• I tablespoon mirin
• I½ tablespoons soy sauce
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Serves: 6
I lb (450 g) new potatoes, peeled and
cut into thin matchsticks
7 oz (200 g) enoki mushrooms,
bottoms trimmed off, separated into
single stalks
I amanatsu [sour-style orange] or
½ orange plus ¼ grapefruit
3 umeboshi
[salted sour plum].
pitted and finely chopped
• I teaspoon soy sauce
• I teaspoon mirin
• I teaspoon sake
I handful mitsuba stems , cut crosswise
into %-inch (r.5 cm) pieces
Red shiso powder or flaky sea salt
GREENS AND CHRYSANTHEMUM
PETALS WITH SESAME
This is a lovely-hued dish and
makes a pretty addition on the table
or even a zensai plate. It is best the
first day , but
holds up well to the
next day if refrigerated.
In a pot , bring 2 cups
(r6 fl oz/
500 ml) water and the vinegar to
a boil over high heat. Set up a bowl
of ice water in the sink. Pull the
petals off of the center portion of
the flower and drop into a wire­
mesh sieve. Dip the sieve in and out
of the pot of boiling water. Shake
off the hot water and plunge into
the bowl of ice water to cool. Once
cool , blot dry in a clean tea towel.
Refresh the bowl ofice water . In
a large pot of salted boiling water,
cook the kikuna 1-3 minutes,
depending on toughness. Scoop
out of the boiling water (but keep
the water boiling) and plunge into
the ice bath. Scoop out and allow
to drain.
Lower the spinach stem ends into
the water (do not let go) for a count
of IO, then submerge the spinach
in the boiling water and cook
30-60 seconds more, depending
on the thickness of the leaves.
Scoop into the i ce bath to cool ,
then drain. Align the stem ends
and squeeze down the length of the
spinach, from the ends to the tips
to remove excess water. Squeeze the
boiled kikuna as well. Cut the greens
across into 3/+-inch (2 cm)
pieces.
Wrap the sesame seeds in a clean tea
towel and crush slightly with the flat
blade of a heavy kitchen knife. Slide
into a bowl and whisk in the sake
and soy sauce. Pull the greens and
flower petals apart with your fingers
to
evenly distribute the yellow
among the green and toss with
the dressing using a pair of saibashi
[cooking chopsticks]. Serve.
NEW POTATOES WITH
SOUR PLUM AND ORANGE
The umeboshi [sour plum] and citrus
notes make this dish a perfect
accompaniment to grilled meat on
a summer afternoon or a bright
addition to a packed lunch.
In a pot of boiling salted water ,
blanch the potatoes until no longer
raw but not mushy, about I minute.
Scoop out with a wire - mesh sieve
and pat dry on a clean tea towel.
Drop the enoki into the pot of boil­
ing water for 20 seconds. Scoop
out and drain well.
Pare off the peel and slice out the
amanatsu sections to remove each
section from its surrounding
membranes. Halve the sections
crosswise but if using grapefruit,
cut into thirds. Scrape the umeboshi
into a small bowl and mix in the soy
sauce, mirin, and sake to loosen the
paste. Toss the potato matchsticks
with the umeboshi dressing and fold
in the enoki, mitsuba stems , and
amanatsu. If the umeboshi dressing is
too sour, drizzle in a little mirin to
rebalance the flavors. Sprinkle with
a few pinches of red shiso powder or
flaky sea salt and serve.
73 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Crispy Green Beans In Sesame Broccoli And Radish Salad
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Serves, 4-6
14 oz
(400 g) green beans, topped
· 6 tablespoons white sesame seeds
2 tablespoons usukuchi shoyu
2 tablespoons mirin
• l pinch flaky salt
Preparation time: QO minutes, plus
l hour chilling
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6
2 tablespoons fine sea salt
11/, lb
(600 g) broccoli , trimmed
3 egg
yolks, at room temperature
• 3 tablespoons rice vinegar
• 3 tablespoons
mirin
• ½ tablespoon potato starch
½ tablespoon grated fresh wasabi
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
8 radishes, sliced into paper-thin
rounds
CRISPY GREEN BEANS
IN SESAME
The white sesame seeds are subtle
in flavor, and pair well with the
saltier, though lighter in color, soy
sauce - usukuchi sh'?J'u (page 443). It
is possible to use the more common
dark soy sauce instead.
In a pot of boiling salted water,
blanch the green beans for 30-
90 seconds, depending on
thickness (they should only be
half cooked). Refresh under cold,
running water until cool to the
touch . Drain, shake off , and pat
dry in a clean tea towel. Cut on
the diagonal into 1½-inch (4 cm)
pieces . If unusually thick, make
acute diagonal cuts so the pieces
are thinner.
In a small, dry frying pan, toast
the sesame seeds over medium heat
until fragrant, shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Transfer
immediately to a
suribachi [grinding
bowl) or spice/nut grinder and
process until the oils come out. Stir
in the usukuchi sh'?)lu, mirin, and salt
until smooth, taking care to scrape
down the si des , so as to not leave
any precious sesame particles.
Toss the green beans with the
dressing and serve.
@ p.75
BROCCOLI AND RADISH SALAD
Broccoli is often served with
hollandaise in Western restaurants,
so this lighter version of an egg
yolk -based sauce is a good match
for broccoli and makes a lovely
dressing, without the richness of
the butter-based hollandai se.
Bring a medium pot of water to a
boil over high heat and add the fine
salt . Cut
off bite-size florets from
the broccoli stem. Cut the tender
part of the stem into similar size
pieces. Blanch in the salted boiling
water for l minute. Scoop out with
a wire-mesh sieve, spread out on
a tea towel-lined plate , and place
the plate in the refrigerator to chill
the broccoli.
Bring the pot of water back to a
boil over high heat. In a metal bowl
(that will fit snugly over the pot
of water), whisk togeth er the egg
yolks, vinegar, mirin, and potato
starc h until smooth. Stir in ½ cup
(5 fl oz/r50 ml)
cold water and set
the bowl over the pot of boiling
water. Continue whisking and cook
until the mixture has thickened
and forms thick ribbons , about
5 minutes. Remove the bowl from
the pot and st ir in the wasabi.
Scrape the kimizu dressing into
a small bowl, cover, and chill.
Toss the broccoli with the flaky salt ,
arrange on a small pretty platter,
and strew with the radish slices.
Drizzle the kimizu dressing over the
salad and serve as a side dish.
74 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Sesame-Dressed Greens And Carrots Steamed Eggplant
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 4
6½
oz (185 g) komatsuna
(Japanese mustard greens]
• I small carrot, scrubbed
r'/• cups
(ro fl oz /3 00 mi) Katsuobushi
Dashi
(page 156)
½ tablespoon mirin
½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
· 2 tab lespoons
soy sa uc e
2 sasami [chicken
tenders] or
(3'/• oz/roo
g) skin less, boneless
chicken breast
4 1/2 tablespoons (r oz/3 0 g) gold
sesame seeds
l ½ tablespoons go ld sesame oil
Preparation time: IO minutes , plus
co oling time
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6
• I lb 2 oz (500 g) , Japanese eggplants
(aubergines) , ste m ends trimmed
· I teaspoon flaky sea salt
• I tablespoon black sesame seeds ,
warmed in a small, dry frying pan
• 2 tablespoons
soy sauce
I large handful freshly shaved
katsuobushi or hanakatsuo
SESAME-DRESSED GREENS
AND CARROTS
This dish is quick to execute , so
works well for lunch or a casual
evening meal. Substitute spinach
or mustard greens if komatsuna
U apanese mustard greens] are not
available.
Bring a lar ge pot of salted water
to a boil over high heat. Lower the
komatsuna stem ends into the water
(do not let go) for a count of
IO seconds , then submerge the
greens in the boiling water and
cook 30 seconds . Drain and
refresh under cold running water
or in an ice bath. Drain well. Pat
dry and cut crosswise into
¾-r¼-inch (2-3 cm) length s.
Cut the carrot into thin
rectangular pieces ½ x r3/• inches
(I cm x 4 cm). Measure out
r ½ tablespoon
of the dashi into a
small bowl and set aside. Add the
rest of the dashi to a saucepan and
add the mirin , ¼ teaspoon of salt ,
and I tablespoon of the soy sauce.
Bring to a simmer over medium­
high heat, drop in the carrot, and
simmer for I minute. Scoop out
with a small wire-mesh sieve and
discard the simmering mixture.
Bring a pot of water to a boil. Place
the chicken tenders in a wire-mesh
sieve and dip into boiling water for
2 minutes.
(if using chicken breast ,
dip in for 7 minutes.) Shake off
excess water an d tear into shreds.
In a sma ll, dry frying pan, toast
the sesame seeds over medium
heat until fragrant , shaking the
pan and lifting off the heat if
needed to avoid scorching. While
still hot , pound the seeds in a
suribachi [grinding bowl] or whirl
the seeds in a spice / nut grinder
until mostly broken down. Whisk
in the remaining I tablespoon soy
sauce and 1/+ teaspoon salt and the
reserved r½ tablespoons dashi. Once
combined, whisk in the sesame oil
until emulsified.
Toss the komatsuna, carrot, and
chicken with the dressing and serve.
[Qj P-77
STEAMED EGGPLANT
WITH SESAME
Though eggplant (aubergine) loves
oil and becomes silky when fried,
steaming it can produce a similar
texture without the grease .
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil. Peel the eggplant
(aubergine) lengthwise at intervals
to crea te a striped effect. Cut
lengthwise into slices ½ inch
(12 mm)
thick. Sprinkle with the
salt. Arrange the eggplant side by
side in the steamer basket, cover,
and steam the eggplant over high
heat for 5 minutes
on each side ,
until softened but not falling apart.
Remove from the steamer and
let cool.
Arrange the eggplant slices
attractively on a platter and sprinkle
with the sesame seeds and soy sa u ce .
Sprinkle the katsuobushi over the
platter and serve immediately with
other Japanese dishes.
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Eggplant In Sesame Miso Walnut-Dressed Chrysanthemum Petals
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes,
plus 20 minutes cooling time
Cooking time: 15 minutes
Serves : 6
I lb 2 oz (500 g) Japanese eggplants
(aubergines), stem ends cut off
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 2 tablespoons sake
4 tablespoons
white sesame seeds
• 2 tablespoons
inaka miso
• I tablespoon mirin
¼ teaspoon ichimi togarashi
[powderedJapanese red chile]
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time: 30 seconds
Serves: 6
2 tablespoons rice vinegar
• (5 ¼ oz/r50 g) fresh edible
chrysanthemum flowers , about
36 medium
• r¾ oz (50 g) walnuts
I tablespoon K.atsuobushi Dashi
(page 156) , plus more as needed
• l tablespoon mirin
I tablespoon brown rice miso
• I pinch of flaky sea salt
EGGPLANT IN SESAME MISO
Eggplant (aubergine), a summer
vegetable, is eaten in myriad ways
inJapan. Although commonly
fried, steaming the eggplant and
dressing it with sesame yields a
naturally light, yet creamy warm ­
weather dish.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil.
Peel the eggplant (aubergine)
lengthwise at intervals to create a
striped effect. Place in a heatproof
dish that will fit in a steamer basket
and rub with the salt. Sprinkle with
the sake. Place in the steamer basket,
cover, and steam until collapsed ,
about 30 minutes. Turn once
after 15 minutes for even cooking.
Drain off the liquid from the dish
and reserve . Allow the eggplant
to cool to room temperature ,
about 20 minutes.
In
a small, dry frying pan, warm the
sesame seeds until fragrant. Slide
into a suribachi [grinding bowl] and
smash until they are powdery and
have partially broken down but are
not paste-like . Mash in the miso,
mirin, and reserved steaming liquid
to make a light, creamy sauce.
Once cool enough to handle , halve
the eggplant crosswise and cut or
tear lengthwise into % - inch (1
cm)
strips. Toss with the sesame sauce,
sprinkle with the ichimi togarashi, and
serve.
[Q'] P-79
WALNUT-DRESSED
CHRYSANTHEMUM PETALS
Chrysanthemum flowers seem
to have fallen out of favor. Still,
they are worth seeking out , as they
can add a bit of spark to a simple
vegetable treatment. They pair
well here with the creamy walnut
dressing.
In a pot, bring 4 cups (32 fl
oz/
I liter) water and the vinegar to a
boil over high heat. Set up a bowl
of ice water in the sink. Pull the
petals off of the center portion of
the flower and drop into a wire­
mesh sieve. Dip the sieve in and out
of the pot of boiling water. Shake
off the hot water and plunge into
the bowl of ice water to cool. Once
cool, blot dry in a clean tea towel.
Warm the walnuts in a small, dry
frying pan until fragrant and
pound in a suribachi [grinding
bowl], or process in a mini-prep
or nut grinder until broken down
to a paste. Leave the nuts in the
suribachi and mash in the dashi, mirin,
miso, and salt . If the mixture is
stiff, dribble in a bit more dashi to
loosen . Fold in the petals until
the dressing is well incorporated
and serve.
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Green Beans With Smashed Tofu And Sesame Carrot With Smashed Tofu
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 40 minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Serves: 6
I (10½ oz/300 g) momendofu or
Japanese-style soft block tofu
¾ lb (350 g) thin green beans, topped
2 usuage
[deep - fried tofu pouches] ,
quartered
3 tablespoons white
sesame seeds
• Q tablespoons mirin
I½ tablespoons usukuchi shoyu
• I large pinch of flaky sea salt
I tablespoon black sesame seeds,
warmed in a small, dry frying pan
Preparation time: 40 minutes
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves: 6
5 oz (150 g) momendofu or Japanese­
style soft block tofu
7 oz (200 g) carrots, scrubbed
• 13/• oz (50 g) walnuts
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
· ½ tablespoon mirin
GREEN BEANS WITH SMASHED
TOFU AND SESAME
Crispy green beans and creamy ,
smashed tofu juxtapose nicely. You
can add a bit of color with some
salt - massaged julienned carrots or
throw in a protein, such as thinly
sliced pork. Cress or mitsuba can also
brighten the dish.
Set the tofu on a cutting board
and prop it up with a small plate
to angle the board into the kitchen
sink (to catch drips). Lay another
cutting board on top of the tofu to
press out moisture for QO minutes.
In a medium pot of boiling water ,
blanch the green beans for
I minute . Scoop out of the water
(but keep it boiling), shake off
the excess, and blot the beans dry
between two clean tea towels. Cut
crosssise, at a diagonal, into
1½-inch (4 cm) pieces . Place the
usuage quarters in a wire-mesh sieve
and dip it in and and of the boiling
water. Cool and blot dry the usuage
pieces. Stack and cut into short
strips¼ inch (6 mm) wide.
In a small , dry frying pan , toast the
white sesame seeds over medium
heat until fragrant , shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Slide into a
suribachi [grinding bowl] or spice /
nut grinder and process until
powdery.
Squeeze the tofu by handfuls to
remove any last liquid and drop
into the suribachi. Sma sh in the mirin,
usukuchi sh~u , and salt using the
surikogi [grinding pestle]. Fold in
the
green beans , usuage, and black
sesame seeds, smooth down the
sides and serve, as is, in the suribachi.
@ p.81
CARROT WITH SMASHED TOFU
AND WALNUTS
While carrots are typically julienned
for smashed tofu treatments,
here cutting the carrots into fine
rectangular pieces gives the dish
more texture .
Set the tofu on a cutting board
and prop it up with a small plate
to angle the board into the kitchen
sink (to catch drips). Lay another
cutting board on top of the tofu to
press out moisture for 20 minutes.
Cut
the carrots into½ x I½-inch
(12 x 40 mm) rectangular pieces
'I• inch (6 mm) thick. In a pot of
boiling salted water , blanch the
carrots for 2 minutes . Scoop
out
with a wire-mesh sieve , refresh
under cold, running water, shake
off, and pat dry in a clean
tea towel .
Gr ind the walnuts in a suribachi
[grinding bowl] or food processor
until almost paste-like . Squeeze the
tofu between two cupped hands to
remove the last bits of moisture and
drop into the suribachi or a medium
bowl. Mash with the salt and mirin
until fluffy. Fold in the carrots and
serve. It holds up well the next day
as leftovers.
80 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Spinach And Enoki With Smashed Tofu Aemono - Dressed
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, I hour
Cooking time, 20 minutes
Serves,
6
2 (10½
oz / 300 g each) momendofu
or Japanese-style soft
block tofu
6 tablespoons white sesame seeds
2 dried shiitake,
soaked in ½ cup
(4 fl oz/125 ml) boiling
water
for 30 minutes
3 tablespoons usukuchi shoyu
· 2 tablespoons mirin
I tablespoon rice vinegar
· 8 tablespoons kigiku [fresh
chrysanthemum petals], from
about 4 large
flowers
• 7 oz
(200 g) shirataki noodles
I cup (8 fl oz/250 mi) Konbu Dashi
(page 156)
½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
· 2 tablespoons fine sea
salt
7 oz (200 g)
enoki mushrooms,
bottoms trimmed off
· 14 oz (400 g) spinach
SPINACH AND ENOKI
WITH SMASHED TOFU
Shira-ae [smashed tofu treatments]
usually contain one or two ingredi­
ents besides the dressing ( -ae) itself .
The combination of ingredients
makes for a gorgeous dish .
Set the tofu on a cutting board and
prop a small plate under it to angle
the board into the kitchen sink (to
catch drips). Lay another cutting
board on top of the tofu to press
out moisture for 20 minutes.
In a small, dry frying pan , toast
the sesame seeds over medium
heat until fragrant, shaking the
pan and lifting off the heat if
needed to avoid scorching. Slide
the seeds into a suribachi [grinding
bowl] or a spice/nut grinder and
grind until well broken down and
almost pastelike. Squeeze the tofu
by handfuls to remove any last
moisture, and drop into the suribachi
along with the ground sesame seeds.
Reserving the soaking liquid, scoop
out the shiitake and thinly slice cross­
wise. Pour the shiitake soaking liquid
into a small saucepan and season
with I tablespoon of the usukuchi sh,zyu
and the mirin. Add the sliced shiitake
and simmer for IO minutes . Let
cool in the simmering liquid.
Bring a medium pot of water to
a boil over high heat. Measure out
a generous 2 cups (17
fl oz/500 ml)
of the boiling water and add the
vinegar to it. (But keep the pot of
water at a boil.) Drop the kigiku into
a wire-mesh sieve and pour the
vinegared hot water over the petals.
Run cold water over to cool. Shake
off the excess water and squeeze
gently in a clean tea towel.
Place the shirataki in a wire-mesh
sieve and dip in and out of the
po t of boiling water (you will use
the pot of boiling water, so keep
it handy). Shake off, cut crosswise
into ¾-inch (2 cm)
lengths,
and blot dry in a tea towel. In a
medium saucepan, bring the dashi,
remaining 2 tablespoons usukuchi
sh£Jlu, and the flaky sea salt to a
simmer over medium heat. Drop
in the shirataki and simmer for
IO minutes to gently absorb flavor.
Cool in the pan.
Fill another medium pot three­
quarters of the way up with water.
Add the fine sea salt,
and bring
back to a boil over high heat. Halve
the enoki crosswise and place in a
wire-mesh sieve. Dip in and out
of the boiling water and cool. Press
gently in a clean tea towel to blot
dry. Hold the spinach stems in the
boiling water used for the enoki for
30 seconds. Drop them all in, push
down to submerge in the water,
and cook for another 30 seconds.
Scoop out from the water with a
wire - mesh sieve and refresh under
cold running water to cool. Pick up
the stem ends and squeeze down to
the leaves to remove excess water.
Drape across a cutting board and
cut crosswise into ¾-inch (2 cm)
lengths .
Drain
the shiitake and shirataki and
mix with a pair of chopsticks into
the tofu-sesame mixture with the
enoki and spinach until all of the
ingredients are well incorporated .
Garnish with the kigiku and serve.
It holds up well for a couple of days
if stored in the refrigerator , though
there will be some seepage.
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Fiddlehead Ferns With Smashed Tofu And Walnuts Natto-Topped
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Serves:
6
5 oz (150 g) momendofu or
Japanese-style soft block tofu
• 3 ½
oz (JOO g) young fiddlehead ferns
· I¾ oz (50 g) walnuts
• I tablespoon soy sauce
• ½ tablespoon mirin
• I pinch of flaky sea salt
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Serves: 4
I teaspoon fine sea salt
I small, sweet apple, peeled and cut
into ¾-inch (1.5 cm) cubes
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
• I small yellow or red onion,
finely chopped
I package (3 oz/85 g) natto, well
aerated (see Note, page 46)
½
cup (4 fl oz/J20 mi) Japanese
Mayonnaise
(page 32)
½ teaspoon mustard powder
I tablespoon usukuchi shoyu
• I teaspoon fresh lemon juice
• 4 crispy
inner leaves of iceberg lettuce
I medium avocado, cut into 5/a-inch
(1.5 cm) cubes
2 1/+ oz (65 g) daikon sprouts ,
cut off their sponge base
I large handful Italian or curly parsley,
finely chopped
2 tablespoons
freshly grated
Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese
FIDDLEHEAD FERNS WITH
SMASHED TOFU AND WALNUTS
The creamy tofu smooths out the
slight bitterness of fiddlehead fe r ns
and the toasted walnuts add a nutty
ri chness.
Set the tofu on a cutting board and
prop a small plate underneath to
angle the board into the kitchen
sink (to catch drips). Lay another
cutting board on top of the tofu to
press out moisture for 20 minutes.
Bring a medium pot filled half
way with water to a boil. Hold the
fiddlehead stems in the water for IO
seconds, then drop in the water and
cook for another 20 seconds.
Drain the fiddleheads and cut cross­
wise into 1½-inch (4 cm)
lengths .
In a small, dry frying pan, warm the
walnuts until fragrant and smash
to a paste in a suribachi U apanese
grinding bowl]. Squeeze the tofu by
handfuls and mash into the walnuts
with the soy sauce, mirin , and salt
until fluffy . Fold in the fiddleheads
and serve.
NATTO-TOPPED
VEGETABLE SALAD
The texture differences between
the different components make this
salad unusual, and the mayonnaise­
based natto sauce ties the ingredients
together . Kraft Parmesan cheese
has been ubiquitous to the Japanese
kitchen since the 1970s , though
here it is updated as freshly grated
Parmigiana- Reggiano .
Stir to dissolve the fine sea salt into
I cup (8 fl oz/250 mi) cold water .
Drop the apple cubes into the
salt water and soak until needed.
Massage ½ teaspoon of the flaky salt
into the chopped onion, drop into
a wire - mesh sieve and rinse quickly
with cold, running water. Shake off
excess water and blot dry in a clean
tea towel.
Scrape the natto onto a chopping
board and chop with a sharp
knife until almost paste-like. In
a small bowl, whisk together the
mayonnaise, mustard powder ,
usukuchi sh'!)'u, and lemon juice .
Stir in the chopped natto to make
a sauce for the salad.
Drain the apple cubes and press off
the residual water inside a clean tea
towel. Take out 4 salad plates and
set I piece of iceberg on each to
act as a cup for the chopped salad.
Divide the salad vegetables among
the 4 plates
in the following order:
avocado , appl e, daikon sprouts,
parsley , and onion . Drizzle with
the natto sauce and sprinkle with
the Parmigiano-Reggiano. Serve
immediately.
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Kabocha With Smashed Tofu 86 Aemono - Dressed
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: I hour
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 6
2 (IO½ oz/300 g each) momendofu or
Japanese -sty le soft block tofu
% cup (3 oz/85 g) gold sesame seeds
• I½ tablespoons soy sauce
• I tablespoon mirin
Neutral oil such as canola (rapeseed),
peanut, or safflower, for deep-frying
% lb (300 g) lightly peeled kabocha
(Japanese pumpkin) , cut into
% - inch (I cm) cubes
2 dried shiitake, soa ked in hot water
for 30 minutes
3 ½ oz (100 g) shirataki noodle
· Boiling water
I small carrot, scrubbed
¼ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• I large handful seri
Qapanese wild parsley]
KABOCHA WITH
SMASHED TOFU
Smashed tofu dishes make protein ­
rich creamy additions to any meal.
Set the tofu on a cutting board and
prop a small plate underneath to
angle the board into the kitchen
sink (to catch drips). Lay another
cutting board on top of the tofu to
press out moisture for 20 minutes.
Heat a large frying pan over
medium - high heat and once the
heat rises from the surface of the
pan, dump in the sesame seeds.
Shake and roast lightly to bring out
the natural oils, taking care not to
scorch or burn. Pulverize well in
a suribachi [grinding bowl] or spice/
nut grinder until broken down but
not yet paste-like. Pass the pressed
tofu through a wire-mesh sieve into
the bowl with the ground sesame
seeds . Fold in I tablespoon of
the soy sauce and ½ tablespoon
of the mirin.
Pour 3 '/• inches ( 8 cm) oil into
a heavy medium pot and heat over
medium-high heat until hot but
not smoking. Working in batches
(do not crowd the pot), drop the
kabocha cubes into the oil and
fry until golden brown. Drain on
absorbent paper towels until cool.
Drain the shiitake, pare off the stems
and discard. Blot the caps dry and
thinly slice. Drain the shirataki in a
wire-mesh sieve and pour boiling
water over for IO seconds. Shake off
excess water, blot dry, and cut into
¾-inch (3 cm) lengths. Place in a
medium bowl with the shiitake. Toss
with the remaining ½ tablespoon
each soy sauce and mirin and fold
into the tofu mixture.
Cut the carrot crosswise into
I 1/•-inch (3 cm) lengths and slice
those into thin slivers. Massage
in the flaky sea salt and drop into
the bowl of smashed tofu and
shirataki along with the cooled , fried
kabocha. Set the seri in a wire-mesh
sieve and pour a steady stream of
boiling water over it for IO seconds.
Cool in cold, running water and
squeeze gently with your hands
to remove excess water. Slice into
¾-inch (2 cm) lengths and mix
into the sesame-tofu mixture with
a pair of chopsticks until all of
the ingredients have been evenly
di stri but ed . Serve immediately.
86 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Okara Potato Salad Aemono - Dressed
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 45 minutes
Cooking time, 15
to 20 minutes
Serves, 6
2 lb IO oz (1. 2 kg) potatoes
• I tablespoon fine sea salt
• I large carrot , scrubbed
I cup (2 ½ oz / 75 g) dried okara
[soy pulp]
I small red onion, slivered
I teaspoon flaky sea salt, plus more
as needed
Q tablespoons rice vinegar
1¼ cups (10 fl oz / 300 ml) Japanese
Mayonnaise
(page 32)
I handful chopped Italian parsley
OKARA POTATO
Okoro is the by-product of making
soy milk and is often called
"soybean pulp " in English. Adding
okoro to this potato salad lightens
this casual side dish . In the
summer, slice Japanese cucumbers
in thin rounds, salt lightly for IO
minutes, squeeze, and add with the
carrot and onion.
Peel the potatoes and cut into large
chunks. Place in a heavy medium
pot, cover with cold water, and
add the fine sea salt . Bring to a
boil over high heat and slip in the
carrot. Boil the carrot until half
cooked , about 7 minutes.
Remove
with a pair of tongs and cool in
a sieve. Continue cooking the
potatoes until they can be pierced
easily with a bamboo skewer or
fork, but are not falling apart,
about 5 more minutes. Drain in
a colander for 8-10 minutes .
Meanwhile, mix scant I cup
(7½ fl oz/225 ml)
cold water into
the dried okoro and let sit for a
few minutes to absorb the water
completely. Toss the red onion
with I pinch of flaky sea salt and
let sit for IO minutes before gently
squeezing out the water.
SALAD
Slide the drained potatoes into a
large bowl and mash with a potato
masher while still hot. Let cool
completely .
Cut off the carrot top end and
tip, halve lengthwise, and slice
crosswise into thin half-moons.
Add the carrot to the potatoes,
along with the reconstituted okoro
and squeezed red onion . Sprinkle
with the flaky sea salt and vinegar
before mixing in the mayonnaise.
Add a few drops of vinegar or
pinches of flaky sea salt to taste.
Fold in the parsley and serve .
AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Tofu Flavored Six Ways 88 Aemono - Dressed
recipes.transcription:

30 minutes soaking time
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves,
6
For the dressing,
2 tablespoons
rice vinegar

gold sesame oil

For the tofu,

handfuls unshelled edamame

crosswise into thin strips

cha tsai

(16 fl oz/500 ml) cold
water
for 30 minutes

toasted in a small, dry frying pan
• I (ro½ oz/300 g) momendofu or
Japanese-style soft block tofu, cut into
%-inch (1 cm) cubes
TOFU FLAVORED SIX WAYS
If possible, seek out the best
handmade artisanal tofu for this
dish, as it makes a big difference.
Make this dish in the summer
when tomatoes and edamame are
in season.
Make the dressing, In a small bowl,
combine the rice vinegar and
usukushi shqyu. Slowly whisk in the
sesame oil and r'!Yu to emulsify.
Prepare the tofu, In a pot of
boiling water, cook the edamame
for 3 minutes. Drain and shell
the beans.
Massage the flaky sea salt into the
shredded cabbage and let sit for
IO minutes, then lift out in
handfuls (leaving the salt in the
bottom of the bowl) and squeeze

Drop the squeezed cabbage into
a medium serving bowl.
Toss the tomato and edamame with
the fine sea
salt and add to the bowl

the cha tsai and sesame seeds into the

Strew the tofu cubes on top of the
salad and serve.
88 AEMONO - DRESSED

recipes.title: Sea Pineapple And Cucumber In Sweet Vinegar Shime Saba
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 25 minutes
Serves, 6
2 fresh sea pineapples (14 oz/ 400 g)
7 oz
(200 g) Japanese cucumbers
• ¼ teaspoon flaky sea salt
2 tablespoons
brown rice vinegar
2 tablespoons
usukuchi shoyu or
soy sauce
Preparation time: 20 minutes,
plus 12 hours marinating time
Serves, 6
l large ultra-fresh mackerel
(11/, lb/600
g) , cleaned
3 tablespoons
fine sea salt
• 3 tablespoons
rice vinegar
• 3 tablespoons
mirin
• 6-inch (15 cm) piece konbu
l tablespoon slivered fresh ginger
Sudachi halves or lemon wedges
(optional)
SEA PINEAPPLE AND CUCUMBER
IN SWEET VINEGAR
Sea pineapple , an edible sea
creature, perhaps because of its
chewy texture or flavor reminiscent
of iodine, can be an acquired
taste. Though aficionados prefer
unadorned sea pineapple , serving
it with cucumbers and dressing
softens the unusual experience of
eating this sea squirt.
Slit the sea pineapple through the
two siphon holes, and about
2 inches
(5 cm) beyond, following
the curve of the body. While
rinsing under cold running water ,
pull out the orange meat inside.
Trim off any discolored portions
or tendril-like filaments from the
meat. Separate the halves, pat dry ,
and cut crosswise into ¼--inch
(5 mm) slices.
SHIME SABA
Shime saba [vinegar-cured mackerel]
is usually prepared by heavily
salting, then treating the fish with
vinegar.
This recipe has less salt
but more vinegar and a longer soak
time. Raw fish treatments, such
as shime saba, cannot be done with
previously frozen fish , and for
safety's sake need to be prepared
with very fresh fish.
Fillet
the mackerel (leave the skin
on) and pluck out any small pin
bones from the flesh with a pair of
flat tweezers. Rinse the fillets well
in cold water and pat dry. Sprinkle
on all sides with the fine sea salt.
In a small bowl, whisk together the
vinegar and mirin.
Roll the cucumbers on a cutting
board to soften, pare the ends off,
and slice into fine rounds.
Toss
with the salt and leave to macerate
for IO minutes.
In a small bowl , stir together the
vinegar and usukuchi sh'!)'U-
Leaving any salt particles that
have not dissolved , pick up the
cucumbers with your fingers , shake
off, and toss in a clean bowl with
the sea pineapple and the vinegar
mixture. Serve immediately for
the crunchiest effect, though if
chilled, this treatment holds up
to the next day .
Spread the
konbu in a container
just large enough to hold the fillets
and lay the fish on
top of the konbu,
skin-side up. Pour the vinegar
mixture over the mackerel, cover ,
and refrigerate for 12 hours.
Remove from the vinegar mixture ,
blot dry with absorbent paper
towels, and cut into diagonal
sashimi slices with a razor-sharp
knife. Slide the knife under the
slices and arrange attractively on
a ceramic salad plate. Sprinkle with
the ginger. Provide sudachi halves
or wedges of lemon if more acid
is desired. The fish is best within
1-2 days
of preparing, though you
should cut as needed for serving.
93 NAMAMONO - RAW

recipes.title: Konnyaku Sashimi With Sesame Miso Mountain Yam With
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 4
I block (9 oz/ 250 g) white konnyaku,
halved crosswise
4 tablespoons brown rice miso
· 2 tablespoons mirin
2 tablespoons
rice vinegar
2 tablespoons
gold sesame seeds
w I teaspoon mustard powder
• A few small sprigs parsley
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6
2½ cups (5¼ oz/200 g) unshelled
edamame
1/2 sheet nori
I medium naga imo [mountain yam],
(12 ½
oz/350 g)
I teaspoon grated fresh wasabi
(optional)
I tablespoon soy sauce
KONNYAKU SASHIMI
WITH SESAME MISO
Mountainous areas separated
from the sea prepare this dish as
a substitute for sashimi.
Set up a bowl of ice water in the
sink. In a pot of rapidly boiling
water, blanch the kon'!}aku for
2 minutes. Scoop out with a wire­
mesh sieve and plunge into the ice
water to cool.
In a small saucepan, stir the miso,
mirin, and vinegar over low heat to
warm . In a small , dry frying pan ,
toast the sesame seeds over medium
heat until fragrant, shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Slide into a
suribachi [grinding bowl] or spice /
nut grinder and grind well until
completely broken down. Scrape
the ground sesame into the miso
mixture , add the mustard, and stir
all together.
Drain the kon'!Yaku and pat dry with
a clean tea towel. Cut into fine
slices . Make individual small plates
for serving each person , Drape
5 slices over a chopstick and lay
them on a small plate so that they
are curled in half. Rest another
5 slices on top of the first row
of
slices, leaving about% inch (r cm)
of the bottom slices peaking out.
Spoon some of the miso sauce onto
the plate for dipping the kon'!Yaku
and garnish with a sprig of parsley.
MOUNTAIN YAM WITH
EDAMAME AND NORI
Grated naga imo [mountain yam] is
a creamy white vehicle for cooked
green soybeans and jet-black nori
threads. The colors in this dish
are particularly vibrant and worth
duplicating, even if the idea of
trying raw, slippery yam seems
offputting-grated mountain
yam is delightfully slurpable and
delicious. Eat as is for a refreshing
pick - me-up or with a bowl of
Japanese rice. Naga imo is itchy, so
don rubber gloves if you want to
avoid a few minutes of lingering
discomfort after grating.
Bring a pot of water to a boil over
high heat. Dump in the fresh
edamame and boil for 3 minutes.
Drain in a colander, cool to room
temperature , and pop the beans
out of their pods . Cut the nori into
quarters and snip crosswise into
fine threads and reserve .
Peel the naga imo and grate it in a
circular motion using an oroshigane
Uapanese grating plate] or a wide,
fine-toothed Microplane into a
medium bowl. Spoon the grated
yams into small individual bowls.
Strew the cooked edamame beans and
nori threads over the grated yam ,
dab with grated wasabi, if you have
it, drizzle with soy sauce, and serve.
Bring the bowl to the mouth and
guide the grated nogo imo in with
chopsticks, using a slurping sound .
The viscosity is unusual-it is at
once slippery and creamy.
@ p.95
94 NAMAMONO - RAW

recipes.title: Grated Daikon With Salmon Roe Vinegared Mackerel
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Serves: 6
I 1/, cups (14 oz/ 400 g) finely grated
daikon, strained
I sac (7 oz/200 g) fresh salmon roe
½ cup (4 fl oz/125 ml) sake
•
½ tablespoon soy sauce
Preparation time: 30 minutes, plus
4 1/2 hours salting and marinating time
Serves: 6
I ultra-fresh mackerel (11h lb/600 g) ,
cleaned
3 tablespoons fine sea
salt
· 6 tablespoons rice vinegar
• 2 tablespoons mirin
• I large pinch of flaky sea salt
3 ½ oz (100 g) daikon, finely julienned
• I small carrot, finely julienned
• 2 tablespoons
slivered scallion
(spring onion)
2 tablespoons
slivered fresh ginger
GRATED DAIKON
WITH SALMON ROE
Salmon roe takes patience to coax
from its sac, but is well worth
the effort. Outside of Japan, it
might be hard to find fresh
roe,
so in that case it is still wise to
wash the cleaned, salted roe in the
sake. lnjapan, there is no better
accompaniment to salmon roe than
grated daikon. If the daikon is fresh,
there is no need to peel it. Scrub
with a tawashi [vegetable brush] and
grate on an oroshigane U apanese
grating plate] before serving. Serve
as an amuse-bouche or as part of
a ,::ensai course (page 28). Best with
chilled sake or champagne.
Spoon the strained daikon into
6 soba dipping cups or small bowls.
Fill a medium bowl with lukewarm
water and slip the roe sac into the
water. Working slowly and patiently ,
pry the roe out of the sac and drop
into a small wire-mesh sieve set
over a bowl to catch drips. Once
all of the roe has been freed from
the sac membranes, rinse the roe
with the sake in a small bowl. Swish
the salmon eggs around for a few
seconds with your fingers and drain.
Spoon the roe over the grated daikon
and drizzle each serving with
1/, teaspoon soy sauce.
@ p.97
VINEGARED MACKEREL
WITH DAIKON
Shime Saba (page 93) is a classic
cure for eating mackerel as sushi
and sashimi. Here it becomes more
of a marinated salad but without
the oil.
Fillet the mackerel, pull the skin
off the fillets, and pluck out the
pin bones with tweezers. Holding
the knife at an angle to the cutting
board, cut the fillets into slices
½ inch (12 mm) thick. Place the
slices in a gallon-size resealable
food storage bag and toss with the
fine salt. Refrigerate for 4 hours.
Whisk
the vinegar and mirin together
and pour over the fish. Allow to
marinate for 30 minutes .
Meanwhile, massage the flaky salt
into the daikon, carrot, scallion
(spring onion), and ginger. Let sit
for IO minutes, then squeeze gently
to remove moisture. Toss in with
the fish for the last IO minutes of
its sweet vinegar soak.
Pull the fish slices out from the
julienned vegetables and arrange
in attractive overlapping lines on a
serving platter. Strew the vegetables
in the free areas around the fish
and serve as a first course or part
of a buffet. (Alternatively , serve on
individual small plates.) This dish
keeps vibrant for 1-2 days.
96 NAMAMONO - RAW

recipes.title: Shirataki Noodles With Cod Roe Oysters In Sweet Vinegar
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 15 minutes
Serves, 6
IO oz (300 g) shirataki noodles
• Boiling water
3½ oz (100 g) enoki mushrooms,
bottoms trimmed off, halved crosswise
• 2 tablespoons usukuchi shoyu
· 2 cod roe sacs (10 ½ oz/ 300 g)
5'/• oz (150 g) Japanese cucumbers,
unpee led , cut
into julienne 1'/• inches
(3 cm ) long
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time, 30 seconds
Serves, 6
• 2 tablespoons fine sea salt
IO oz (300 g) freshly shucked oysters
· 3 tablespoons
rice vinegar
• I tablespoon usukuchi shoyu
• I tablespoon mirin
14 oz (400 g)
daikon, scrubbed, finely
grated,
and drained
2 teaspoons finely slivered yuzu or
Meyer lemon zest
SHIRATAKI NOODLES
WITH COD ROE
Cod roe is readily available in Japan
and the sacs are easily prepared (as
opposed to the time-consuming
job of prying salmon roe from its
sac). Raw cod roe has a mild flavor
with a creamy texture.
Cut the shirataki noodles crosswise
into 2-inch (5 cm) lengths. Drop
into a wire-mesh sieve and pour a
steady stream of boiling water over
them for I minute. Shake off excess
water and, while still hot, slide
into a medium serving bowl with
the enoki mushrooms. Toss with the
usukuchi sh~u.
Break open the roe sacs and
scrape small pieces of roe into the
noodles with your fingers. Toss
the cucumbers with the noodles
and serve.
OYSTERS IN SWEET VINEGAR
WITH YUZU
Ultra - fresh oysters are essential for
this bright dish.
Place a medium bowl in the kitchen
sink . Add I quart (32 fl oz/r liter)
cold water and stir in the fine salt.
Place
the oysters in a wire - mesh
sieve and plunge into the salt water.
Swish around a little, then rinse
with cold , running water. Shake off
excess water.
Set up a bowl of ice water in the
sink, Bring a medium pot of water
to a boil. Dunk the sieve holding
the oysters into the boiling water
and hold them there until the
outside of the oysters start to turn
white , about 30 seconds. Pull them
out of the water and plunge into the
ice bath to shock and refresh . Once
cool to the touch, scoop the oysters
out of the ice water and shake off. If
lar ge, halve those oysters crosswise
on the diagonal.
In a small bowl , stir together the
vinegar, usukuchi sh'?,Yu, and mirin.
In a smallish serving bowl, toss
the sieved grated daikon with the
dressing. Fold in the oysters, gar­
nish with the yuzu zest , and serve
right away.
@ p.99
98 NAMAMONO - RAW

recipes.title: Squid And Jellyfish With Mustard Vinegar Mustard-Dressed Squid
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 45 minutes, plus
20 minutes soaking time and 20 minutes
marinating time
Serves, 6
r3/+ oz
(50 g) salted jellyfish
I small squid (5 1/+ oz/r50 g), cleaned
(see Note on the following recipe below)
• Boiling water
3 ½ oz (roo g) Japanese cucumber
• I tablespoon rice vinegar
• I tablespoon soy sauce
• ¾, teaspoon mirin
I teaspoon mustard powder
½ teaspoon gold sesame oil
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Serves, 6
I ultrafresh squid (5¼ oz/r50 g) ,
cleaned (see Note)
7 oz (200 g) Japanese cucumbers,
halved lengthwise
1/+ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• I½ tablespoons soy sauce
• I teaspoon sake
• I teaspoon gold sesame oil
• ½ teaspoon mustard powder
SQUID AND JELLYFISH
WITH MUSTARD VINEGAR
Finding packaged salted jellyfish
without additives or MSG might
be challenging , but if you do,
this crunchy salad will pleasantly
surprise you.
Soak the jellyfish in several changes
of cold water for 20 minutes
to
remove the salt. Scoop the jellyfish
out with a wire-mesh sieve and
rinse one last time under cold,
running water. Pat dry .
Set up a bowl of ice water in the
sink. Put the squid body, tentacles,
and tail fin into a wire-mesh sieve
and pour boiling water over for
IO seconds. Immediately plunge
into the ice bath to refresh. Pat dry
and cut into thin strips r¼ inches
(3 cm) long.
Roll the cucumber on a cutting
board to soften, then finely
julienne . In a small bowl, whisk
together the vinegar, soy sauce,
mirin, mustard powder, and sesame
oil. Toss the dressing with the
jellyfish, cucumber, and squid and
leave to marinate for 20 minutes
before serving. This is best the first
day, but also fine the next.
MUSTARD-DRESSED SQUID
AND CUCUMBER
Japanese squid is pristinely white
with a mild flavor and a pleasantly
creamy texture. Here, crisp
cucumber makes an exceptional foil.
Set up a bowl of ice water in the
sink. Bring a pot of water to a boil.
Put the cut-up squid into a wire­
mesh sieve. Dip the sieve in and out
of the boiling water. Immediately
plunge into the ice bath to cool.
Drain and pat dry. Cut the body
and fin into thin strips
1/+ inch
(5 mm) wide and r¼-r3/+ inches
(3-4 cm)
long. Slice the top
connected area of the tentacles to
separate and if any tentacles are
too long too eat in one bite, cut in
half diagonally.
Slice the cucumber crosswise at
an acute diagonal into ¼-inch
(5 mm) pieces. Sprinkle with the
salt, toss to distribute , and let sit for
5 minutes . Pick out the cucumber
pieces with your hands (rather than
dumping) and strew on a couple of
pieces of paper towel. Blot off the
excess moisture and salt.
In a bowl, stir the soy sauce, sake,
and sesame oil into the mustard
powder until emulsified. Toss the
squid and cucumbers with the
dressing and serve immediately.
(Alternatively, add the dressing
to the squid, refrigerate the
squid and cucumbers in separate
containers, and toss together when
ready to serve.)
Note , To
clean squid , grasp the
tentacles and pull the guts out of
the squid. Pull out the plastic­
stick-like "pen" (gladius)
as well.
Slice the tentacle portion off of the
guts and discard the guts. Tear the
tail fin off the body. Slice the body ,
lengthwise to open up flat. Rinse
under cold , running water, pulling
off any lingering tendrils. Peel off
the skin as well .
(Q] p.IOI
IOO NAMAMONO - RAW

recipes.title: Chopped Sardines With Miso Citrus- And Ume-Dressed Daikon And Sardines
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 15 minutes
Serves, 4
6
fresh sardines (18½ oz/525 g)
• 2 teaspoons brown rice miso
• I teaspoon white sesame seeds
2 teaspoons finely chopped negi or
scallion (spring onion)
2 teaspoons grated
fresh ginger or
julienned green shiso leaves
• I teaspoon rice vinegar
½ teaspoon soy sauce
• ½ teaspoon mirin
Preparation time: 50 minutes , plus
3 hours marinating time
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6-8
For the sardines,
4 fresh
sardines (121/, oz/350 g)
· 6-inch
(15 cm) piece konbu
· 2 ½ teaspoons flaky sea salt
• 4 tablespoons rice vinegar
• I tablespoon mirin
10½ oz (300 g) daikon , scrubbed and
finely julienned
I small carrot, scrubbed and
finely julienned
½ stalk peeled udo (see Note) or I stalk
celery, julienned
3 heaping tablespoons
dried wakame,
soaked in cold water for 20 minutes
• 314, natsumikan (substitute 3/+ sour
orange or ½ grapefruit), sectioned and
membranes removed (if using grapefruit,
cut the sections in half)
• 2 tablespoons white sesame see ds ,
lightly toasted and coarsely ground
2 umeboshi [salted sour
plum]. pitted
For the dressing,
2
tablespoons rice vinegar
• I tablespoon mirin
2 teaspoons natsumikan juice (squeezed
from
the remaining ¼ natsumikan) or
sour orange or grapefruit juce
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
CHOPPED SARDINES WITH MISO
This is a popular dish with the
fishermen of the Boso and Izu
peninsulas and is served alongside
a bowl of hot rice.
Cut the heads off of the sardines
and slice down through the belly .
Pull out the guts, vertebrae, and
tail and discard. Rinse the cleaned
fish under cold running water
and pat dry . Lay the fish on a
cutting board and slice into thin
strips lengthwise, then finely dice
crosswise.
While the fish is still on the cutting
board, spoon the miso, sesa me
seeds, scallion (spring onion), and
ginger or shiso over the chopped
sardines. In a small measuring cup
(jug), mix the vinegar, soy sauce,
and mirin and sprinkle on the fish as
well. Chop the ingredients into the
sardine using a very sharp fish or
butcher knife until the mixture has
amalgamated. It i s best served when
freshly made.
[Qj p.103
CITRUS- AND UME-DRESSED
DAIKON AND SARDINES
The classic version of namasu is
made from daikon and carrots and
is served during Japanese New
Year. The addition of ume, citrus,
and sardines here makes the
combination unforgettable .
Prepare the sard ines , Slice off the
heads of the sardines and cu t down
through the belly. Pull out the guts,
vertebrae, and tail and discard.
Rinse under cold running water
and pat dry. (Alternatively, have
the fishmonger perform this task
for you.) Lay the konbu in a shallow
rectangular contai ner and arrange
the fillets on top . Sprinkle both
sides of the fish lightly with
½ teaspoon of the flaky salt.
Sprinkle with the vinegar and mirin,
cover, and leave in a cool place
or the refrigerator for 3 hours.
If possible, turn every 45 minutes
for even marinating.
About I hour before the sardines
have finished marinating, slide
the daikon, carrot, and udo into a
medium bowl and massage in the
remaining I teaspoon flaky salt.
Let sit for IO minutes, then squeeze
gently and drop by handfuls into
a clean bowl. Drain the wakame in
a wire-mesh sieve, lay out on a
cutting board, and cut crosswise
at 1¼-inch (3 cm) intervals. Blot
dry with a clean tea towel.
Make the dressing, In a small bowl ,
whisk together the vinegar, mirin,
natsumikan juice, and salt to emulsify.
Toss the wakame with the dressing.
When the fish have marinated
for 3 hours, remove
the sardines
and discard the marinade and
konbu. Cut the fillets crosswise
into %-inch (1 cm) slices. In a
large salad bowl, toss together
the sardines, daikon, carrot, udo,
natsumikan, and sesame seeds. Tear
the pitted umeboshi by hand and
drop in to distribute evenly (the
flesh tends to clump if chopped
with a knife) .
Add the dressed wakame to the salad,
toss to coat the vegetables, and serve.
Note, If you don 't plan on using
the udo right away after cutting, soak
in a small bowl of cold water with
a littl e lemon juice or rice vinegar.
Drain and pat dry before using.

recipes.title: Daikon And Dried Persimmon With Mitsuba Vinegared Turnips
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 20 minutes, plus
I hour macerating time
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6
I lb (450 g) daikon, scrubbed and
julienned
Boiling water
4 shiitake,
stems discarded
• I yuzu or ½ Meyer lemon
• 3 tablespoons
sake
2 tablespoons
usukuchi shoyu
4 hoshigaki
[dried persimmons] ,
topped, seeded, and julienned
• I small bunch mitsuba
Preparation time: 40 minutes
Serves, 6
6 small turnips, with tops
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
2 tablespoons rice vinegar
• 2 tablespoons mirin
• I teaspoon soy sauce
2 hoshigaki [dried persimmons]
Finely slivered zest of ½ yuzu
or 1/+ Meyer lemon
DAIKON AND DRIED
PERSIMMON WITH MITSUBA
Daikon is in season in late winter ,
just in time to be paired with dried
persimmon. The mitsuba adds a
bright spark to this dish .
Place the daikon slivers in a wire­
mesh sieve and pour a steady stream
of boiling water over them for
IO seconds. Shake once or twice to
remove excess water and pat dry in
a clean tea towel.
In a medium heavy frying pan,
lightly grill the shiitake caps over
medium heat for 2-3 minutes. Cut
into fine slices. Remove the yUsu
zest with a sharp knife and slice into
fine slivers . Squeeze the juice for
another dish, if you like.
In a small saucepan , combine the
sake and usukuchi shczyu and bring to
a boil over high heat. Remove from
the heat. In a medum bowl , toss the
sake mixture with the hoshigaki, daikon,
shiitake, and yUsu zest. Let macerate
at room temperature for I hour.
Cut the mitsuba crosswise into
¾-inch (2 cm) pieces . Fold the
mitsuba into the ma c erated mixture
and serve. It is best the first day,
but still good the next (though the
daikon will release a bit of liquid) .
VINEGARED TURNIPS
WITH DRIED PERSIMMONS
Turnips and fresh persimmons
complement each other beautifully ,
both in flavor and color. This dish
uses hoshigaki [dried persimmons] ,
so it is a bit of a twist. These
rolls make for an elegant passed
appetizer, but the turnip and
hoshigaki can just as easily be tossed
as a casual salad.
Cut the roots and tops off of the
turnips , leaving about ¾ inch
(I cm) of green stem. Scrub the
turnips and cut from stem to root
end into rounds 1/+ inch (6 mm)
thick. Massage in the salt and let sit
for IO minutes. Squeeze gently by
handfuls , without breaking,
and drop into a clean bowl. Toss
with the vinegar, mirin , and soy
sauce and leave to marinate for
IO minutes.
Meanwhile , cut the hoshigaki in half
lengthwis e and remove the pits.
Spread the hoshigaki halves out on
a cutting board and slice into strips
1/+ inch (6 mm) wide.
Reserving the marinade , drain
the turnip slices. Lay the turnip
slices out on a clean baking sheet
or a piece of parchment paper and
divide the hoshigaki strips among
them , arranging the strips across
the bottom third of each turnip
round. Roll each round up and
secure with a cocktail pick .
Arrange on an attractive platter,
drizzle with the reserved marinade ,
strew with yu.zu zest, and serve.
These stay well for several hours
at room temperature.

UDO AND WAKAME IN VINEGAR
Udo (page 442) is ajapanese
mountain vegetable with soft ,
furry skin and a pleasantly bitter
aftertaste. Substitute celery if udo
is not available .
Slice the udo into % x l ½-inch
(1 x 4 cm) thick slices . Place in a
medium bowl, fill with
cold water
to cover, and add the l tablespoon
rice vinegar Cut the wakame
crosswise into 1¼-inch (4 cm)
pieces. If using fresh wakame, place
in a wire-mesh sieve, and dip in

under cool, running water and
shake off.
In a small saucepan, combine the
brown rice vinegar , dashi, mirin,
usukuchi sh'!J'u, and salt and bring to

Stir in the katsuobushi, remove from
the heat , and let the dressing cool.
Drain the udo, pat dry , and toss

VINEGARED OCTOPUS
AND WAKAME
Octopus has a chewy yet creamy
texture that holds up well in vinegar
treatments such as this one.
Place the octopus in a wire- mesh
sieve and pour a steady stream of
boiling water over it for a count
of 5. Pat dry and cut at a diagonal
into slices ¼ inch (5 cm) wide . If
using fresh wakame, cut crosswise
