boiling water. Refresh in cold ,
running water until cool to the
touch and drain well. (If using
reconstituted dried wakame, drain ,
and cut crosswise into 11/.+-inch
[3 cm] pieces if not already cut.)
In either case, blot the wakame
dry in a tea towel. Stir the dashi,
vinegar, mirin, soy sauce , and salt
together. Toss with the octopus and
wakame, and serve . This salad keeps
for 2-3 days, if stored chilled in
the refrigerator .

6
fresh sardines (18 ½ oz/ 5 2 5 g)

VINEGARED SARDINES
Sardines need to be eaten quickly
after catching and cleaning, so
treating them with vinegar makes
sense because it is a natural
preserving process .
Cut the heads off the sardines and
slice open the gut sac with a sharp
knife. Remove the guts by running
your finger down the stomach
cavity-and discard them. Rinse
the fish under cold running water
and place in a small saucepan. Add
water halfwa y up to the top of the
fish , about½ cup (4¼ fl oz/
125
ml) along with the vinegar , soy
sauce, sake, and ginger. Cover with
a lid or piece of parchment paper
on top of the fish and bring to
a simmer over high heat. Reduce
the heat to low and cook until the
liquid is reduced and the fish has
cooked through, 5-7 minutes.
Cool in the simmering liquid and
serve with vegetable side dishes.
These sardines keep well in the
refrigerator for several days.
VINEGARED CRAB AND
CUCUMBER WITH YUZU
This crab and cucumber treatment
has less vinegar than Vinegared
Cucumber and Crab with Ginger
(below) , and is more of a salad. It
is a good accompaniment to pre­
dinner drinks in the summer.
Place the cucumbers in a medium
bowl and massage in the salt gently
and thoroughly , taking care not to
bruise. Let sit for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile , in a bowl, whisk
together the vinegar, mirin, and
soy sauce and toss with the crab .
Set aside to marinate while the
cucumbers are salting .
Squeeze the cucu mbers in large
handfuls to remove excess liquid
and drop into the bowl with the
crab . Toss, strew with theyuzu zest,
and serve.
(QI p.llI
VINEGARED CUCUMBER
AND CRAB WITH GINGER
This refreshingly cooling dish is
lovely in the summer. Small boiled
and chilled shrimp work as a nice
substitute for the crab.
Toss the cucumbers with the
ginger and massage in the salt.
Leave to macerate for IO minutes.
Meanwhile, whisk togeth er the
vinegar, soy sauce, and mirin.
Squeeze the cucumbers and ginger
gently but firm ly, to remove excess
liquid , then drop into a medium
serving bowl. Toss with the crab
and sweet vinegar dressing . Serve
immediately . This salad holds up
for a few days , but the cucumbers
will release liquid, so the dressing
will become diluted.

Leaving a part of the turnip

While still not mainstream , celery

Cut the daikon and carrot into

pieces . Cut those pieces into

Holding the knife at a 45-degree

In a large mixing bowl, massage the
In a small, dry frying pan, toast

into a suribachi [grinding bowl] or

recipes.title: Asparagus With Sesame Vinegar Dressing Cucumber And Bean
recipes.transcription:

I lb 5 oz (600 g) asparagus

• 2 teaspoons
gold sesame seeds

mirin

minutes

moyashi [mung bean

ASPARAGUS WITH SESAME
VINEGAR DRESSING
A trio of sesame seeds brightens up
asparagus with its subtle flavor and
pretty combination of colors.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil
over high heat. Snap the bottoms
off of the asparagus where they
naturally want to break. Blanch
until crisp-tender, 2-5 minutes
depending on the thickness.
Refresh under cold, running
water. Pat dry in a clean tea towel.
Cut on the diagonal into ¾-inch
(2 cm) pieces.
In a small frying pan , heat the oil
over medium-low heat. Add the
sesame seeds when you can feel
some heat rising from the pan.
Cook, stirring until you can smell
the aroma of sesame, about
I minute. Scrape into a small bowl
to cool.
Toss the asparagus pieces with the
cooled sesame seeds, vinegar, mirin,
soy sauce, and salt. Serve at room
temperature, or cold the next day
as a salad or vegetable side dish.
@ p.n5
CUCUMBER AND BEAN
SPROUTS IN SESAME-VINEGAR
Quick to put together, this dish
benefits from using top-quality
sesame seeds and rice vinegar to
elevate it above the ordinary .
Roll the cucumber on a cutting
board to soften and cut into thin
flat strips ½ x r¼ inches (12 mm
x 3 cm).
Toss with ½ teaspoon
of the flaky salt and let sit for IO
minutes. Blot off excess salt and
place in a medium serving bowl.
Fill a medium pot three-quarters
with water. Add the 4 tablespoons
rice
vinegar and fine salt and bring
to a boil over high heat. Blanch the
bean sprouts for I minute. Scoop
out with a wire-mesh sieve and lay
out on a tea towel to cool and blot
dry . Place the usuage in a wire-mesh
sieve and dip in and out of the
same boiling water. Pat dry and
slice the usuage crosswise into thin
strips. Add the bean sprouts and
usuage to the bowl of cucumbers.
In a small, dry frying pan , warm
the sesame seeds over medium­
high heat, shaking the pan , until
you get a faint whiff of sesame,
2-3 minutes. Slide into a suribachi
[grinding bowl] or spice/nut
grinder and smash until completely
broken down to a powdery semi­
paste-like consistency. Stir in the
rice vinegar , mirin, soy sauce, and
remaining ½ teaspoon flaky salt ,
scraping down the sides to make
a smooth dressing .
Toss the m'!Yashi, usuage, and
cucumbers with the dressing right
before serving since the cucumbers
tend to release liquid .

time: 5 minutes

14 oz
(400 g) Japanese cucumbers

KYURIMOMI
]0,urimomi is made all over Japan
and there are countless variations ,
depending on area and the
individual style of the cook. This
version comes from Kansai ,
where usukuchi sh~u is commonly
used , and it does not contain miso,
making it more of a sesame-vinegar
treatment.
Slice the cucumbers into fine
rounds. Massage in the salt and let
sit for IO minutes. Squeeze gently
to express liquid , but not bruise
excessively, and drop into
a medium serving bowl.
In a small, dry frying pan, toast
the sesame seeds over medium heat
until fragrant, shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Slide into a
suribachi [grinding bowl] or spice/
nut grinder and process until fully
broken down .
Smash the vinegar , mirin, and
usukuchi sh~u into the ground
sesame, and add the shiso and
cucumbers. Toss until the
ingredients are well distributed and
serve as a bright summer salad .
TARO STEMS IN SESAME
VINEGAR DRESSING
Zi,iki [dried taro stems] are available
online . They are also used in
Korean cooking, so inquire about
availability at Asian groceries
outside of Japan.
Wash and massage the
zuiki in
cold water. Lay in the kitchen
sink and pour a steady stream
of boiling water over them for
IO seconds. Let cool in the sink.
Once completely cool , rinse in
cold water, and cut crosswise into
I¼-inch (3 cm) pieces .
In a medium sauc epan, bring the
dashi, 2 tablespoons of the soy sauce,
and I tablespoon mirin to a simmer.
Slide in the zuiki pieces and simmer
until softened, but not falling
apart, about 15 minutes. Allow
to cool in the simmering liquids.
Halve the usuage lengthwise, set in
a wire-mesh sieve , and pour a
steady stream of boiling water over
them for IO seconds. Stack on
a cutting board and cut crosswise
into fine strips . Drain the shiitake,
pare off and discard the stems, and
finely slice the caps. Pat dry and
put in
a small bowl with
½ tablespoon
of the mirin and the remaining
½ tablespoon soy sauce.
In a small, dry frying pan, toast
the sesame seeds over medium heat
until fragrant, shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Slide the seeds
into a suribachi [grinding bowl] or
spice/nut grinder and grind until
broken down and the oils are
released. Stir in the vinegar to make
a paste . Sweeten with the remaining
½ tablespoon mirin .
Drain the zuiki and toss with the
usuage, shiitake, and the sesame­
vinegar dressing. Serve .

recipes.title: Daikon With Sesame-Vinegar Burdock In Sesame-Vinegar
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Cooking time : 5 minutes
Serves:
6
I lb (450 g) daikon,
scrubbed and
julienned
3/+ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 6 fresh anchovies
4 tablespoons gold sesame
seeds
• ½ tablespoon mirin
I tablespoon rice vinegar

Cooking time, IO minutes

7 oz (200 g) burdock root , scrubbed
and cut into 2-inch (5 cm) lengths
½ tablespoon white sesame seeds
• ½ tablespoon black sesame seeds

2 tablespoons brown rice vinegar
• I tablespo .on mirin
.Q tablespoons rice vinegar
8 kigiku [edible chrysanthemum
flowers]
DAIKON WITH
SESAME-VINEGAR
This dish is a traditional preparation
from Kanagawa prefecture . Daikon
is one of the most important
vegetables in Japanese cuisine grown
by seemingly every farm. Grated ,
pickled, simmered, seared, dressed­
there are myriad preparations,
and a dizzying number of heritage
varieties never make their way to the
mainstream market.
Scrape the daikon into a medium
bowl and massage in the salt. Let sit
for IO minutes . Squeeze by handfuls
and drop into a clean bowl.
Pinch off the heads and tear down
toward the belly of the anchovies
and pull out the guts , vertebrae,
and tail. Separate into fillets , rinse
under cold running water, and pat
dry in a clean tea towel.
In a small, dry frying pan , toast
the sesame seeds over medium heat
until fragrant, shaking the pan and
lifting off the heat, if needed , to
avoid scorching . Slide the seeds
in a suribachi [grinding bowl) or
spice/nut grinder and grind until
broken down and almost paste - like.
Mash the mirin and vinegar into the
ground sesame seeds, fold in the
squeezed daikon and anchovy fillets.
Serve immediately .
BURDOCK IN SESAME-VINEGAR
Dishes with gobo [burdock, which
is a hardy root vegetable] stand up
well over the course of several days
and this dish is no exception . The
kigiku [bitter chrysanthemum petals]
provide contrast to the earthy
burdock , and the yellow against the
brown is stunning.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil.
If the burdock is about the
circumference of a pencil, leave
whole . Otherwise, quarter or halve
lengthwise. Arrange the burdock in
the steamer basket, cover , and steam
until pliable , about 8 minutes.
In a small, dry frying pan, warm
both sesame seeds for I-2 minutes.
In a medium bowl, toss together
the still-hot burdock , salt, sesame
seeds, brown rice vinegar , and
mirin.
In a small pot, bring 2 cups
(16 fl oz/ 500 ml) water with
the
rice vinegar to a simmer. Pull the
petals off the flowers and place in
a small wire-mesh sieve . Dip in and
out of the simmering water, then
plunge into a bowl of cold water to
cool. Drain and blot dry in a clean
tea towel. Sprinkle in with the gobo,
toss , and serve.
II7 SUNOMONO - VINEGARED

long as you keep dried daikon and
squid in your pantry. Filipino
grocery stores might be a good
so ur ce for the dried squid.
Bring a pot of water to a rapid
boil. Cut the dried squid into
fine julienne
strips with a sharp
butcher knife or strong pair of
kitchen shears and drop into a
wire-mesh sieve. Dip in and out
of the boiling water and pat dry
in a clean tea towel.
Place a medium bowl in the kitchen
sink and fill with
hot water. Quickly
swish the kiriboshi daikon in the water,
scoop out with a wire-mesh sieve ,
and drain. Cut the wakame crosswise
into I 1/•-inch (3 cm) pieces.
In a bowl, stir together the vinegar,
mirin, and soy sauce. Add the daikon,
squid , carrot, and wakame and toss.
This dish holds up well for several
days, if refrigerated .
n8 SUNOMONO - VINEGARED

recipes.title: Simmered Hijiki Seaweed Simmered Dried Daikon Threads
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 35 minutes
Cooking time , 15 minutes
Serves, 6
r% cups
(r oz / 30 g) dried hijiki
2 tablespoons
canola (rapeseed) oil
• 3½ oz (roo g) pork shoulder , thinly
sliced and cut into thin strips I¼ inches
(3 cm) long
• I small carrot (3½ oz / roo g), scrubbed
and julienned
r¼ cups (ro fl oz / 300 ml) Katsuobushi
Dashi
(page 156)
3 tablespoons
soy sauce
• r½ tablespoons mirin
• r½ tablespoons sake
Preparation time, 40 minutes
Cooking time , 5 minutes
Serves, 6
r'/• oz
(50 g) kiriboshi daikon [dried
daikon threads)
I (7-inch/I8 cm)
square konbu
I usuage [deep-fried tofu pouch),
halved lengthwise
• Boiling water
2 tablespoons
ca_nola (rapeseed) oil
• I small dried red japones chile , sliced
into fine rings
• I medium carrot , scrubbed and finely
julienned
% cup
(5 fl oz/I50 ml) Katsuobushi
Dashi
(page 156)
2 tablespoons
soy sauce
• 2 tablespoons
sake
• I tablespoon mirin
SIMMERED HIJIKI SEAWEED
Hijiki [a seaweed) has a bad rap in
some countries, because of trace
inorganic arsenic contained in the
dried form (which incidentally is
never consumed as such). Soaking
the hijiki removes any food safety
worries and thejapanese have been
eating it for centuries without
issues. Hijiki contains a high amount
of fiber and
adds texture to salads
or croquette s such as ganmodoki
(page 234),
Place the hijiki in a wire- mesh sieve
and rinse under cold running
water. Place the sieve of hijiki into a
large bowl of cold water and let soak
for IO minutes . Scoop out, dump
the water , refill to
the top of the
bowl, and soak the hijiki for another
IO minutes. Drain and shake off
excess water.
In a heavy medium pot, heat the
oil over medium heat. Add the
pork and stir-fry until the meat
has whitened and curled up into
small clumps , about 2 minutes.
Add
the drained hijiki and toss
over high heat until the hijiki
is glossy from the oil, another
I-2 minutes. Stir in the carrot,
dashi, soy sauce, mirin, and sake.
Cook over medium - high heat ,
stirring occasionally, until most
of the liquid has evaporated, for
about 5 minutes. Serve hot or at
room temperature.
SIMMERED DRIED
DAIKON THREADS
Kiriboshi daikon [dried daikon threads)
are useful to have around the
kitchen as an instant starter for
a dish on the fly .
Soak the kiriboshi daikon in a large
bowl of water for IO minutes.
Drain, fill the
bowl again , and
soak for IO more minutes. Drain ,
blot dry, and cut crosswise into
r' /•-inch (3
cm) pieces. Soak the
konbu in a shallow, flat pan with
water to cover for IO minutes .
Drain and snip , following the
lengthwise grain , into thin r¼­
inch (3
cm) long threads . Lay the
usuage in a wire-mesh sieve and
pour a steady stream of boiling
water over it for IO seconds.
Slice crosswise into strips 'I• inch
(6 mm) wide.
In a heavy medium pot , heat the
oil over medium-low heat. Add the
reconstituted kiriboshi daikon, usuage,
chile, konbu, and carrot and stir-
fry over medium heat until glossy,
I-2 minutes. Stir in the dashi, soy
sauce, sake, and mirin and cook ,
stirring, over medium-high heat
until all the ingredients have
softened and the simmering liquids
have evaporated, 2-3 minutes.
Serve hot or at room temperature .
123 NIM ONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Simmered Shiitake And Sweet Potato Simmered Daikon With Miso
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 45 minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 6
6
donko [thick-capped dried shiitake]
• Boiling water
5 1/• oz (150 g) head bok choy , pulled
in half lengthwise
• I lb 5 oz (600 g) sweet potatoes, well
scrubbed but not peeled
Generous 2 cups (17 fl oz/500 mi)
chicken
stock
• I teaspoon salt
I tablespoon finely slivered cha tsai
[ Chinese pickled mustard
stem] (page 429)
2
tablespoons chopped Italian or
curly parsley
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time, 30 minutes
Serves, 6
14 oz
(400 g) daikon, peeled (see Note)
I (6-inch1I5 cm) piece konbu
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
·
3 tablespoons sake
• ;! tablespoons mirin
• 6 tablespoons Katsuobushi Dashi
(page 156)
• I egg yolk
2 tablespoons grated fresh ginger
• 6 tablespoons brown rice miso
6 tablespoons white miso or inaka miso
• 6 sprigs sansho leaves
SIMMERED SHIITAKE
AND SWEET POTATO
This dish has an interesting and
delicious combination of flavors.
Sweet potatoes are a good foil for
earthy shiitake, while the chicken
stock gives the dish depth and the
pickled cha tsai [mustard stem]
lend pop .
Soak the shiitake in I cup
(8 fl oz/250 mi) boiling water for
30 minutes.
Meanwhile, slice the torn bok choy
in half crosswise where the leaves
meet the stems. Cut the sweet
potato into ¾-inch (2 cm) pieces .
Reserving the soaking liquid , drain
the shiitake, pare off the stems and
discard. Slice the caps into ¼-inch
(6 mm) pieces. In a medium pot ,
comb ine the chicken stock and the
soaking liquid. Slide in the shiitake,
bok choy stems, and sweet potatoes
with the salt and cha tsai. Bring to
a lively simmer over medium -
high heat and cook until the sweet
potatoes have softened, about
7 minutes.
Stir in the bok choy
leaves cook until they are wilted ,
1-2 more minutes . Spoon into
a pretty serving bowl and garnish
with chopped parsley.
[Qj p.125
SIMMERED DAIKON WITH MISO
This homey dish is stunningly
lovely, and can be served alone to
accompany drinks before dinner
or as a vegetable side dish .
Starting from the top , cut the
daikon
crosswise into 6 rounds. Bevel the
cut edges with a sharp paring knife.
Lay the konbu across the bottom of a
heavy medium pot. Put the daikon in
the pot, add cold water to cover by
about 3/• inch (2 cm), and sprinkle
with the salt. Set an otoshibuta [dr op
lid] or pan lid directly on top of
the water surface (to keep the daikon
submerged) and bring to a boil over
high heat. Adjust to a simmer and
cook until the daikon has softened in
the center but is not mushy, about
20 minutes.
In a small bowl , slowly whisk the
sake, mirin, and dashi into the egg
yolk. Transfer to a small stainless
steel bowl set over a saucepan of
simmering water and stir in the
ginger and miso. Cook, stirring ,
until thickened and fragrant,
I-2 minutes.
Cool until just barely warm and
spoon the sauce over the top of each
daikon piece, smoothing it across the
surface in a circular motion with the
back of your spoon. Garnish with
a small sprig of sansho leaf, but cut
out the hard stems.
Nate, Save
the peels to make
Daikon Peel Kinpira (page 32).
124 NIMONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Dashi-Simmered Taro Root Dashi-Steamed Eggs With Spinach
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time , 20 minutes
Serves : 6
I lb 2oz (500 g) medium taro roots,
peeled
2½ cups (20 fl oz/600 ml)
K.atsuobushi
Dashi (page 156)
• 2 tablespoons
mirin
• ¼ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 2 tablespoon s soy sauce
Shichimi togarashi [seven-spice
powder]. optional
Preparation time: 20 minut es
Cooking time, 20 minutes
Serves,
6-8
6 eggs, at room temperature
5 cups (40 fl oz/I. 2 liters) Katsuobushi
Dashi (page 156)
• 1/• teaspoon salt
3 tablespoons usukuchi shoyu
· 2 teaspoons mirin
I (7-oz/200 g) bunch spinach, leave s
only, cut crosswise into 3/•-inch
(2 cm) length s
I teaspoon finely slivered yuzu
or Meyer lemon zest
DASHI-SIMMERED TARO ROOT
Taro root is silky and satisfying ,
and is one of those quintessential
Japanese vegetables with a naturally
slippery texture , which lends well
to simmered treatments.
Place the peeled ta ro in a medium
pot, fill with
water to cover by
r½ inches (4 cm), and bring to
a boil over high heat. Cook for
about 5 minutes over
medium
heat (the taro tends to bubble up
so stay close), un til half cooked.
Drain, return to the pot, and
add the dashi, mirin, and sal t. Set
an otoshibuta [drop lid) or piece of
parchment paper on top and bring
to a simmer over medium-high
heat. Adjust to a brisk simmer
and cook until the taro is cooked
through and soft in the middle,
about 5 more minutes. Remove
the drop lid or paper, swirl in
the soy sauce , and once the liquid
returns to a simmer, remove from
the heat. Serve hot or at room
temperature. Sprinkle with shichimi
togarashi, if using .
[Qj p.127
DASHI-STEAMED EGGS
WITH SPINACH
This is a pretty, deconstructed egg
custard that makes an excellent
starter to a meal.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil.
In a bowl, whisk together the eggs,
scant 2 cups
(15 fl oz/ 450 ml) of
the dashi, the salt, and I teaspoon
each of the usukuchi sh'!J'u and mirin.
Pour into a foil-lined 8-inch (20
cm) square pan with a removable
bottom. Cover with foil, place
in the steamer insert, and steam,
covered , for 20 minutes.
In a pot, combine the remaining
3 cups (24 fl oz/710 ml) dashi,
2 teaspoons usukuchi sh'!J'u, and
I teaspoon of mirin and bring to
a simmer over medium heat .
Drop in the spinach leaves and
cook for I minute. Scoop them
out and set to drain in a sieve set
over ii small bowl. Do not discard
the simmering dashi.
Slide a knife around th e outside of
the custard and unmold carefully.
Cut into 6 or 8 squares and
remove from the foil-lined pan
bottom with a thin metal spatula
into shallow soup bowls. Drape
the spinach leaves attractively
around the custard and ladle in the
simmering
dashi. Garnish with a few
slivers ofy"-<:u zest
and serve hot.
NIMONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Fragrant Miso­ Simmered Daikon Shirataki Bundles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6
I lb (450 g) daikon, peeled
• 3 tablespoons
soybean miso
l large pinch ground sansho pepper
• l tablespoon mirin
· 2 tablespoons sake
Preparation time, 45 minutes
Cooking time, 20 minutes
Makes, 8 bundles
2 strands kanpyo
[dried gourd)
• 5 oz (150 g) shirataki noodles, cut
crosswise into 1½-inch (4 cm) lengths
· Boiling
water
• 4 usuage
[deep-fried tofu pouches),
halved crosswise
• 7 oz (200 g) ground (minced) chicken
2 medium shiitake , stems
discarded,
caps thinly sliced
2½ cups (20' /• fl oz/600 ml)
Katsuobushi Dashi (page 156)
2 tablespoons soy
sauce
• I tablespoon mirin
FRAGRANT MISO­
SIMMERED DAIKON
Julienned daikon appears often in
country-style miso soups . Here the
pieces are cut thick and simmered
with seasonings rather than in the
more usual dashi-based soup. The
sansho can be substituted by a spoonful
of ground black sesame seeds.
C ut the daikon into batonnets
'/•-inch (6
mm) thick and
2½ - inches (6 cm) long.
In a large frying pan , combine
the miso and sansho pepper. Slowly
whisk in the mirin, sake, and l cup
(8 fl oz/ 250 ml) cold water. Bring
to a simmer over medium heat
and drop in the daikon b ; tonnets .
Simmer
until the center of the
daikon is just cooked, about
I minute . Drain and serve hot or at
room temperature in rustic ceramic
bowls napped with a little of the
simmering liquid .
Im p.129
SHIRATAKI BUNDLES
These little bundles are time­
consuming to prepare, but
make for a pretty presentation
as a first course.
Drop the kanpyo into a small bowl
and fill with cold water. Let soak
for 20 minutes to reconstitute.
Place the shirataki in a wire-mesh
sieve and pour a steady stream of
boiling water over the noodles for
IO seconds . Shake off the excess
water and slide the noodles into
a medium bowl.
Put the usuage in a wire - mesh sieve
and pour a steady stream of boiling
water over it for IO seconds . When
coo l , set the usuage on your work
space and roll over it with a heavy
rolling pin to help it separate more
easily . Pry the pouches open with
your fingers, without tearing the
sides, to make an envelope for
stuffing. Drain the kanpya.
Dividing evenly , stuff the halved
usuage with shirataki, chicken , and
shiitake. Close the flap to create a
package and tie securely with a half
strand of kanpyo. Nestle the bundles
into a small saucepan. Add the
dashi, soy sauce, and mirin. Cover
and simmer gently for 20 minutes.
Serve
hot or at room temperature.
128 NIM
ONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Kenchin Tofu-Stuffed Napa Cabbage Nimono - Simmered
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 45 minutes
Cooking time, 20 minutes
Serves,
6
I (ro½ oz/300 g) momendofu
or Japanese-style soft block tofu
6 large or I2 small
napa cabbage
( Chinese leaO leaves
I teaspoon flaky sea salt
I heaping tablespoon dried wood ear
mushrooms, soaked in cold water for
20 minutes
• I small carrot, scrubbed
I¾ oz (50 g) gobo [burdock]. scrubbed
• 2 tablespoons
pine nuts, warmed in
a dry frying pan over low heat until
the oils come out
• I tablespoon potato starch
(13/+ oz/50 g) dried hijiki, soaked
in cold water for 20 minutes
l quart (32 fl oz/r liter) Japanese
Chicken Broth (page r6o)
• 4 tablespoons
sake
I tablespoon usukuchi shoyu
Shichimi togarashi [seven-spice
powder]. optional
KENCHIN TOFU-STUFFED
NAPA CABBAGE
Kenchin refers to dishes that have
their roots in shojin ryori [Buddhist
temple food]. Konbu Dashi
(page 156) or Katsuobushi Dashi
(page 156) can be substituted for
the chicken stock . These rolls are
also good cold the following day for
a quick lunch on the fly.
Set the tofu on a cutting board and
prop a small plate underneath
it
to angle the board into the kitchen
sink (to catch drips). Lay another
cutting board on top of the tofu to
press out moisture for 20 minutes.
Bring
a large pot of water to a boil.
Hold the stem ends of the napa
cabbage ( Chinese leaO leaves in
the boiling water for a count of IO,
then submerge the leaves in the
boiling water and cook until the
stem ends have softened, about
2 minutes .
Drain, pat dry, and sprinkle with
½ teaspoon of the salt.
Drain the wood ear mushrooms
and finely slice. Cut the carrot and
burdock into medium dice.
Scrape the tofu into a medium
bowl and sift in the potato starch .
Beat well with a wooden spoon to
incorporate. Fold in the wood ear
mushrooms, carrot, gobo, and pine
nuts. Drain the hijiki and add. Stir
until all the ingredients are well
distributed.
Lay the cabbage leaves out on a
large baking sheet. Dividing evenly ,
spoon the tofu mixture onto the
base of each leaf, about ½ inch
(12 mm)
up from the stem end.
Roll each leaf up one rotation,
fold in the sides of the leaves , and
continue rolling all the way up.
In a medium pot, combine the
chicken broth, sake, usukuchi sh'!)'u,
and the remaining scant
½ teaspoon of salt. Nestle the
cabbage rolls into the bottom of
the pot and cook, covered , at a
lively simmer until the rolls have
set , about 15 minutes. Serve hot
or at room temperature, with
a sprinkling of shichimi togarashi,
if using.
NIMONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Napa Cabbage Rolls Simmered In Tomato 131 Ni Mono - Simmered
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 25 minutes
Cooking time, 45 minutes
Serves,
6
For the tomato sauce,
l tablespoon extra virgin olive oil
• l (28 oz/794 g) can whole organic
Roma tomatoes packed in tomato juice,
finely chopped
¼ teaspoon flaky sea salt
For the cabbage ro lls,
l lb 2 oz (500 g) large black tiger
shrimp (prawns)
7 oz (200 g) naga imo [mountain yam].
peeled and cut into rounds % inch
(1 cm) thick
6 large or 12 small leaves napa cabbage
( Chinese leaf)
1¼ cups (ro fl oz/300 ml) Katsuobushi
Dashi (page 156 )
I½ teaspoons flaky sea salt
1/+ teaspoon freshly ground black
pepper
I small handful fresh Italian or curly
parsley, chopped
NAPA CABBAGE ROLLS
SIMMERED IN TOMATO
Noga imo [mountain yam] is an
unexpected ingredient in these
unusual cabbage rolls .
Make the tomato sauce: In a large
frying pan set over high h eat ,
add the oil and tomatoes. Cook,
stirring, for 5 minutes . Decrease
the heat to medium-low and
cook for 5 minutes more, stirring
occasionally.
Measure out the
1% cups
(400 ml) of the sauce and
reserve the rest for another use.
Make the cabbage rolls: Rinse
the shrimp (prawns) under cold,
running water, make a shallow
cut in the back of the shells, and
remove the veins with a small
bamboo skewer.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil . Arrange the shrimp
and
naga imo in the steamer ba sket,
cover, and steam for IO minutes.
Mash the steamed shrimp and naga
imo in a suribachi [grinding bowl] to
form a paste (or pulse in a food
processor). Keep the steamer going
(replenish with water if necessary).
Separate the cabbage leaves one by
one and tenderize the hard stem
areas by pounding with a rolling
pin. Ad d to the steamer basket and
cook until soft and pliable, about
5 minutes.
Stir
the dashi, salt, and pepper
into the r% cups
(400 ml) of
tomato sauce.
Lay the cabbage leaves out on a
couple of baking sheets. Dividing
evenly, spoon a dollop of shrimp­
naga imo mixture onto each leaf
about ½ inch (12 mm) from the
base of the stem end. Roll up one
rotation, fold in the side leav es,
and continue rolling up to form
a neat package. Place the rolls in a
la rge frying pan , add 1% cups (13 ½
fl oz/ 400 ml) of
the tomato sauce,
and place an otoshibuta [drop lid] or
saucepan lid on top of the rolls.
Set the pan over medium-high
heat, bring to a slow boil, lower
the heat , and simmer , covered, for
20 minutes. Spoon onto a platter
and sprinkle with the parsley
before serving.
131 NI MONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Tofu-Stuffed Cabbage Rolls 132 Ni Mono - Simmered
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 40 minutes
Cooking time , 25 minutes
Serves , 6
l (ro½ oz/300 g) momendofu or
Japanese-style soft block tofu
12 small
or 6 large green cabbage leaves
• l small carrot , scrubbed
l usuage [deep-fried tofu pouch],
halved lengthwise
• 4 sh
ii take , stems discarded and caps
finely chopped
2 tablespoons
finely chopped thin negi
or fat scallion (spring onion)
l egg, at room temperature ,
lightly beaten
l tablespoon sake
¾ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 2½ cups (20 fl oz/600 mi)
Katsuobushi Dashi (page 156)
· l tablespoon soy sauce
• I teaspoon mirin
¼ teaspoon freshly ground
black pepper
l tablespoon chopped parsley
TOFU-STUFFED
CABBAGE ROLLS
Cabbage rolls are universally loved
worldwide, and Japan i s no excep ­
tion. The variations are myriad
but due to the predominance of
Japanese seasonings, this one is
particularly Japanese in flavoring
and style .
Set the tofu on a cutting board and
prop a small saucer underneath to
angle the board into the kitchen
sink (to catch drips). Lay another
cutting board on top of the tofu to
press out moisture for 20 minutes.
Bring a medium pot of water to
a boil. Stack the cabbage leaves
together and hold the stem ends
in the boiling water for
l minute ,
then submerge the leave s in the
boiling water and cook for 30 more
seconds. Scoop out with a wire­
mesh sieve and let drain in the sink .
Drop the carrot into the boiling
water and cook for 3 minutes, or
until half done, and drain. Set the
usuage halves in a wire-mesh sieve
and dip them into the boiling
water for IO seconds. Drain in the
sink and blot dry with a clean tea
towel. Cut the carrot and usuage into
1/+-inch (6 mm) dice.
Squeeze the tofu to remove excess
liquid and drop into a suribachi
[grinding bowl] or medium bowl.
Grind with a surigoki [wooden pestle]
or whip with a wooden spoon until
creamy. Fold in the carrot , usu age,
shiitake, negi, beaten egg , sake, and salt
until well incorporated.
Lay the cabbage leaves out on
two baking sheets and spoon the
tofu filling into the curled section
of the leaf about ¾ inch (2 cm)
in from the stem end. Smooth
out the filling to make a fat
sausage-like shape. Roll one
rotation
up , fold
the sides of the
leaf in toward the center , and
continue rolling up until you have
formed a tight packet.
Nestle these packets into a medium
pot and pour in the dashi, soy
sauce, and mirin. Place an otoshibuta
[drop lid] or piece of parchment
paper on top of the cabbage rolls
and bring the pot almost to a boil
over high heat. Adjust the heat to
medium, cover, and simmer for
20 minutes. Let the rolls rest for
5 minutes before serving with the
simmering liquid. Serve whole
or slice and serve, sprinkled with
the black pepper and parsley, in
individual small saucers.
132 NI MONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Dashi-Simmered Cabbage Rolls 134 Nim Ono - Simmered
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time, 20 minutes
Serves, 6
6 large green cabbage leave s
31. lb (350 g) finely ground (minced)
pork
½ medium negi or 2 fat scallions
(spring onions) , finely chopped
• I 1/2 teaspoons flaky sea salt
• 1½ tablespoons mirin
2 small eggs , at room temperature
• 2 ½ cups (20 fl oz/ 600 ml)
Katsuobushi
Dashi (page 156)
• 2 tablespoons
sake
• 2 table spoons soy sauce
• I medium carrot , scrubbed and cut
crosswise into ¼ - inch (6 mm) rounds
• 12 green beans , topped and cut
crosswise into 1½-inch (4 cm) pieces
Ichimi togarashi [powdered Japanese
red chile] , optional
DASHI-SIMMERED
CABBAGE ROLLS
There are several variations of
cabbage rolls in this book. Here,
the meat is rolled up with the
cabbage for a spiral effect when cut.
Western cabbage is called for , but
napa cabbage ( Chinese leaf) can
just as easily be substituted .
Lay the cabbage leaves on a cutting
board and rap the thick stem ends
of each one with a wooden mallet
or
surikogi [grinding pestle] to
break down the fibers a
little. Fill
a medium pot with water and bring
to a boil. Hold the stem ends in
the boiling water for 30 seconds ,
then submerge the leaves in the
boiling water and cook for 30
seconds more. Scoop out with
a wire - mesh sieve and run cold
water over to refresh.
In a medium bowl , mix together
the pork , negi, I teaspoon of the
salt , I tablespoon of the mirin, and
the egg until all of the ingredients
are well incorporated. The meat
mixture will be fairly loose.
Arrange the cooled cabbage leaves
side by side on two baking sheets .
Dividing evenly , top the leaves with
the meat filling about 3/+ inch
(2 cm) up from the stem end.
Spoon the meat into base of the
leaf, leaving at l east 4 inches
(10 cm) free at the tip of the leaves.
Roll the stem up one rotation, fold
in the sides of the leaves , and keep
rolling to make a tight package.
In a heavy medium pot , combine
the dashi, sake, soy sauce, and
remaining ½ teaspoon salt and ½
tablespoon mirin and bring to a boil.
Remove the pot from the heat and
nestle the rolls in the bottom of the
pot. They should fit snugly, but you
will still need to place an otoshibuta
[drop lid] or pan lid directly on
top of the rolls to keep them from
jumping around and unraveling.
Simmer over medium - low heat
for 15 minutes. Drop the carrot
and green beans into the pot of
simmering cabbage rolls and cook
until the carrots and green beans
have softened , 3-5 minutes.
Remove the rolls with a slotted
spoon to a carving board (with
grooves to catch the juices). Scoop
the green beans and carrot into a
small bowl. Cut the rolls in half or
quarters crosswise and arrange in
a shallow soup bowl or salad plate
per person. Strew with the carrot
and green beans. Reheat the broth
over high heat, and ladle over a
scoop of broth. Sprinkle with ichimi
togarashi, if using. Do not cut until
serving. Serve hot wi th chopsticks
and a soup spoon . (The roll s can
be made ahead and reheated the
following day for a warm lunch or
casual supper .)
134 NIM ONO - SIMMERED

recipes.title: Creamy Napa Cabbage Nimono - Simmered
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time: 20 minutes
Serves : 6
5 1/+ oz (150 g) cauliflower , separated
into small florets
3 1/ 2 oz (100 g) broccoli, separated into
small florets
14 oz
(400 g) napa cabbage (Chinese
leaf), halved
lengthwise
l medium carrot, scrubbed and
quartered lengthwise
l large onion, peeled and halved
lengthwise
l tablespoon canola (rapeseed) oil
• 3 ½ oz (100 g) unsmoked bacon, cut
crosswise into 1½-inch (4 cm) pieces

The cabbage combines well with the

dish served over rice.

and onion and continue to stir­

they have softened. Stir in the
milk , chicken stock, I cup (8 fl
oz/ 250 ml) water,
the cauliflower,
broccoli, napa cabbage, and salt
and bring to a gentle simmer .
CABBAGE
In a small saucepan , melt the butter
over medium heat. Sprinkle in
the flour and scrape and stir the
row, for
2 minutes . Ladle in a
scoop of the liquid from the pot of
vegetables and whisk until smooth.
Whisk in 4 or
5 more scoops of
liquid, then incorporate the sauce
slowly back into the simmering pot
of vegetables. If you are feeling
harried with the two bubbling pots ,
turn off the pot of vegetables while
you get the cream sauce made .
Simmer the vegetables for IO more
minutes .
Mound a generous portion of rice
on a dinner plate and spoon the
creamy vegetables over the rice .
Serve hot. (If using as a leftover the
following day, reheat.) Sprinkle
with ichimi togarashi if spice sounds
appealing.

This is a quintessentialJapanese

Once the pan liquids return to a

Shimi daikon, which resembles

irresistible ability to soak up
simmering juices, might be hard to
find outside of
Japan.
Soak the herring in water (ideally

(3 cm) lengths.

Add the miso paste and reconsti­

[cooking chopsticks]. Return to
a slow simmer and cook until the
earthy fragrance of miso and mirin
lifts from the pot, another 3-5
minutes. Spoon into small bowls
and serve.

l lb 2 oz (500 g) pork belly , cut into
¾- to 1¼-inch (2-3 cm)
cubes
13 oz (375 g) fat green beans, cut
crosswise into ¾-inch (2 cm)
lengths
• 2 tablespoons
finely chopped
fresh ginger
· % cup (5 fl oz/r50 ml) Katsuobushi
Dashi
(page 156)
• 6 tablespoons sake
4-tablespoons soy sauce
· 2 tablespoons mirin
1/2 teaspoon brown rice vinegar
SIMMERED PORK BELLY
Although commonly consumed in
the winter, some say the richness
of this dish makes for energy food
during the hot and muggy Japanese
summer. Good as a small bite with
a beer in the late afternoon when
feeling droopy. Pork belly should
always have its rind removed before
being used in Japanese dishes .
In a heavy medium pot , combine
the pork belly , chile , and okara
and add cold water to cover by
4-inches (ro cm) . Bring to a boil
over medium-high eat, then set an
otoshibuta [drop lid] on top of the
meat, reduce the heat to low, and
simmer for 5 hours.
In a small saucepan, combine
1¼ cups (ro fl oz/ 300 ml) water,
the sake, soy sauce, and mirin . Bring
to a simmer, then remove from
the heat.
Scoop the meat out of the
simmering liquid with a slotted
spoon, discard the liquid, and
rinse the
okara solids off of the meat
with cold water. Put the meat in
the small saucepan of seasonings,
place an otoshibuta [drop lid] or
piece of parchment paper on top,
and simmer for 20-30 minutes
to absorb flavor.
To serve, spoon into a bowl with the
mustard on the side, to be dabbed
on as desired.
PORK BELLY WITH
GREEN BEANS
Pork belly is a versatile and easily
obtainable cut both inJapan and
abroad. (Though injapan, we
never use pork belly that still has its
rind, so be sure to ask the butcher
to remove it.) The trick is to render
out enough fat so the pork becomes
meltingly soft. Adding a vegetable
to the dish makes a big difference.
While daikon and negi are possible,
here green beans add a pleasant
vegetal note to the dish.
Place the pork belly in a small
saucepan and add water to just
cover. Bring to a boil over high
heat , reduce the heat to a simmer,
cover, and cook for 30 minutes.
Remove the pork and cooking
liquid to a small bowl and allow
to cool for about 30 minutes.
Meanwhile , bring a medium pot of
water to a boil and blanch the green
beans for 3 minutes.
Scoop out and
refresh under cold, running water.
Shake off excess water and set aside .
Skim the cooled pork pieces out
of the cooking liquid, discard the
liquid, and put the pork in the
medium pot. Add the dashi, sake,
soy sauce, mirin , and ginger. Set
an otoshibuta [drop lid] or piece
of parchment paper across the
surface and bring to a simmer over
medium-high heat. Adjust the heat
and cook at a simmer, swirling the
pot occasionally, until the liquids
have reduced by more than half ,
10- 15 minutes .
Stir
in the green beans and vinegar,
replace the otoshibuta, and cook for
just enough time to absorb flavor
but not discolor, l-2 minutes.
Serve
immediately.

NIKUJAGA
Nikujaga (soy - simmered pork and
potatoes) is a much-loved dish that
benefits from some green to give
it color . If peas are out of season,
two-minute blanched green beans
make an excellent substitute.
In a large pot of salted boiling
water, blanch the peas for about
30 seconds. Scoop out with a large
wire-mesh sieve and refresh under

shirataki noodles into the pot and

Scoop

In a heavy medium pot, combine

SOY-SIMMERED BEEF
AND BURDOCK
At Japanese New Year, some people
make beef and burdock rolls, which
require a little work to assemble.
Here the basic ingredients are the

Cut the meat into roughly

In a heavy medium saucepan ,

ginger , chile , and beef and simmer ,
stirring, until all of the liquid has
evaporated. Serve hot or at room
temperature.

Beef and burdock are a classic

Quarter the burdock lengthwise,

Avoid the unappealing versions

In a pot of boiling water, boil the

2 minutes more , while stirring

BAMBOO SHOOT
WITH KATSUOBUSHI
Boiled fresh bamboo shoots
smothered in delicately smoky
katsuobushi is an example of how
seasonal ingredients only need
a light hand to bring out their
natural nuances.
Place the bamboo shoot in a large
pot with the rice bran and chile .
Fill with cold water to cover by
4 inches
(10 cm) and add an
otoshibuta [drop lid] or saucepan
lid to keep the bamboo shoot
submerged . Bring to a boil over
medium-high heat, adjust to a
brisk simmer, and cook for l hour.
Remove from the heat and allow
to cool overnight in the simmering
liquid.
The following day , remove the
bamboo shoot from the pot and
discard the liquid . Rinse off any
lingering rice bran solids and peel.
Cut the bamboo shoot into thin
wedges 2½ inches
(6 cm) long .
Place in a medium pot with the
katsuobushi, dashi, soy sauce, sake,
mirin, and salt. Top with an otoshibuta
[drop lid] or pot lid and bring to
a simmer over medium-high heat.
Adjust to a lively simmer and cook
for 8-10 minutes to absorb flavor
and reduce the simmering liquid.
Serve hot or at room temperature,

bamboo shoot and just a little of
the simmering liquid to keep the
dish glossy and appealing.
SOY DASHI-SIMMERED
MUSHROOMS
Make this earthy dish in the fall
when mushrooms are springing
up in wooded areas . Use any
combination of mushrooms

In a medium pot , heat the soy

heat , stirring and tossing gently
with a pair of saibashi [cooking
chopsticks] to distribute heat, until
a large portion of the simmering
liquids has reduced , and the
mushrooms are cooked through
and glossy brown, 5-6 minutes.
Serve hot or at room temperature .

SUMO-STYLE CHICKEN SOUP
The thinner-bodied Sumo
wrestlers are called "Soppu-type,"
since they resemble chicken bones
compared to the typical hefty­
bodied wrestlers. The Japanese
name of this soup , Soppu-daki, is a
play on words evoking the "soppu­
type" sumo wrestlers and the Dutch
name for soup-borrowed from
Dutch traders. The chicken broth
base is meant to add richness to fill
the
bellies of the hungry wrestlers .
The garlic chives add an integral
flavoring note , so be sure to use
the six whole chives and not just
six leaves.
Make the broth: Rinse the chicken
bones with plenty of cold water .
Drop them into a heavy medium
pot and add
4 quarts
(about
4 liter s)
cold water. Throw in
the onions, celery, carrot, and
parsley and bring to a near boil
over high heat. Adjust to a gentle
simmer and cook uncovered for
I½ hours . Every 30 minutes, skim
off the scum that accumulates on
the surface of the broth. Strain
the broth into a medium pot or
donabe [flameproof earthenware
casserole], season with the soy sauce
and mirin, and set the pot over low
heat to keep warm.
Make the soup: Cut the reconsti­
tuted k<!Jadofu into 4 pieces each.
Drop the kon'!)'aku into a wire-mesh
sieve and pour a steady stream of
boiling water over it for IO seconds.
Cut the carrots crosswise into
r½-inch (4 cm) lengths . Slice those
pieces lengthwise into slabs ¾ inch
(2 cm)
thick. Stack the slabs and cut
lengthwise into batonnets % inch
(r cm) wide . Cut the chicken into
¾ - inch (2 cm)
pieces.
Adjust the heat under the broth
to medium and add the chicken ,
k<!Jadofu, kon'!)'aku, usuage, and carrot
batonnets. Cook at a lively simmer
until all of the ingredients have
absorbed flavor and the carrot has
softened ,
7-8 minutes. Drop in
the napa cabbage ( Chinese leaf),
shungiku, and garlic chives. Stir once
or twice to distribute and cook for
about I more minute, until the
greens have wilted.
To serve , ladle into large, donburi
[deep soup bowls]. Sprinkle with
shichimi togarashi, if you are looking for
a little heat. Serve with individual
bowls of Japanese rice on the side.
Note: This soup makes excellent
leftovers, but if intending to save
some for later , don't add all of
the greens . Just add enough for
the portions you are serving and
reserve the .rest to stir in when
reheating the soup.

Use for dipping simple boiled

Use this broth for dipping tempura

CLAM BROTH
Small clams make for less work ,
since they can be left whole for

fine if they are cut down to bite-size
pieces. Don't skip the soaking and
rinsing of the clams: It's important
for removing any sand .
Scrub the clams in several changes

about
IO minutes in salty water to

remove the broth from the heat.
If any grains of sand escaped into
the broth, strain through a double
layer of cheesecloth.
Use as a base for miso soup or season
with salt and serve reheated with the
clams and garnished with chopped

Clams and spinach always go well

course before dinner.

recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time: 45 minutes
Makes:
5 cups (40 fl oz/1.2 liters)
• l lb 2 oz (500 g) snapper head and
center bones (with flesh still clinging on)
• ½ teaspoons flaky sea salt
• l large negi or 4 fat scallions (spring
onions), cut crosswise into 2-inch (5
cm) pieces
• l ¼-inch (3 cm) piece fresh ginger ,
scrubbed and cut crosswise into '/•-inch
( 6
mm) slices
· l teaspoon fine sea salt
l ½ tablespoons finely chopped fresh
chives or scallions (spring onions)
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time : 1'/• hours
Makes: 3 quarts (3 liters)
12 oz (350
g) uncooked chicken bones

(spring onions) , cut crosswise into
2-inch (5 cm) pieces

scrubbed and cut crosswise into '/•-inch
(
6 mm) slices
CLEAR FISH BROTH
This clear fish broth is one of
the most quintessentialJapanese
dishes.
Position a rack 6 inches (15 cm)
from the top of the oven and
preheat the broiler (grill).
Pull out the snapper gills and whack
the head in half to split into two
cheeks. Cut the center bone into
thirds. Rinse the bones and heads
under cool , running water and pat
dry . Line a baking sheet with foil
and set the fish bones
and heads on
the foil. Holding your hand
12 inches (30 cm) above the bones ,
sprinkle both sides with the flaky
sea salt (this ensures a light even
coating) .
Broil (grill) for about 7 minutes
on
each side, or until the oils have
been released and there is some
browning, but not blackening, on
the surface of the head and bones .
Meanwhile , bring 2 quarts
(64
fl oz/2 liters) water to a boil
over high heat.
Drop the broiled fish bones
and
head pieces, negi, and ginger into
the hot water and simmer gently
for 30 minutes. Strain, season with
the fine salt, and
reheat for serving.
Ladle into individual soup bowls
and garnish with the chives.
JAPANESE CHICKEN BROTH
Japanese stocks and broths are
generally much lighter in taste
than Western ones; so Japanese
chicken broth is similarly subtler
and less chicken-forward than
typical chicken broth. Duck or
turkey bones can substitute for
the chicken .
Rinse the bones under cold
running water and drop into a large
stockpot. Add the
negi and ginger
and fill with 4 quarts
(4 liters)
cold water . Cover and bring to an
almost boil over high heat, 10-15
minutes. Watch the pot so that it
does not boil since boiling will
result in a cloudy broth . (That said,
this broth tends to be cloudy from
the negi.) Immediately reduce the
heat so the broth gently simmers ,
uncover, and cook for about 1½
hours, skimming occasionally.
Strain the broth (di scard the bones
and aromatics).

This is a light , lovely soup , but its

Halve the usuage crosswise, place

CARROT SOUP
Vegetable soups need no additional
stock if your vegetables are seasonal
and flavorful. This soup freezes well
and is convenient to have on hand.
Cut the celery , carrots, potatoes ,

MISO SOUP WITH
GRATED CARROT
The finely grated carrots add a
note of sweetness to this soup and
balance well against the miso broth.
Finely grate the carrot on an
oroshigane Uapanese grating plate].
Quarter the daikon lengthwise , then
slice it crosswise into thin slices
(itchogiri; see page 446) .
In a medium pot, heat the dashi
over medium-high heat and slip
in the daikon. Cook at a lively (but
not crazy) simmer until the daikon
has softened, 2-3 minutes. Scoop
up a ladle of dashi and whisk the miso
into the ladle of dashi. Dunk the
ladle back into the soup and stir
in the seri and grated carrot. Heat
for I minute or so , but no longer,
since heat destroys the probiotic
propertie s of miso. Serve hot.
CABBAGE MISO SOUP
Excellent miso soup relies on
homemade dashi, resist the
temptation to use instant dashi.
While farming families sometimes
make big pots of miso soup full of
root vegetables and cabbage, for a
thrifty meal to feed a crowd, more
often miso soup relies on only two
or three ingredients.
Slice the usuage crosswise into strips
1/+ inch (6
mm) wide. Place in a
wire-mesh sieve and pour a steady
stream of boiling water over it for
about IO seconds. Shake off excess
water.
In a medium pot, bring the dashi
to an almost simmer over medium­
high heat. Add the usuage and
cabbage, reduce the heat to low ,
and simmer for about I minute.
Whisk a small scoop of hot dashi
into the miso to emulsify. Scrape
back into the soup, stir once to
distribute, remove from the heat ,
and serve immediately.

recipes.transcription:

MISO SOUP WITH
POACHED EGG
Adding egg to miso soup gives it
richness and substance.
Break each egg into a small bowl.
In medium saucepan, bring the
dashi to a simmer over medium­
high heat and add the onion slices.
Reduce the heat to low and simmer
until soft, 2-3 minutes. Drain the
wakame. Dollop the miso into a soup
ladle and whisk in a little of the
dashi to emulsify. Stir the miso into
the dashi with the wakame.
When the soup has returned to
a gentle simmer , slip in the eggs ,
one by one. Cover and cook at
a bare simmer for I minute, swirl­
ing the pan a little to encourage
the soup to slurp over the egg to
aid the cooking process. Remove
the soup from the heat. Allow the
egg to "cook " by the heat of the
covered saucepan until partially set,
2 minutes. Ladle gently
into 4 bowls
and
serve immediately.
GRILLED EGGPLANT
MISO SOUP
While still delicious pan-grilled or
broiled, if the eggplant is charcoal
grilled, this soup is spectacular.
The proportion of miso to dashi is
purposely light, since this is
a summer dish.
Place the eggplants (aubergines)
on a grate directly over a medium­
high gas burner or in a cast iron
pan over medium - high heat. Grill
until blackened on all sides and
collapsed , 5-6 minutes. Peel off the
blackened skin and tear into long
strips. Divide the eggplant among
4 to
6 miso soup bowls.
In a small saucepan , heat the dashi
over medium heat. Spoon the miso
into a ladle and dip the ladle into
the warm dashi to catch up a little
of the liquid. Whisk the dashi into
the miso to emulsify and dunk the
ladle all the way into the dashi. Give
the soup one more whisk, and ladle
over the eggplant. Sprinkle with the
sesame and serve hot.
[ variation]
Chill all the ingredients and serve
cold.

EGGPLANT AND PEANUT SOUP
Peanuts perhaps do not come to
mind as a conventional Japanese
ingredient, but they are grown
all over Japan and are eaten as a
snack or as a protein in shojin ryori
Uapanese temple food].
Halve the eggplants (aubergines)

NATTO SOUP
Though popular inJapan, many
people living elsewhere do not care
for natto. Nonetheless, this soup
is delicious and should be given
a chance . If you are fortunate,
you can source good-quality natto
made outside of Japan. The nameko
mushrooms have a similar slippery
characteristic as the natto, and are
essential to this soup .
Finely chop the natto and scrape

Pound to a paste, then mash in the

In a medium saucepan, simmer the

low to low heat until soft, 7-I0
minutes. Scrape in the peanut miso

eggplant piece in a small lacquer
bowl , ladle in the soup , sprinkle

In a medium saucepan , heat the

SWEET POTATO COUNTRY SOUP
Kenchinjiru [country soup] is the soup
we make whenever a crowd comes
to pound mochi. Sweet potato,
ginger, and miso are an appealing
combination in this version.
Set the tofu on a cutting board
and place a small saucer underneath

COUNTRY MISO
Serve this soup in the winter when
craving a big bowl of broth and
vegetables .

In a medium pot, heat the dashi over

Potato starch adds a subtle silkiness

(Or quick-soak, Bring

Ozoni is a soup that is made only at

for breakfast on the morning of
January I. Squares of mochi (page

heated up in the broth

the elderly are warned to take heed
not to cho ke , because the mochi
can stick in one 's throat. With that
warning in mind, the ooey-gooey

the soup's clean simplicity makes

of shichimi togarashi, if using.

I pinch of shichimi

KENCHINJIRU
Kenchiryiru [rustic vegetable soup]
is made all over Japan. This chunky
version is from Iwate prefecture,
a mountainous area in the north of
the country. Doubling or tripling
the recipe makes sense, since the
soup is traditionally served at large
gatherings, and leftovers are eaten
for several days afterward .
Rub ½ teaspoon of the salt into the
kon19aku, place in a wire-mesh sieve ,

or

chopped mitsuba. Serve hot.

recipes.title: "Raccoon Dog" Soup Shirumono - Soups
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 6
2 (6-inch/15 cm) squares
konbu

konnyaku, torn into
bite-size pieces

"RACCOON DOG" SOUP
The raccoon dog is a beloved
creature whose statue stands in
front of restaurants for good
luck. Since eating these animals
is no longer in fashion, kon191aku
(also known as devil's tongue)­
gelatinous blocks made from a
zero-calorie corm-now replaces
raccoon dog in this traditional
soup. If turnip greens are not
available, substitute mustard
greens.
In a medium pot , combine the
konbu and 11/, quarts (42 fl oz/
1.25 liters) cold water
and bring
to a near boil. Remove the pot
from the heat. Pluck the konbu out
with a pair of tongs and cut into
thin strips. Add the konbu back to
the pot of dashi.
Set the kon191aku pieces in a wire­
mesh sieve and pour a steady
stream of boiling water over them
for IO seconds. Add it to the pot
of dashi and place the pot over
medium-low heat.
With your nondominant hand,
hold the burdock above the pot of
dashi and use a sharp knife to shave
thin slices off the end of it as you
rotate it (sasagaki; see page 446), like
sharpening the end of a stick. Bring
the pot of soup to a simmer over
medium-high heat and stir in the
grated daikon. Cook for 5 minutes
over medium-low heat. Drop in
the greens, stir until wilted, and
remove from the heat. Measure
both misos into a large ladle and dip
it into the soup to capture some
broth. Stir the broth into the miso
in the ladle to loosen the paste ,
then dunk back into the soup and
stir to emulsify and serve hot with
a sprinkling of shichimi togarashi.

FISH DUMPLING SOUP
WITH MISO
A bit like aJapanese-style quenelle,
shinjo are poached fish or seafood
"balls" (for want of a better word),
but can be formed into spheres ,
obelisks, or small patties.
Cut the fish fillet into
½-inch
(12 mm) pieces and pound in a
suribachi [grinding bowl) or pulse
in a food processor until a smooth
paste has formed . In a small bowl,
whisk together the flour, potato
starch, and salt. In another small
bowl , whisk together the sake and
egg whites . Add the wet and dry
ingredients alternately to the fish
paste
by pounding or processing
them until incorporated into
a stiff paste.
Fill a medium saucepan three ­
quarters of the way up with cold
water and bring to a boil over high
heat. Dip two small spoons into
cold water and fashion teaspoon
amounts of the fish paste
into
rounded balls . Drop the fish balls
into the boiling
water as they are
formed. Cook at a lively simmer ,
skimming out the balls as they bob
to the surface, about 3 minutes.
In
a medium pot, bring the dashi to
a simmer over high heat. Drop in
the shiitake slices and scallion pieces
and cook for 3 minutes
over low
heat. Whisk a small ladle of broth
into the miso to loosen the paste .
Scrape the diluted miso into the
soup, add the fish balls, and
serve
immediately. Garnish with the
mitsuba leaves, if using.
GARLIC CHIVE SOUP
Garlic chives and eggs are a classic
pairing, the addition of cod, how­
ever, lends a note of richness. This
is clearly a restorative , delicious,
soup. Use eight whole garlic chives,
not eight garlic chive leaves.
Place the cod pieces in a wire-mesh
sieve and pour a steady stream of
boiling water over them for
IO seconds to remove any residual
smells.
In a medium saucepan, combine
the dashi, salt , usukuchi sh'!J'u, and
sake and bring to a simmer over
medium heat.
In a small bowl, beat the eggs and
the garlic chives with a fork or
chopsticks. Slide the cod into the
simmering broth and return to a
boil. Give the eggs a quick whisk
to re-emulsify and swirl into the
soup . Adjust to a low simmer and
cook until the eggs are just set , but
still runny in places, another 1-2
minutes . Grind black pepper over
the top and serve by ladling into
small bowls or over a bowl of rice.

HERRING AND
CHRYSANTHEMUM SOUP
The knotted herring fillets make
for an attractive presentation. If
you are unable to source edible
chrysanthemum leaves, you can
substitute spinach.
Halve each herring fillet lengthwise
to make 12 strips,
rinse briefly in
cold water, and pat dry. Tie the
fillets into loose single knots and
sprinkle with the salt. Fill a medium
pot three-quarters of the way up
with water and bring to a boil
over high heat. Poach the knotted
fillets over medium-low heat for
2 minutes, then remove with
a slotted spoon to a small bowl.
Slice a shallow V-cut cross (hanagiri;
see page 446) in the tops of the
shiitake. Drop into a small, shallow
bowl , sprinkle with the soy sauce,
and rub the soy sauce over the
shiitake to distribute. Tear the
chrysanthemum leaves from the
stems and slice crosswise into
2-inch (5 cm) pieces.
In a medium saucepan, combine
the fish broth and shiitake and bring
to a bare simmer over medium
heat. Place an otoshibuta [drop lid]
or piece of parchment on top of the
surface of the soup and cook until
the
shiitake are soft , about 5 minutes .
Prepare 6 small soup bowls and
place 2 herring knots, a piece of
yu zu zest , and a shiitoke cap in each
one. Drop the greens into the
barely simmering broth and cook
until wilted. Divide the greens
among the bowls, taste the soup for
added salt or a dash of soy sauce,
and ladle into the bowls. Serve
immediately.
JAPANESE EGG DROP SOUP
Adding beaten eggs to soup
increases its richness for a gorgeous
light meal.
In a medium pot, bring the chicken
broth to a simmer over medium­
high heat. Stir in the salt, sake,
and soy sauce and adjust the heat
to low . Whisk the eggs until frothy
and spoon gently onto the surface
of the soup, endeavoring to keep
them from sinking. Cook at a bare
simmer for 2 minutes, then ladle
into
4 donburi [deep soup bowls].
Squeeze the ginger to add a few
drops of ginger juice to each bowl
and garnish with the mitsuba.
Serve hot.

SOYBEAN SOUP
Using soy milk as the base for this
soybean soup makes it extra rich
with pr o tein . Double the recipe
and freeze for an instant dinne r
when you have no time to cook .
Soak th e soy beans overnight in a
generous amount of water. Drain.
Place the beans in a heavy pot and

inches
(ro cm) . Bring to a

and cook until soft, and the beans

In batch es, pulse the bean s, potato ,

or blend er with the salt and the

forms a smooth paste . Scrape into

Bring to a simmer , keeping it warm
until ready to serve , but taking care
not to scorch the bottom .
In a large frying pan , heat the olive

PORK AND MUSTARD
GREENS SOUP WITH MISO
Flavoring this casual soupy stew with

for a light dinner.
Massage the pork lightly with the

COLD PREVENTION SOUP
This textured chicken broth with
tofu and ham has restorative powers
when you feel like you're coming
down with a cold or the flu . Reheat
leftovers the following day for
lunch or a light supper.
In a medium pot, heat the chicken
broth and sake and season with
the salt. Slide in the smashed

low heat to soften the negi, about

This is a quick, rustic miso soup,
comforting in the late fall when the
weather begins to cool.
Grate the daikon on an oroshigane
0 apanese grating plate]. Squeeze

In medium saucepan , bring the

GINGER PORK AND
MUSTARD GREENS SOUP
Pork and mustard greens are iconic
in the American South, but are just
as delicious prepared withjapanese
flavors . This soup has a clarity
from the konbu base and the delicate
ginger flavoring .
Place the pork in a small bowl and
massage in the usukuchi sh'!Y" · Squeeze
the grated ginger into a small bowl
to extract the juice.
In a heavy medium pot or donabe
[flameproof earthenware casserole],
combine the konbu, salt, and 6½
cups (1. 5 liters) water. Bring to a
boil over high heat and slide in the
pork pieces , komatsuna, and ginger
juice. Cook until the komatsuna has
softened and the pork is no longer
pink, I-2 minutes. Pluck out the
konbu pieces and discard. Ladle
the soup into 6 bowls , sprinkle
with the black pepper , and serve
immediately.
TARO ROOT COUNTRY SOUP
The texture neba-neba, which can be
translated as "sticky" in English ,
is prized injapanese food. Taro
root and naga imo are two of those
naturally viscous foods and, when
simmered in a soup, soften to an
appealing creamy texture. Wear
rubber gloves when peeling and
cutting naga imo, or wash your hands
and forearms immediately with
hot water and soap after handling .
Prepare this soup in the late
autumn when root vegetables are
starting to appear and mushrooms
are still in their peak season.
Cut the taro and naga imo into
3/+-inch (2 cm) triangular chunks
(rangiri; see page 446). Quarter
the
carrot and daikon lengthwise. Slice
into ¼-inch (6 mm) quarter ­
rounds. With your nondominant
hand, hold the burdock above the
cutting board and use a sharp knife
to shave thin slices off the end of
it as you rotate it (sasagaki; see page
446), like sharpening the end
of
a stick. Drop the kon'!J'aku into a
wire-mesh sieve and the usuage into
another. Pour a steady stream of
boiling water over each sieve for

into ¾-inch (2 cm) squares .
Pour the dashi into a large heavy
pot and set over high heat. Slide
in the burdock , carrot, daikon, and
kon'!Yaku. After the dashi comes to a
boil , stir in the taro, naga imo, tofu ,
shiitake, shimeji, enoki, usuage, and negi.
Adjust the heat and cook at a lively
simmer until the vegetables and
mushrooms have softened , 10-15
minutes. Add the komatsuna and seri
in the last 2 minutes of cooking.
Remove
from the heat. Measure
the miso into a large ladle . Dip the
ladle into the soup to fill with dashi.
Whisk the miso and dashi together in
the ladle , stir into the soup, and
serve in large , donburi [deep soup
bowls] as a warming supper.

NAPA CABBAGE AND
SPINACH ROLLS
These are versatile little rolls . Serve
as is napped with soy sauce, por,zu,
or any Japanese dressing of your
choice. Or use in aJapanese soup
or nobe [one - pot dish].
Bring a medium pot of water to
a boil over high heat. Stack the
cabbage leaves and lower the stem
ends into the water for about
l minute , then submerge the
whole leaves in the boiling water
and coo k for 30 more secon ds.
Scoop the leaves out and slide
them into a colander to drain in
the kitchen sink .
Grasp the whole bunch of spinach
between two hands and lower
the stems into the boiling wat er.
Cook the stems for 30 seconds
to l minute , depending on how
thick they are . Drop the leaves into
th e water and blanch for 30 more
seconds. Scoop out with a sieve and
refresh under cold, running water
until cool to the touch . Align the
stem ends together and, gras ping
a quarter of the spinach at a tim e,
squeeze down the leaves to remove
excess water.
Set out a couple of baking sheets as
your workspace and patch together
two 7-inch (17 .5 cm) squares of
cabbage leaves , with the leaves all
po sitioned horizontally. Split
the spinach clumps in half , and
rearrange with half of the stems
at one end and half at the other.
Drape the spinach in a neat line
horizontally across the cabbage
square, about ¾ - inch (2 cm) up
from the bottom. Roll the cabbage
up into a tight roll . Squeeze gently ,
but firmly in
a clean tea towel ,
and let rest for 15 minutes before
cutting each roll crosswise into
6 pieces.
LAYERED NAPA CABBAGE
AND SPINACH
In stead of rolling the spinach in
the n apa cabbage ( Chinese le aO ,
as in the previous recipe, her e the

Salmon Nabe (page 356).
Bring a medium pot of water to
a boil over high heat. U sing tongs,
lower the napa cabbag e (Chinese
lea0 stem ends into the water and
cook for l minute , then su bmerge
the leaves in the boiling water
and cook for 30 seconds. Place the
leave s in a wire-mesh sieve
to drain.
Set up a bowl of cold water . Hold
the spinach stems in the boiling
water for 30 seconds, then
submerge the whole leave s for
another 30 seconds . Scoop out
with a wir e- mesh sieve and plunge
into the cold water to refre sh . Run
ext ra cold water , if needed .
Divid e the napa cabbage into
4 piles
equal in surface area, and
the spinach into 3 piles. Smooth a

the bottom of an 8-inch (20 cm)
square pan with removable bottom.
Do the same with a layer of spinach .
Repeat layering the cabbage and
spinach , ending with the cabbage .
Set the pan in the sink and pr ess

recipes.title: Miso-Stuffed Steamed Turnips Miso-Flavored Onion
recipes.transcription:

Cooking time , 15
to 20 min utes
Serves, 6
2 teaspoons gold
sesame seeds
6 medium turnips (1½ lb /685 g) ,
scrubbed and tops removed leaving
3/+ inch (2 cm) of stem
• 4 tablespoons
white or inaka miso
2 teaspoons
finely slivered yuzu peel

Cooking time, 15 minutes

a sma ll bite

g) small onions, halved and
thinly slice d
2 tablespoons

powder). optional
MISO-STUFFED
STEAMED TURNIPS
Miso and turnips pair well together
because of their complementary
flavors and textures. Sub stituting
inaka miso [country-style miso] for
the white miso will give you an
earthier result . Also, the leftovers
are delicious , co ld or warm .
In a small , dry frying pan , toast
the sesame seeds over medium heat
until fragrant, shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Slide into a
suribachi [grinding bowl) or spice
grinder and grind to a coar se
powder.
Turn the turnips on their sides
and slice off the tops about one ­
quarter of the way down from
the top to form a lid (try to keep
track of which top goes with which
turnip bottom). Scoop out the
inside of the turnip bottom to
form a receptacle for stuffing. Push
the scooped out turnip through
a coarse sieve (or pulse in a food
processor) and divide the smashed
turnip between two small bowls .
Fold half of the miso into one bowl
of smashed turnip and half into
the other. Mash theyuzu peel into
one bowl and the ground sesame
seeds and sesame oil into the
other. Spoon theyuzu miso into
3 of the scooped-out turnips and
the sesame miso into the remaining
turnips. Cover with the tops of the
turnips.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil. Arrange the stuffed
turn ips in the steamer basket ,
cover , and steam until softened
but not mushy when poked with
a bamboo skewer, 15-18 minutes.
Serve warm on individual ceramic
plates as a large appetizer .
@ p.189
MISO-FLAVORED ONION
Finding a well grown onion is
wor:th the effort for
this recipe.
The best way to tell the difference
between a large-scale grown onion
and a small , responsible farmer ­
grown onion is to taste them raw.
If the onion is unplea santly hot
or insistent, then maybe it is not
what you want to use in cooking
either . Mild , sweet onions yield
mild , sweet results . Negi (Japanese
leeks , an allium more similar to fat
scallions than Western leeks) sliced
into thin rounds can be substituted
for the onion. This dish works well
as a salty bite before dinner or
a condiment to a bowl of rice.
Strew the sliced onions in the
bottom of a heavy medium pot.
Dollop the miso on top of the
onions but do not mix , otherwise
the miso will burn. Cover the pot
and steam the onions over low
heat until they have released their
juices and have softened , but still
have a pleasant crunch, about 15
minutes. (Take care not to scorch
th e bottom . Using a flame retarder
could be advantageous.)
Stir the miso into the softened
onions and scrape into a bowl
for serving. Sprinkle with shichimi
togarashi, if you like .

recipes.title: Soy Milk Chawan Mush! Steamed Egg Custard Pots 190 Mushimono - Steamed
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking
time, 20 minutes
Serves,
6
I teaspoon fine sea salt
2 1/2 cups (20 fl oz/600 ml) best-quality
or homemade soy milk (see page 56)
• 2 eggs, beaten, at room temperature
• ½ cup (4 fl oz/125 ml) Konbu Dashi
(page 156)
· 3 oz
(75 g) sasami [chicken tenders] or
boneless, skinless chicken breast, cut into
1/2-inch (1 cm) cubes
6 ginkgo nuts, shelled and skinned
(see Note, page 202)
I small handful shimeji, torn apart
by hand
6 slices ('/e inch/3
mm) kamaboko
[fish cake]. halved crosswise, optional
I small handful mitsuba , cut crosswise
into ¾-inch (2 cm)
pieces
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time, 30 minutes
Serves: 6
I small lily bulb (optional), brown parts
pared off , separated into 12 "petals"
• ½ teaspoon fine sea salt
3 large sea scallops, quartered, or
6 small scallops , halved
• I tablespoon sake
5 oz (150 g) momendofu or Japanese­
style soft block tofu, cut into 6 pieces
3 large
shiitake , stems discarded and
caps quartered
I small handful mitsuba leaves, or
3 spinach leaves , cut crosswise into
I'/• -inch (3 cm) pieces
• 3 eggs, at room temperature
Generous 1¾ cups (15 fl oz/ 450 ml)
Katsuobushi
Dashi (page 156), at room
temperature
I teaspoon usukuchi shoyu, or
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
SOY MILK CHAWAN MUSH!
Using the best soy milk is extremely
important for this delicate dish so
be sure to use one without additives
or make homemade soy milk,
following the method in the recipe
for Tofu (page 56).
In a large glass measuring cup (jug)
with a spout, stir together the salt ,
soy milk, eggs, and dashi. Divide the
chicken, ginkgo nuts, shimeji, and
kamaboko among six 7 fl oz (200 ml)
chawan mushi or handleless teacups
(preferably with lids) . Pour 1/2 cup
(4 fl oz/120 ml) of the soy milk­
konbu dashi mixture into each cup ,
cover with the lid (or plastic wrap
[clingfilm]).
Set up a steamer and bring the
wat,;~ to
a boil. Arrange the chawan
mushi in the steamer basket , cover,
and steam for 15 minutes. Uncover ,
drop 1-2 pieces
of mitsuba on top of
each chawan mushi, replace the lids,
re-cover the steamer and steam
until set, about 5 more minutes.
[Q'I p.191
STEAMED EGG CUSTARD POTS
These savory egg custard pots take
more planning than actual work.
Prepare these when you have dashi
and scallops on hand for another
. dish
since you only need a small
amount for this recipe.
Bring a small saucepan of water to a
boil. Rub the lily bulb "petals" with
1/+ teaspoon of the fine sea salt
and blanch in the boiling water for
3 minutes.
Toss the scallop pieces with the sake
and remaining 'I• teaspoon of the
fine salt . Put I piece each of tofu in
the bottom of six 7 fl oz (200 ml)
chawan mushi or handleless teacups
with lids. Alternating between the
ingredients, drop the lily "petals,"
scallops , shiitake, and mitsuba into
each cup so that they are evenly
distributed.
In a bowl, whisk the eggs until well
emulsified , then slowly whisk in
the
dashi and usukuchi sh'!)'u, Pour the
egg mixture through a wire-mesh
sieve into a large glass measuring
cup (jug) with a spout. Pour the
mixture into the cups. Cover the
cups with their lids (or plastic wrap
[clingfilm]).
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil. Arrange the cups
in the steamer basket, cover, and
steam over medium-high heat for
about 25 minutes.
Serve warm.
