recipes.title: Spinach Gratin Sea Urchin-Glazed Flounder
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 15 minutes
Cooking time, 45 minutes
Serves,
6
ro½ oz (300 g) spinach
7 oz (200 g) potato , peeled and
halved lengthwise
3½ oz (100 g) lightly smoked bacon
• 2½ tablespoons (r¼ oz/35 g)
unsalted butter
• 3 '/,
tablespoons unbleached all­
purpose (plain) flour
2 cups
(16 fl oz / 500 mi) whole
milk
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 'I• teaspoon freshly ground
black pepper
I large tomato, halved lengthwise and
cut crosswise into ¼ - inch (6 mm)
half-moons
• 4 tablespoons
panko
Preparation time: IO minutes, including
IO minutes of salting time
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 4
2 flounder
or sole fillets
(about 4¾ oz/r35
g each), halved
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
I egg yolk, at room temperature
• 4 sea
urchin, sma shed
(about 2 tablespoons)
SPINACH GRATIN
In modern Japan , gratin has
come to mean a dish that is made
with a store-bought white sauce ,
which comes in a vacuum-packed
plastic envelope. But a homemade
bechamel sauce is easy to prepare,
and is the perfect medium for
spinach gratins-here the potato ,
tomato , and bacon add texture and
lusciousness .
Position a rack in the top third
of the oven and preheat to 400°F
(205°C/Gas Mark 6).
In a pot of well - salted boiling
water, blanch the spinach stems for
30 seconds , then drop in the leaves
and cook 30 seconds more . Scoop
out to drain. (Keep the water
boiling for the potatoes.) Once
cooled, squeeze the spinach down
the length of the greens and cut
crosswise into 2-inch (5 cm) pieces.
Slice the potatoes into 1/,-inch
(6
mm) half-moons and boil in
the salted water used for cooking
the spinach until just softened, but
not falling apart, about 2 minutes.
Drain.
Heat
a large frying pan over
medium-high heat and cook the
bacon until there is a bit of fat
rendering and coloring, but the
pieces are still not fully cooked ,
2-3 minutes . Cut crosswise into
r¼-inch (3 cm) pieces .
In a heavy medium saucepan, melt
the butter over medium heat until
bubbling . Add the flour and scrape
across the bottom of the pan with
a flat wooden spoon for 2 minutes
to cook the flour, taking care
not to brown. Whisk the milk in
slowly and gently simmer, stirring
occasionally, for IO minutes. Fold
in the spinach , potato, and bacon.
Season with the salt and pepper.
Scrape the mixture into a
7 x IO-inch (17 .5 x 25 cm)
oval
gratin dish . Smooth the top with a
rubber spatula, arrange the tomato
half-moons on top , and sprinkle
with the panko. Bake the gratin until
bubbling around the edges and the
panko is golden brown , about
25 minutes.
@ p.257
SEA URCHIN-GLAZED
FLOUNDER
This creamy sea urchin glaze makes
an elegant presentation and pairs
well with the soft-fleshed, mild
fish. This
is a great side dish .
Holding your hand 12 inches
(30
cm) above the fish, sprinkle
on
both sides with salt (this
ensures a light even coating). Let
sit IO minutes before blotting off
excess moisture with absorbent
paper towels.
In a small bowl , mash the egg
yolk into the sea urchin to make
a smooth paste (or whirl in a mini
food processor) .
Position a rack 6 inches (15 cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill).
Place the fish , skin
side down , on
a foil-lined rack set over a rimmed
baking sheet and broil (grill) for
I minute on each side. Brush
generously with the sea urchin/egg
sauce and cook I minute more on
each side. Brush 2 more times to
u se up the sauce and cook I more
minute on each side after brushing ,
until glossy and golden with
intermittent brown spotting. Serve
I fillet per person .
YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Foil-Grilled Garlic Foil-Grilled Crab And Eggplant
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time : IO minutes
Cooking time, 20 minutes
Serves, 4
2 tablespoons
canola (rapeseed) oil
I medium onion , halved lengthwise and
thinly sliced crosswise
• 4 shiitake,
stems dis carded and caps
thinly sliced
• 2 oz
(60 g) thinly sliced nonsmoky or
lightly smoked bacon, cut crosswise into
¾-inch (2 cm)
pieces
16 small garlic cloves, thinly sliced
lengthwise
1/+ teaspoon flaky sea salt
½ teaspoon freshly ground black
pepper
Preparation time, 15 minutes
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Serves, 6
I teaspoon canola (rapeseed) oil
• 9 oz (250 g)
mediumJapanese
eggplants (aubergines), stem ends
trimmed
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
4 1/, oz (120 g) fresh crabmeat, picked
over for shells and cartilage
• 2¼ oz
(75 g) shimeji
· 2 tablespoons
sake

¼ teaspoon ichimi togarashi [powdered
Japanese red chilel
FOIL-GRILLED GARLIC
An excellent afternoon snack, this Broil (grill) until the garlic
grilled garlic is quick to prepare has caramelized , the onion has
and goes equally well with Brown softened, and the bacon is sizzling,
Rice (page 291) or
on toast. about 5 minutes .
Position a rack 4 inches (IO cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill) .
Line a rimmed baking sheet with a
12- inch (30
cm) piece of foil and
smooth the oil evenly into a
IO - inch (25 cm)
circle in the
center of the foil . Strew the onions
onto the oil circle, followed by the
shiitake, then the bacon, finishing
with the garlic. Sprinkle with the
salt and pepper .
FOIL-GRILLED CRAB
AND EGGPLANT
Grilling food wrapped in foil is
an effective way to seal in juices
and needs only some sake to add a
delicate flavor and cook by steam.
Here a bare film of
oil is used so
this makes a light , fresh appetizer
in the summer . Any kind of
complementary mushroom can
be substituted for the shim~i.
Tear off six 12- inch (30 cm)
lengths of foil and line up across
your workspace . Lightly oil th e
center area of each piece of foil.
Shave off the sides of the eggplant
(aubergine) where it bulges out to
make the eggplant straight - sided ,
then halve the eggplant lengthwise
to make %-inch (I
cm) thick slabs .
Lay an eggplant slab in the center
of the oiled portion of each piece
of foil and sprinkle lightly with the
salt. Strew the crabmeat across each
slice of eggplant and top with
2 or 3
shim~i. Sprinkle I teaspoon sake, 1-2
drops
of usukuchi sh~u, and I pinch
of ichimi togarashi onto the shimeji and
fold the sides of the foil in to the
center. Bring the top and bottom
pieces together and roll down to
seal the packet.
Position a rack 6 inches (15 cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill) .
Set the foil packets on a rack set
over a rimmed baking sheet and
broil (grill) for 15 minutes .
Serve on salad plates and let each
person unwrap his or her packet
to get the full affect of the fragrant
steam wafting up.
YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Sweet Miso-Grilled Eggplant Grilled Natto Pouches
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves: 6
14 oz (400
g) medium Japanese
eggplants (aubergines), stem ends
trimmed
· I tablespoon gold sesame oil
2 tablespoons brown rice miso
• ½ tablespoon mirin
• ½ tablespoon sake
I tablespoon shiso chiffonade
(optional)
Preparation time, 15
minutes
Cooking time, 5
minutes
Serves: 4
2 packages (3 oz/85 g each) natto, well
aerated (see Note, page 436)
2 tablespoons finely chopped negi or
scallion (spring onion)
½ cup (11/• oz/35 g) chirimen jakko
[semi-dried
juvenile fishes]
• I tablespoon soy sauce
• 1/2 teaspoon mustard powder
6-inch (15 cm) piece tororo konbu
2 usuage
[deep-fried tofu pouches],
halved crosswise
SWEET MISO-GRILLED
EGGPLANT
Eggplant (aubergine) smothered in
sweet miso is a harbinger of summer.
When the eggplant is ripe, this
dish is a favorite to make over and
over. While typically fried, here the
eggplant is oil-grilled .
Shave off the sides of the eggplants
(aubergines) where it bulges out
to make it straight-sided, then
cut lengthwise into slabs ½ inch
(12 mm) thick.
Heat a cast - iron pan over medium ­
low heat. Brush the eggplant with
the sesame oil, add to the pan, and
cook, covered, for 2 minutes on
each side, until softened and brown
speckled.
Position a rack 4 inches (10 cm)
from the heat source
and preheat
the broiler (grill) .
In a small saucepan, whisk together
the miso, mirin, and sake and warm
briefly over low heat. Scrape into
a small bowl , cool for 5 minutes,
then fold
in the shiso, if using .
Transfer the eggplant pieces to a
rack set over a rimmed baking sheet
and spread the miso mixture across
the surface of the eggplant slices.
Broil (grill) until bubbling and
slightly glossy, about 3 minutes .
Serve hot or at room temperature.
GRILLED NATTO POUCHES
Grilling natto [fermented soybeans]
brings out some of its funky
characteristics , but the mild chirimen
jakko [tiny semi-dried fish] and
usuage [deep-fried tofu pouches]
provide a counterpoint. Serve for
breakfast or as a healthy snack with
a glass of beer in the afternoon .
In a bowl, stir together the natto,
negi, and chirimen jakko. In a small
bowl, whisk the soy sauce into the
mustard powder. Scrape into the
natto and mix well.
In a heavy frying pan , toast the
tororo konbu over low heat until it has
crisped up (turn once or twice).
Crumble into the natto.
Position a rack 4 inches (ro cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill).
Roll a wooden dowel across the
surface of each usuage half to aid
in separating the sides to make a
pocket. Stuff with the natto mixture,
secure by threading a toothpick
(cocktail stick) through the
opening. Place on a rack set over
a rimmed baking sheet and broil
(grill), turning once, until the
usuage is sizzling and lightly colored
in spots, about 2 minutes per side.
Alternatively, grill over low ember
coals.
259 YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Salt-Grilled Turban Shells Pine Needle-Grilled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 5 minutes
Cooking time: IO minutes
Serves: 4
4 fresh
turban shells
¼ teaspoon flaky sea salt
'I• teaspoon shichimi togarashi [seven­
spice powder), optional
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking
time: 20 minutes
Serves : 6
• I (1'/• lb/800 g) fresh snapper , cleaned
and scaled
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
7 oz (200 g) red or black headless,
unpeeled shrimp (prawns), about 6
• Small pebbles
• 2 large handfuls
long pine
needles, washed
6 vacuum-packed peeled chestnuts,
3 oz (90 g)
6 medium-to-large shiitake,
stems discarded
I teaspoon soy sauce
I yuzu or ½ Meyer lemon
SALT-GRILLED
TURBAN SHELLS
Grill freshly gathered turban shells
over a fire by the seaside for the
most wildly, rustic taste. In such
a case, the natural salt contained
in the seawater is all the flavoring
needed. Removing the grilled meat
from the shells can be a bit messy,
so lay some newspapers down for
this operation.
Position a rack 4 inches
(ro cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill).
Rinse the turban shells in cold,
running water and shake off exc ess
water. Sprinkle I pinch of salt into
each shell and place on a rack set
over a rimmed baking sheet . Broil
(grill) until sizzling and fragrant ,
about 8 minutes. If desired , pinch
a bit of shichimi togarashi into each
shell. Serve hot, I per person,
with an oyster fork to remove each
mollusk from its shell.
PINE NEEDLE-GRILLED
SNAPPER
Salt-grilling over a bed of pebbles
and pine needles is not an everyday
occasion . Make this dish when
company is coming. When you
open the top after baking, the
room will be filled with the heady
aroma of pine needles.
Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C/
Gas Mark
6).
Score a crosshatch pattern through
the skin of the fish with a
sharp
knife to allow
the flesh to cook
evenly. Massage with 1/2 teaspoon
of the salt. Snip through the back
shells of the shrimp (prawns) with
a pair of kitchen shears and remove
the veins.
Strew a layer of clean small pebbles
in the bottom of an oven proof
earthenware casserole . Make a bed
of pine branch tips on top of the
pebbles, moisten the pine needles
to prevent burning, and set the
snapper across the pine needles.
Nestle the shrimp, chestnuts, and
shiitake around the fish and sprinlcle
with the remaining ½ teaspoon
salt. Dribble in the soy sauce.
Cover and bake in the center of the
oven until the fish and shrimp have
cooked through, about 20 minutes.
Serve
from the casserole, but warn
the guests that the casserole is hot!
Eat with a squeeze of yuzu or Meyer
lemon juice.
YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Salt-Grilled Snapper Black Sesame-Grilled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation tim e , IO minutes
C o oking time , 20 minutes
Serves,
6
I (2 ¼ lb/r kg) snapper or sea bream ,
cleaned and scaled
I tablespoon flaky s ea salt
I yuzu, 2 sudachi, or ½ Meyer lemon ,
halved
Preparation time, 25 minutes
Cooking time, 5
minutes
Serves , 6
I lb (450 g) unpeeled, headless spot
prawns or Gulf shrimp , about 18
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 2 tablespoons
sake
I tablespoon black sesame seeds,
warmed in a small, dry frying pan
• Ponzu , for serving
SALT-GRILLED
Salt-grilling is an excellent method
to crisp up the skin and seal in the
fish juices,
leaving the flesh moist
and taut.
Rinse the fish inside
and out
under cold water, brushing off any
lingering pieces of gut tendrils from
the inside spine bone with a clean
toothbrush . Pat dry , including the
inside body cavity. Evenly sprinkle
about I teaspoon of the salt in the
cavity.
Thread two metal skewers through
the mouth of the fish, out
the back
at the collarbone, and back through
to the front between the bottom fin
and
tail. Rub the remaining 2 tea­
spoons
salt onto the skin of the fish ,
taking
care to be a bit more generous
on the tail and fin sections.
Light
the charcoal in an outdoor grill
(barbecue) and let reduce to ash­
covered embers . (Or position a rack
6 inches/r5 cm from the heat source
and preheat the broiler [grill].)
SNAPPER
Grill the fish over embers for
IO minutes on each side, until the
flesh is moist and flaky . Use the
metal skewers to help flip the fish .
(If cooking under the broiler,
suspend the fish over
a rimmed
baking sheet by resting the skewers
on the edges of the pan [or set a
rack inside of the pan and place
the fish on
the rack]. This will aid
maneuverability since the skin can
stick. Broil for
8-ro minutes on
each side .)
Trans fer to a large platter and
remove the skewers . Garnish with
the yuzu halves. The fish head
should
point to the left and the
belly should be directly in front of
your most honored guest. People
serve themselves as neatly as possible
using individual chopsticks .
BLACK SESAME-GRILLED
SPOT PRAWNS
Spot prawns and Gulf shrimp are
experiencing a revival as they have
become more readily available .
Avoid farmed prawns, if possible ,
since they are raised in water
pens that require heavy doses of
antibiotics to keep the prawns
healthy. This dish makes for a great
appetizer.
Snip through the back shell with
a
pair of kitchen scissors and slice
about halfway through the back
of the prawns with a sharp knife .
Remove the ve in, and butterfly ,
leaving the shells intact.
Cover a wire rack with foil and
place over a rimmed baking sheet.
Arrange the prawns , shell side
down, on top . Sprinkle the exposed
portion of the prawns with the salt
and leave for 5 minutes . Dribble
on
the sake and let sit for 5 more
minutes to absorb flavor.
Position a rack 4 inches (ro cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill).
Carefully strew the sesame seeds
evenly over the prawns and broil
(grill) for 2 minutes.
Flip, and
broil the shell side for 2 more
minutes.
Serve 3 shrimp per person, on
individual plates , with a small
saucer of ponzu on the side for
dipping .
YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Sweet Soy-Grilled Spanish Mackerel Mackerel Teriyaki
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minute s
Cooking time: IO minutes
Serves: 6
4 tablespoons soy
sauce
· 4 tabl espoo n s Katsuobushi
Dashi
(page 156)
• 4 tablespoons mirin
• 2 tablespoons
sake
I fre sh Spanish mackerel (1½ lb/
700 g), cleaned and filleted
• ¼ te aspoo n fine sea salt
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time , 20 minutes
Serves: 6
½ cup (4 fl oz/J25 ml) soy sauce
• ½ cup (4 fl oz/J25 ml) mirin
4 tablespoons finely
grated fresh
ginger , squeezed to make juice
I fresh mackerel (11/3 lb/600 g) , cleaned
and filleted
1/• teaspoon flaky sea salt
SWEET SOY-GRILLED
SPANISH MACKEREL
Unagi [river eel] is on the "avoi d "
list of the Monterey Bay Aquarium
Seafood Watch, so here Spanish
mackerel stands in for the traditional
unagi. Eating unagi in the summer is a
Japanese custom that dates from the
early nineteenth century . However,
the global appetite has depleted
the wild eel population. These
grilled fillets can be eaten as they
are, on rice, or on a salad.
Soak 12 thin bamboo skewers in
water for 20 minutes .
In a small saucepan, simmer the
soy sauce, dashi, mirin, and sake until
large bubbles form and the sauce
thickens and reduces by two-thirds,
about 3 minutes. Pour the sauce
into a small bowl to cool.
Rin se the mackerel fillets in
cold
water and pat dry. Cut in thirds
crosswise. Line a wire rack with foil.
Thread 2 bamboo
skewers lengthwise
through each fillet, I on either side
of the centerline. Holding your
hand 12 inches (30 cm) above the
fillets , sprinkle both sides with the
salt (to ensure a light, even coating).
Light the charcoal in an outdoor
grill (barbecue) and let reduce to
ash - covered embers . (Or position
a rack 6 inches/J5 cm from the
h eat source and preheat the broiler
[grill] .)
Brush the fillets with the sauce and
grill over embers, skin side up, for
2 minutes
(or under the broiler
skin side down). Brush again with
the sauce and grill for 2 more
minutes.
Flip , brush , and grill for
2 minutes,
skin side down, (or skin
side up under the broiler). Brush
again with the sauce and grill for
2 more minutes , until the
skin is
sizzling and browned .
Serve hot or at room temperature.
MACKEREL TERIYAKI
Oily fish do well with a terjyaki
glaze and this is a classic way to
pr epare mackerel. The alternative
to broiling here is to cook slowly
over charcoal embers in a shichirin
[brazier] .
In a small saucepan, bring the soy
sauce, mirin, and ginger juice to
a lively simmer over medium - low
heat and cook , swirling the pan,
for about IO minutes, until large
bubbles appear and the liquid has
reduced to a thick syrup-about a
quarter of the original amount.
Cut the mackerel fillets into thirds.
Holding your hand 12 inches
(30 cm)
above the fish, sprinkle
both sides with
the flaky salt (this
ensures a light even coating).
Po sition a rack 4 inches
(10 cm)
from the heat source and preheat
th e broiler (grill).
Lay a piece of foil over a wire rack
and set in a rimmed baking sheet.
Broil (grill) the mackerel for
I minute on each side , starting with
the skin side up. Remove from the
broiler and brush with the terjyaki
sauce on the flesh side . Broil for
I minute, flip, brush the skin side,
and broil I more minute. Repeat
the bru sh-and-broil method on
each side. Brush and broil each side
for 30 seconds more , ending with
the skin-side up .
Serve hot or at room temperature
on individual plates as part of a
Japanese meal.
YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Grilled Sesame Chicken Yakitori 266 Yakimono - Grilled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes, plus
45 minutes
marinating time
Cooking time: 20 minutes
Serves:
6
r teaspoon flaky sea salt
l½ lb (700 g) chicken breasts
· 4 tablespoons sake
3 tablespoons gold
or white
sesame seeds
2 tablespoons soy sauce
• l tablespoon mirin
½ tablespoon brown rice vinegar
• l tablespoon gold sesame oil
Preparation time: IO minutes , p1us
30 minutes marinating time
Cooking time : 15 minutes
Serves: 6
½ cup (4 fl oz/125 ml) soy sauce
• 4 tablespoons
mirin
· 4 tablespoons
sake
2 tablespoons
grated fresh ginger
r lb 2 oz (500 g) boneless chi cken
thigh, skin on, cut into %-inch
(2 cm) cubes
4 medium
negi or 12 fat scallions
(spring
onions), white and light green
parts only , cut crosswise into 3/•-inch
(2 cm) pieces
GRILLED SESAME CHICKEN
Sesame is a crucia) flavoring in
Japan and high-grade seeds are
hard to come by , though certainly
not impossible. Sourcing makes all
of the difference when approaching
simple dishes such as this one ,
so put some effort into finding
the
best choice within reach. Oils
should be bright and flavorful and
seeds should never be cracked or
discolored.
Rub the salt into the chicken breasts
and place in a quart -s ize (1 liter)
resealable food storage bag. Add the
sake and marinate for 15 minutes .
Meanwhile, in a small , dry frying
pan, toast the sesame seeds over
medium heat until fragrant,
shaking the pan and lifting off the
heat if needed to avoid scorching .
Transfer while still hot to a suribachi
[grinding bowl) or spice / nut
grinder and grind to a powder.
Stir in the soy sauce, mirin, and
rice vinegar.
YAKITORI
There are many sty les ofyakitori,
[grilled chicken on a stick] though
this sweet soy sauce-marinated
one with negi is arguably one of the
most classic ones. Slow grilling over
charcoal embers, with frequent
turning and basting, render these
skewers sublime, the broiler (grill)
method is more practical.
In a small saucepan, bring the soy
sauce , mirin, sake, and ginger to
a brisk simmer over medium-high
heat and cook until slightly syrupy
and reduced by half, about
7 minutes . Pour into a medium
bowl to cool.
Remove the chicken from the sake
m ari nade and place in a clean
resealable food storage bag with
the sesame mixture and marinate
30 minutes.
Light the charcoa l in an outdoor
grill (barbecue) and let reduce to
ash -co vered embers . (Or position
a rack 6 inches/r5 cm from the
heat source and preheat the broiler
[grill].)
Reserving the marinade, remove
the chicken and pat the pieces dry
with absorbent paper towels. Rub
the chicken with the sesame oil to
seal the meat. Brush lightly with the
marinade and grill until the meat
sizzles and the flesh firms up
with
just a little give when touched in the
middle, 15- 20 minutes , turning
and brushing as they cook . ( Or
if
broiling, arrange the breasts, skin
side down, on a wire rack set over a
rimmed baking sh eet and broil for
7 minutes on each side.) Let rest
for 5 minutes , then slice , and serve.
Once the marinade has cooled ,
add the chicken and negi pieces and
toss to distribute and marinate for
30 minutes
Position a rack 4 inches (IO cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill).
Reserving the marinade , thread the
chicken and negi onto metal skewers,
alternating them . Line the skewers
across a wire rack set over a rimmed
baking sheet. Broil (grill) for
7 minutes
on each side , brushing
periodically with the marinade .
266 YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Miso-Marinated Grilled Cod Grilled Duck Breast With Turnip
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 15 minutes, plus
4 hours curing time
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 6
½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
6 (3 oz/8 5 g each) cod fillets
• 3 tablespoons mirin
¾ cup (r8o g) inaka or white miso
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 4
4 small duck breasts (4 ½ oz/r2 5 g each)
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
ro½ oz (300 g) small turnips, with tops
· 2 medium
negi or 6 fat scallions
(spring onions) , cut at a diagonal, into
r½-inch (4 cm) pieces
MISO-MARINATED GRILLED COD
If cod is not available, yellowtail or
swordfish make good substitutes.
Salt the fillets on both sides and let
sit for IO minutes. While the fish is
salting,
whisk the mirin into the miso.
Pat the fillets dry with a clean tea
towel or absorbent paper towels.
Smear half of the
miso in a shallow
refrigerator container that will just
hold the fillets side by side. Spread
two layers of cheesecloth across the
miso and arrange the fillets on top
of the cloth. Lay another two layers
of cheesecloth across the
fish and
smooth it down flat. Spread the
remaining miso on top of the cloth
and press down gently to compact.
Cure in the refrigerator 4 hours.
The fish can
hold in the mash for
up to 2 days .
Position
a rack 6 inches (ro cm)
from the heat source and preheat
the broiler (grill) .
Remove the fish from
the
cheesecloth layers and wipe off
any miso that might have adhered
to the fish . Place,
skin side down,
on a rack set in a rimmed baking
sheet. Broil (grill) for 4 minutes on
each side. (Alternatively, grill over
charcoal embers for spectacular
results.) Serve hot or at room
temperature.
GRILLED DUCK BREAST
WITH TURNIP
Try to find small duck breasts since
they are more tender and milder
in flavor than larger ones. This
is good as an appetizer or part
of a full meal that includes other
vegetable dishes and some rice or
noodles. Duck breast should always
be cooked with the skin on, since
the skin protects the delicate meat
and also crisps up nicely.
Trim off the overhanging fat on
the duck breasts and score the
skin in a crosshatch pattern, only
cutting partially into the fat layer
and not all the way down to the
meat. Sprinkle both sides with
½ teaspoon of the salt.
Scrub the turnips and lop off their
tails and leaves, leaving ¾ inch
(2 cm)
of the stem. Save the tops
for another dish. Quarter the
turnips from stem to tail into
wedges. Fill a heavy (cast iron)
medium pot with water and bring
to a boil. Blanch the turnip wedges
for I minute. Scoop out and drain.
Discard the water.
Heat a cast-iron frying pan over
medium-high heat. Add the duck
skin side down, weight with the
heavy pot used to cook the turnips,
and sear for 2 minutes. Remove
the pot , flip the breasts, and cook
I minute more on the second side.
Remove the pan from the heat and
use a pair of tongs to place the
cooked breasts on a cutting board to
rest for 5 minutes.
Pour off the excess fat and return
the pan to medium heat. Drop in
the blanched turnips and the negi
and sprinkle with the remaining
½ teaspoon salt. Sear, turning with
the tongs , until evenly browned,
about 2 minutes .
Cut the duck into slices ¼ inch
(6 mm) thick and arrange
attractively on 6 individual salad
plates with the vegetables nudged
up next to the meat.

recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 25 minutes
Cooking
time: I5 minutes
Serve s, 4
ro½
oz (300 g) Japane se eggpl ants
(aubergines) , stem ends removed
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 5 oz (145 g)
piman or small gre en
pepper s , cut into quarter s or sixths
(d epending on the size of the pepper)

stems di scarded

cut crosswise into ½ inch (12 mm)
thick
slice s
r lb 2 oz (500 g) slightly marbled beef
sirloin steak , cut crosswise into slices
¼ inch (6 mm) thick
I tabl espoon canola (rapeseed) oil
• I tablespoon gold sesame oil
• Ponzu sauce, for serving
• Japanese Rice (page 291), for serving
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time: IO minutes
Serves: 6
2 ('l+ - inch / 2 cm)
pieces suet
· 3 bonele ss beef steaks (ro oz/
300 g each), r'/+ inches (3 cm) thick
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
24 shishito or padr6n peppers
• 12 shiitake ,
stem s discarded
2 medium
negi or 6 fat scallions
(spring onion) , cut crosswise into
I 1/2- inch (4 cm) pieces
• Ponzu, for serving
TEPPAN-YAKI
This is a fun , communal cooking
affair that tends to create a lot of
smoke , so be sure to open the win­
dows if cooking this indoor s. Give
each per son a small plate for their
meat and vegetables , a small saucer
for pon,,_u to dip, and a bowl of rice .
Trim the curved sides off both
sides of the eggplant (aubergine)
lengthwi se (to facilitate making
slices without surface skin) . Cut the
eggplant lengthwise into slabs ½
inch (12 mm)
thick. Toss with the
salt in a medium bowl and let sit for
IO minute s. Remove from the bowl ,
shake off any adhering salt crystals,
and blot off excess moisture with
absorbent paper towels.
Mound the eggplant ,
piman
U apanese green pepper]. sh ii take,
and cabbage on a large platter.
Arrange the sliced steak on a
dinner plate . Bring the v egetables,
meat , and pon,,_u to the table . Set
a cast-iron teppan-yaki or grill pan
on a portable tabletop burn er and
heat over low for 5 minutes.
Film 1/2 tablespoon each of the
canola (rapeseed) and sesame oil
on the pan, adjust the heat to
medium-high , and drop a handful
of each vegetabl e on the pan ,
keeping them s eparate. Using saibashi
[cooking chopsticks] or tongs,
turn the v egetables after about
2 minute s.
Let them sizzle for
about I minute longer before lay ing
several meat piece s directly on th e
pan surface (rather than over some
vegetables). If the vegetables are
almost ready, move to the edges
of the pan away from direct heat.
Each person should cook the meat
to his or her preference , 15-30
seconds on each side , depending on
desired doneness , and serve him o,r
herself
some vegetables along with
the meat. Dip, but don 't drench ,
th e cooked ingredients in the ponzu
sauce before eating . Serve with rice .
QUICK TEPPAN-YAKI
A cast - iron pan or grill pan
(griddle pan) is essential for
searing. If shishito or padr6n peppers
are not available , substitute with
a medium piman Uapanese green
pepper] quartered, per person.
In a large cast-iron frying pan
or grill pan (griddle pan) , melt I
piece of the suet over medium-low
heat. Lay the steaks on a plate
and salt lightly on both sides with
½ tea spoon of the salt.
Increase the heat to high and sear
the meat on both sides for
2 minute s for rare, or 3 minutes
for medium-rare. Transfer the
steaks immediately
to a large
cutting board .
Discard the used piece of suet,
replace with a new one, and set
the pan over medium heat. Once
the suet starts to melt, carefully
arrange the shishito, shiitake, and negi
in the pan , keeping them separate ­
each in their own area. Sprinkle
with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt
and sear slowly while the m eat rests ,
turning with a pair of tongs to allow
even b r owning until the vegetables
have softened and are cooked
through , 3 minutes
on each side .
To serve , cut the steaks cro sswise
into slices 1/2 inch ( 6 mm) thick.
Serve on salad plates with the seared
vegetables alongside. Pool a small
amount of pon,,_u for each person on
individual soy sauce plates . Dip a
corner of the meat and vegetables in
the pon,,_u before eating.

recipes.title: Okonomiyaki 272 Yakimono - Grilled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time: 20 minutes
Makes: 2 large pancakes
I (ro½ oz/300 g) boneless pork chop,
I¼ inches (3 cm) thick
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
2 tablespoons Worcestershire sauce
• 2 tablespoons tomato ketchup
r'h cups (7 oz/ 200 g) udon flour or
unbleached pastry flour
ro½ oz (300 g) green cabbage, cut
crosswise into fine threads
I medium negi or 3 fat scallions
(spring onions),
finely chopped
• 4 tablespoons sakura e bi
[small dried shrimp]
4 eggs, at room temperature
2 tablespoons canola (rapeseed) oil
• I tablespoon aonori
[powdered green nori]
2 tablespoons finely julienned
benishoga [pickled red ginger]
2 handfuls freshly shaved katsuobushi
or hanalcatsuo
2 tablespoons Japanese Mayonnaise
(optiorurl; page
32)
OKONOMIYAKI
Most popular in the area around
Osaka and Hiroshima, there are
myriad regional variations of these
jam-packed pancakes. Prepare
for a casual family meal , or have
a make-your-own party using a
portable tabletop burner. Feel free
to omit or substitute the pork or
dried shrimp.
Sprinkle the pork with ½ teaspoon
of the salt. In a small, heavy frying
pan, stand the pork up, fat side
down, while holding it upright
with a pair of tongs, and sear over
high heat for 30 seconds to render
the fat. Lay the chop down and
sear I minute on both sides. Cover
and cook over medium heat for
30 seconds more on each side.
Remove to a cutting board and let
rest 5 minutes . Then cut into fine
"sticks" .
In a small bowl, stir the
Worcestershire sauce and ketchup
together .
In a larg e bowl, whisk together the
flour and remaining ½ teaspoon
salt . Add the pork, cabbage , negi,
shrimp, and eggs using a pair of
saibashi [cooking chopsticks] . Slowly
mix in ½ cup (4 fl oz/125 mi) water
to
form a loose, chunky batter .
Heat 2 large
lightweight frying
pans over medium-low heat. Once
you can feel the heat rising from
the pans, add I tablespoon canola
(rapeseed) oil to each pan . Ladle
half of the batter into each pan,
smearing it around in a circular
motion to evenly distribute the
ingredients across the surface of
the pan . Cover and cook slowly
until the edges have dried a little
and the pancake is golden brown
on the bottom , about 8 minutes .
Steam will accumulate on the inside
of the lid , so take care to wipe the
water droplets off every once in
a while .
Invert a large dinner plate over a
pan and using two pot holders or
oven mitts (gloves) , flip the pan
upside down so the pancake is on
the plate . Then slide the pancake
back into the pan. Cook over
medium heat until cooked through
and the bottom is lightly browned,
about
4 more minutes. Repeat for
the second pancake.
Slide each okonomjyaki onto a larg e
clean plate . Smear each with
2 tablespoons
of the Worcestershire­
ketchup mixture (this takes the
place of okonomjyaki sauce), sprinkle
with ½ tablespoon aonori,
I tablespoon benishoga, and a handful
of katsuobushi. Squeeze a little
Japanese mayonnaise, if using,
over the top in a crosshatch or
wiggly pattern . Cut into wedges
and serve hot.
272 YAKIMONO - GRILLED

recipes.title: Hittsumi One-Pot Seafood Udon 277 Menrui - Noodles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time , 30 minutes, plus
2 hours
resting time
Cooking time, 10-15 minutes
Serves, 6
1% cups (8¾ oz/250 g)
udon flour
• l pinch fine sea salt
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, 15 minutes
- Serves,
6
½ lb (225 g) maitake
7 oz (200 g) spinach
5 ½ cups (45 fl
oz/ r. 32 liters)
Hot
Noodle Broth (Kaketsuyu , page 157)
• Udon (page 280) or l lb 2 oz (500 g)
dried udon noodles, cooked according to
the package directions
• 12 large shrimp (prawns), peeled
and deveined
• 4 thin
negi or 6 fat scallions (spring
onions), cut crosswise into 1½-inch
(3 cm) pieces
7 oz (200 g) fresh crabmeat, picked
over for shells and cartilage
• Ponzu (optional)
HITTSUMI
Called hittsumi in Iwate prefecture,
the basic preparation for these
dumplings is found all over
Japan. Although the shape
varies by region , th e dumplings
are commonly eaten in hearty
country vegetable soups. They are
equally good as a bed for a cold
summer salad (Summer Salad with
Dumpling s, page 68). This is a
great group cooking experience
if you have some able hands at
the ready.
Measure the flour and salt into a
medium bowl. Work in ½ cup
(4 fl
oz/ 125 ml) warm water to form
a stiff, yet pliable d o ugh. Knead the
dough for about 100 turns , drop
into a reseal able food storage bag,
and let rest for at least 2 hours.
(The dough can be made the night
before .)
Fill a large , wide pot with water and
bring to a boil over high heat. Fill a
large bowl with cold water and place
near the pot of boiling water.
Working quickly, pinch off a
small piece of dough and flatten
it into a 4-inch (10 cm) square
about ¼-inch (6 mm) thin. Tear
off small ragged pieces of dough
(roughly ¾-inch /2 cm strips),
dropping them into the pot as you
go. Continue dropping the flat
pieces of dough into the boiling
water , but do not crowd. Once
the dough pieces bob back up to
the surface of the water , cook for
3-5 minutes more before fishing
them
out and sliding into the bowl
of cold water. Drain and shake off
before using.
ONE-POT SEAFOOD UDON
A cross between nabe (one-pot dish)
and udon, unusually, this dish is
baked in the oven .
Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C/
Gas Mark 5) .
Slice the ends off of the maitake and
break into pieces about the size of
the shrimp . Slice the spinach stems
into 3/+- inch (2 cm) pieces and the
leaves into 1½-inch (4 cm) pieces .
In
a medium donabe [flameproof
casserole] or Dutch oven
(casserole), heat the broth over
medium-high heat. Add the
cooked
udon, shrimp (prawns),
maitake, and negi. Cover and bake
for IO minutes . Remove from the
oven, stir in the crab and spinach,
cover, and return to the oven for
5 minutes .
Serve in 6 large, donburi [de ep
soup bowls] , distributing all of the
ingredients evenly. Splash in a little
pom:.u to taste, if desired.
277 MENRUI - NOODLES

chicken thighs, cut the into ½-inch
(12 mm) cubes
• 7 oz (200 g) medium-thick negi or
9 fat scallions (spring onions), cut
crosswise, into ¾-inch (2 cm) pieces
2% oz
(75 g) shimeji, bottoms sliced
off, broken apart
7 oz (200 g) dried udon noodles,
cooked according to the package
directions
Shichimi togarashi [seven-spice
powder], optional
ONE-POT CHICKEN WITH UDON
The clams add a depth to this
warming
nabe. Serve on a cold
winter night when you have
company to help . Substitute dried
udon if you want to save a little time,
though using homemade makes a
big difference.
Scrub the clams and soak in a bowl
with 5 cups (42 fl
oz/1.25 liters)
cold water and the fine sea
salt for
I hour. Drain and flush with several
changes of cold water to get rid of
the sand. Scoop out of the water
and place in a wire-mesh sieve
to drain .
Make the udon and cook according
to the recipe directions. Leave in
the bowl of cold water until ready
to use .
In a small bowl, toss the chicken
pieces with the flaky salt, then the
sake. In a small pitcher, stir together
the dashi, soy sauce , and mirin.
Pour 3 1h cups (27 fl oz/800 mi)
of
the seasoned dashi into a donabe
[flameproof earthenware casserole]
or enameled cast-iron pot and heat
over medium heat on a portable
tabletop burner.
Drain the
udon, place on a dinner
plate , and take to the table. Put the
clams in a bowl and arrange the
chicken, shiitake, and cabbage and
spinach rolls on a platter. Bring the
bowl with the clams and the platter
to the table with the negi, ponzu, and
a bowl for discarded clamshells.
Give each person a small bowl for
eating the nabe. Put about half of
each ingredient into the casserole ,
each in its own place, and cook at a
brisk simmer over medium heat for
about 5 minutes. Ladle out some
of each ingredient, along with the
broth, into the small bowls and
season with a dash of ponzu and a
sprinkle of negi. Eat hot. Once all
of the first half of ingredients have
been served, replenish with the
remaining dashi and ingredients and
cook and serve .
UDON WITH CHICKEN
AND NEGI
Using Hot Noodle Broth (page
157) instead of chicken broth makes
this dish possible to be assembled
on the fly when in a hurry.
In a medium pot, heat the broth
over medium-high heat. Add the
chicken, negi, and shimeji and once
the soup returns to a simmer ,
adjust to medium heat and cook
until the negi and mushrooms have
softened and the chicken is cooked
through, 3-5 minutes .
Divide
the cooked udon among 6
large, donburi [deep soup bowls],
portion out the soup, sprinkle with
shichimi togarashi (if using) , and serve .

recipes.title: Nikomi Udon Suigyoza 279 Menrui - Noodles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time , 5 minutes
Cooking time, 5
minutes
Serves, 6
Udon (page 280)
Hearty Japanese broth-based soup ,
Sweet Potato Country Soup (page 168) or
"Raccoon Dog " Soup (page 172)
Preparation
time, 30 minutes, plus
30 minutes resting time
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Makes , 20
l cup (150 g) unbleached bread
(strong) flour
IO oz (300 g) finely ground
(minced) pork
½ tablespoon potato starch
2% oz (75 g) Japanese cucumber,
finely chopped
3 tablespoons
finely chopped negi or
scallions (spring onions)
l tablespoon finely chopped
fresh ginger
I egg, at room temperature
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
½ teaspoon freshly ground
black pepper
I tablespoon gold sesame oil
• Soy sauce, for serving
• Rice vinegar, for serving
Rayu [red chile oil], for serving
NIKOMI UDON
Nikomi udon (simmered udon) is
the ultimate Japanese farmhouse
comfort food, and can be reheated
and eaten over the course of a few
days. Hittsumi (page 277) can be
used in place of the homemade udon
because they inflate and melt in
the same way , but don't substitute
dried udon here. If the soup you
select (see ingredients) is thickened
with potato starch , omit it , as the
noodles will add starch to the soup.
SUIGYOZA
Suigyo{ll [dumplings] are typically
stuffed with pork and shrimp ,
but here they are lighter and
juicier, thanks to the addition of
cucumber. You will find homemade
gyoza to be chewier than those made
from store-bought wrappers,
but this gives them an appealing
heartiness .
Measure the flour into a medium
bowl and slowly incorporate ½ cup
(4 fl oz/ 125 ml) water.
Knead on a
well-floured board until the dough
achieves the soft give of an earlobe .
(Depending on weather and flour,
you might need to add more flour.)
Cover with a dampened non­
terrycloth towel and leave to rest for
30 minutes .
Place the pork in a bowl and sift
the potato starch over it. Add
the cucumber, negi, ginger, egg,
salt , pepper , and sesame oil and
mix thoroughly until all of the
ingredients are distributed and the
meat is a well-amalgamated mass.
On a floured work surface, roll the
dough into a log with a 2-inch
(5 cm) diameter. Cut the dough
into I 1/•-inch (3 cm) pieces with
a pastry scraper or pizza cutter.
Roll the dough pieces out into
thin rounds 4 inches (ro cm) in
diameter. Flour lightly, and line
up on your work space.
Cook and cool the udon according
to the recipe. Place the soup in a
saucepan. Drain the noodles and
slide into the soup. Simmer to heat
up , then ladle into large donburi
[deep soup bowls] to serve.
Place one wrapper in the palm of
your hand and spoon I tablespoon
of the filling onto the center of the
dough . Dip an index finger into
cold water, and wet the perimeter
of the dough round. Pull the edges
of the dough round up so they meet
in the center over the filling. Close
the dumpling by folding over the
front flap to make 1/•-inch (5
mm)
pleats at 11•-inch (5
mm) intervals,
while pressing the pleated front
side to the smooth backside to make
a well-sealed dumpling. (If this
technique eludes you, no need to
obsess , just wet the inside edges and
press closed to make a smooth half
moon dumpling.)
Bring a large pot of water to a
boil over high heat. Drop the
suigyoza into the pot and cook until
they bob back up to the surface,
5-7 minutes. Cook for 5-7 more
minutes , then scoop out into
individual small bowls with a bit
of the simmering water .
Give each person a small dish for
mixing their own dipping sauce,
about equal parts soy sauce and
vinegar , with a drizzle of r'!Yu.

recipes.title: Island Somen With Red Chile And Garlic Chives Udon
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, IO minutes
Cooking time, I minute
Serves, 6
33/• cups (30 fl oz/900 mi) Iriko Dashi
(page 157)
½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
• 1/.+ teaspoon soy sauce

japones , sliced into fine rounds

ISLAND SOMEN WITH RED
CHILE AND GARLIC CHIVES
Somen noodles are the quintessential
summer food and are all about
the aromatics you serve alongside.
Typical garnishes include any of
the following, slivered cucumber,
ginger, ":!)logo, finely chopped
scallions (spring onions), thin egg
threads, shiso, and nori. OnAmami
Oshima, an island between Kyushu
and Okinawa in Southern Japan,
they prepare
,omen with only a few
garnishes, but the result is bright
and flavorful. Somen can be served
with either warm or cold broth­
here it is warm . Be sure to use two
whole charlic chives, not just two leaves.
In a saucepan , warm the dashi and
season with the salt and soy sauce.
UDON
Although hand-rolled udon
might seem intimidating to the
uninitiated, it is a fairly easy noodle
to make at home . Nonetheless, you
will achieve the best results if you
use a noodle rolling machine. Serve
with the dipping sauce of your
choice or slide into the leftovers of
a nabe (page 349) for a last filling
bite .
In a bowl, whisk the salt into the
flour and mix in ½ cup
(4 fl oz/ 120 ml)
water with a pair
of saibashi [cooking chopsticks].
Once the dough becomes too
difficult to mix, switch to your
hands . Knead on a lightly floured
board, dropping in a little more
water if necessary , to form a stiff ,
smooth dough. Knead for a total
of 10-15 minutes to activate the
gluten. Wet a non-terrycloth tea
towel, squeeze dry , and wrap around
the dough . Let rest for 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, fill a large pot with hot
water and bring to a boil.
(To compensate for the blandness
of the noodles, the dashi should
be a touch saltier than you would
normally make it.) Keep warm. Or
if it is summer and you' re serving
the noodles cold, chill the
dashi.
In a pot of boiling water, cook
the somen for I minute. Drain and
refresh in icy water .
Drop a dollop of noodles into
each of 6 round bowls, ladle in the
warm broth, sprinkle with I pinch
of chile , and a scattering of garlic
chives. Serve immediately.
Flatten the dough into a disk,
sprinkle both sides lightly with
flour, and roll out to a rectangle
1/1• inch (2 mm) thick. Slice into
noodles % inch (r cm) wide and
toss with some flour. Alternatively,
u se a seimenki [noodle-rolling
machine] or a pasta machine.
Place 2 large
bowls in the kitchen
sink and fill with cold water. Cook
the noodles in 2 batches,
Toss half
of the noodles into the boiling
water and gently agitate to separate
the noodles. Boil for 2 minutes,
scoop
out with a bamboo noodle
scooper or wire-mesh sieve, and
plunge into the first bowl of cold
water. Swish around to cool, then
scoop out and drop into the second
bowl of cold water. (If the water
in either bowl has warmed , run
cold water in to cool.) Repeat with
remaining noodles.
Scoop each batch of udon onto
a z.aru [bamboo noodle basket]
lined with a dinner plate , or
swirled into three piles directly
on the dinner plate .

recipes.title: Spinach And Udon Soup Five-Color Udon Menrui - Noodles
recipes.transcription:

Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves,
6
3 eggs, at room temperature

(400 g) spinach

finely sliced

chrysanthemum greens] or spinach
5¼ oz
(150 g) thin negi or 5 fat
scallions
(spring onions)

Generous 4 cups (33 fl oz / 990 ml) Hot

Broth (Kaketsuyu, page 157)

caps quartered

cooked according to the directions on

red chile], for serving
SPINACH AND UDON SOUP
Spinach came to Japan from China
during the Muromachi period
(1336 - 1573), and this soup has its
roots in China as well. The chicken
_ soup
and egg lend richness to this
quick noodle soup. Spinach is the
dominant ingredient with small
amount of
udon to add a bit of
starch. Fresh eggs are impossible
to peel , so cutting through the
shell and scooping them out makes
swift work of this onerous task .
Conversely, old eggs peel easily.
Bring a small saucepan of water
to a boil. Add the eggs and cook
until just set , but not runny,
8 minutes . Cool completely under
cold, running water. Slice in half
(through the shell) with a sharp
knife and scoop out the egg halves
with a spoon .
In a separate large pot of boiling
water, cook the spinach for
l minute, refresh under cold
running water, then squeeze dry.
Cut crosswise into thirds.
In the same pot of boiling water,
cook the udon according to the
package directions. Rinse in a large
bowl of cold water .
To serve, portion out the udon into
6 large donburi [deep soup bowls].
Top each bowl with the spinach and
½egg.Pour the hot chicken broth
into the bowl and sprinkle with 1-
2 pinches
of salt and shichimi togarashi
or black pepper, if desired. Serve
immediately.
FIVE-COLOR UDON
-- - Using top - quality dried udon or
soba noodles makes this an excellent
quick and easy supper when you are
busy. Preparing these with fresh
Udon (page 280), however, will
make this a truly gorgeous meal.
Cut the pork , shungiku, and negi
crosswise into ¾-inch (2 cm)
pieces . Cut the carrot into 1/-te-inch
(6 mm) half- or quarter-rounds,
depending on the thickness of its
diameter.
In a heavy medium pot, heat the
broth over high heat. Add the negi,
carrot, and shiitake. Reduce the heat
to medium-high and cook at a
brisk simmer until softened, about
3 minutes.
Stir in the pork and
shungiku and cook for l additional
minute.
Portion the cooked udon noodles
into 6 large donburi [deep soup
bowls] and ladle the hot soup over
the noodles . Serve immediately,
sprinkled with ichimi togarashi.

recipes.title: Ramen Menrui - Noodles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 2 hours plus
30 minutes resting time
Cooking time , 2 hours
15 minutes
Serves, 6
For the broth,
4 bone-in,
skin-on chicken thighs
(1½ lb/675 g total)
2 small carrots, cut into
1¼-inch
(3 cm) lengths
7 oz (200 g) small negi or fat scallions

Brown rice miso

8 minutes , refreshed, peeled, and halved
lengthwise
· I sheet nori, cut into sixths

RAMEN
lnjapan, there are ramen shops
in every town. However , here
is a home-style ramen recipe for
those who want to try making it
themselves .
Make the broth,
Position a rack in the center of
the oven and preheat to 450°F
(230°C/Gas Mark 8).
In a large bowl , toss the chicken ,
carrots, negi, and ginger with the
salt. Rub with the sesame oil and
dump onto a rimmed baking sheet.
Roast for 35 minutes until nicely
browned .
Scrape the roasted chicken and
vegetables into a large heavy pot
and add 4 quarts
(4 liters) cold
water. Bring almost to a boil over
high heat, reduce to a simmer , and
cook, covered, for I hour.
Scoop out the chicken thighs and
shred the meat off the bones into
a medium bowl. Wet the chicken
meat with a small scoop of broth .
Return the bones to the pot and
continue simmering the broth,
uncovered, for 30 minutes. Strain
into a clean medium pot and
discard the bones and vegetables.
Meanwhile , make the noodles,
Place the flour in a large bowl
and drizzle in the sesame oil. Mix
with your fingers until
pebbly .
Make a well and break in the whole
eggs and yolks. Mix with your
fingers until the eggs and
flour
are incorporated, but the dough
is still a bit crumbly . Turn out
onto a work surface and knead
until smooth and pliable , about
5 minutes. Let the dough rest for
at least 30 minutes.
Roll the dough out using a seimenki
[no od le -rolling machine] or Italian
pasta machine . Then cut the dough
into thin noodles 1/s inch (3 mm)
wide. Cut those noodles crosswise
into 9-inch (22 cm) lengths with
a pizza cutter. Sprinkle the noodles
generously with flour and toss
the flour into th e noodles , to help
prevent sticking, but keep the
noodles aligned.
Fill a large pot three-quarters full
of water and bring to a boil over
high heat.
Bring the broth to a simmer over
medium-high heat and adjust to
a bare simmer . Prepare 6 large
donburi [deep soup bowls]. Measure
in one salt flavoring of choice
per bowl, 2 tablespoons miso, 4
teaspoons soy sauce, or 3/+ teaspoon
salt. Whisk 4 table spoons broth
into
each bowl to emulsify the
flavoring.
Add the noodles to the boiling
water and cook for 2 minutes.
While
the noodles are cooking, add
about I½ cups (12 fl oz/350 ml)
broth into each bowl and whisk to
combine with the flavoring liquid.
Drain the noodles and divide the
noodles among the bowls. Working
quickly (so the broth does not
cool), keeping each ingredient
in its own area, add 2 heaping
tablespoons chicken
meat ,
2 heaping
tablespoons greens,
½ tablespoon negi, an egg half , and
a small piece of nori. If desired, add
spice with rcryu (for soy sauce ramen),
y= kosho (for salt ramen) or shichimi
togarashi (for miso ramen).

recipes.title: Soba 286 Menrui - Noodles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Serves: 6
2% cups
(14 oz/400 g) soba ko [fine
buckwheat
flour]
% cup
(3 1/2 oz/Joo g) unbleached
all-purpose
(plain) flour
l cup (3'h oz/J50 g) uchiko flour
or potato starch, for dusting

onion), for serving (optional)
Finely grated fresh wasabi, for serving
(optional)
SOBA
This recipe and method for nihachi­
style soba was graciously shared by
Sonoko Sakai, a Los Angeles-based
soba "guru" who has dedicated
the last several years to perfecting
her craft and to improving the
buckwheat flour in the United
States. Nihachi-style soba contains
8 parts soba ko (fine buckwheat
flour)
and 2 parts
all-purpose
(plain) flour.
In a large bowl, combine the soba
ko and all-purpose (plain) flour
with your fingers . For the water ,
you will need 45-50 percent of
the total weight of the flours:
For 500 g (17 1/2 oz) flour, that
translates to 225 - 250 g (8 - 9 oz)
water , which is a generous ¾-I cup
(7-8½ fl oz/210-250 ml) . Measure
the maximum amount into a cup /
jug with a pour spout.
Sprinkle ¾ cup plus 2 tablespoons
(7
fl oz/210 ml) of the water over
the flours in the bowl and scissor
your fingers through the dough
until crumbly. Press the dough
together with both hands to form a
rough ball and transfer it to a large,
flat work surface . Knead the dough
until smooth and pliable , about
5 minutes. This will take some
elbow grease because the dough will
be stiff, but don ' t flag or lose heart.
Depending on the weather and the
flours , the dough might want a bit
more moisture . If the dough feels
dry or continues to have cracks, dip
your fingertips in the remaining
water and rub it around the dough.
Continue kneading and adding
water , if needed, until the dough
achieves the desired consistency.
Form the dough into a disk ½ inch
(12 mm) thick and sprinkle with a
small amount of uchiko flour. Using
a long , thin rolling pin or dowel,
roll the dough back and forth from
the center into a rectangle 1/16 inch
(r.5 mm) thick . Dust the dough
and work surface generously with
the uchiko flour and flip the dough
to make sure it is well covered in
the flour.
Fold the dough in halflengthwise,
then in half again to form a long
thin folded log. With a
fine, sharp
knife , cut
into thin noodles
1/ 1• inch (r.5 mm) wide. Dust the
noodles with more of the uchiko,
making sure some of the flour
gets between the noodle strands
to prevent them from sticking
together . If not cooking right away,
gently gather handfuls of noodles
and align straight in a wooden
or plastic container. Cover and
refrigerate up to
2 days.
Fill
a large pot three-quarters
of the way with water and bring to
a rolling boil over high heat.
Prepare a large bowl of cold water
in the sink and a medium bowl of
ice water.
Gather the soba noodles up gently
in two hands and drop into the
boiling water. As soon as the water
returns to a boil, cook for
60-90 seconds, depending on
thickness. Scoop out the noodles
and plunge into the bowl of cold
water . Rinse under cold running
water for several minutes to remove
starch. Scoop the soba out of the
water with a wire-mesh sieve and
dip the sieve in and out of the bowl
of ice water to shock. Shake off and
serve with noodle dipping broth ,
chopped negi, and a dab of freshly
grated wasabi, or with one of the
soba soups in this chapter.

OSAKA KITSUNE SOBA
This traditional dish can be made
with either soba or udon noodles .
Here dried noodles are specified,
but fresh noodles are also an option.
Place the usuage in a wire-mesh
sieve . Pour a steady stream of
boiling water over them for
IO seconds to remove oil odors .
Cut the usuage crosswise into strips
¼ inch (6 mm) wide. Reserving
the soaking liquid , pluck out the
shiitake, discard the stems, and and
thickly slice the caps.
In a medium pot, heat the broth

to avoid adding the sediment at

JAPANESE CHICKEN
NOODLE SOUP
This soup comes together quickly
if you have chicken stock in the
freezer . It is good to serve to
someone who is feeling poorly.
In a soup pot, bring the chicken
broth to a simmer over medium­
high heat. Stir in the soy sauce, salt,
shiitake, and chicken . Reduce the
heat to medium-low and cook for
5 minutes at a gentle simmer.
Divide the cooked udon among
4 large donburi [deep soup bowls]
and ladle in the soup. Garnish with
the scallions (spring onions), chile,
and yuzu zest.

JAPANESE RICE
The unit of measure for rice is a
go, which i s 6 fl oz/180 ml , and
h ere the recipe is for 3 -go (18 fl
oz/54 0 ml) of rice. Whil e the go
measurement is still used in Japan
in certain applications, most
modern Japanese use a 200-ml
cup (about 7 fl oz). Nonetheles s,
the go measurement is quite handy,
as it is measured using calibrated
wooden boxes useful for scooping,
in unit s of 1-go, 3- go, 5-go , IO-go.
Sometimes the old way is bett er
than the new .

BROWN RICE
Brown rice is not as popular in
Japan a s abroad, but it is slowly
gaining ground.
Rinse the rice in a medium h eavy

with 2½ cups (20 fl oz/600 ml)
SUSHI RICE
Japanese rice is often labeled "sushi

SCATTERED SUSHI
Prepared for festive days, chirashi zushi
is a form of deconstructed su shi
where the ingredients are scattered
over the surface of the sushi rice,
rather than rolled together inside
a sheet of nori. In its most glorious
rendition, chirashi zushi involve s many
different ingredients. Simplify by
selecting a handful of the treatments
below. Breaking down this recipe is
th e key to rendering it less daunting.
Prepare the rice: Wash the rice
according to the directions in
Japanese Rice (page 291) ; drain.
Place in a heavy
medium pot and
add the konbu dashi. Soak for 20
minutes.
In a small bowl, combine
th e vinegar , sugar, and salt .
Meanwhile, prepare the vegetables,
In a small saucepan, combine

katsuobushi dashi, I tablespoon of the
mirin, and 'I• teaspoon of the salt
and bring to a lively simmer. Add
the carrot and cook until the liquid

Massage ½
teaspoon of the salt into

Thinly

In a small pan of boiling salted

l-2 minutes , depending on
their

(5 fl oz/r50 ml) of the katsuobushi

to a simmer. Add in the beans and
cook for I minute . Remove the

spoon, slice on the bias into

In a small saucepan, combine the
remaining% cup (5 fl oz/150 ml)

and the remaining ½ tablespoon
mirin and bring to a rolling boil
over high heat. Add the bamboo

Make
the egg threads, Beat the
eggs with a fork until emulsified
but not frothy . Stir in the mirin and
salt. In a large frying pan, heat
l teaspoon oil over medium heat,
until shimmering. Pour in a third
of the egg mixture, and swirl it
around to achieve an even coating.
Cook for l minute, flip, and cook
for 30 seconds. Turn out onto a
board to cool. Repeat twice with the
remaining oil and eggs. Once cool ,
roll up like cigars and cut cro sswise
into 'I• inch (6 mm) wide ribbons.
Toss to separate.
Cook the rice, Cook and rest
the rice according to the general
directions for Japanese Rice (page
291), but adjust the cooking
time.
The rice will take 3 minutes to boil
and cooks for 8 minutes on low
heat. Turn out into a handai [flat
wooden tub] or onto a large wooden
cutting board , and spread out while
wafting with an uchiwa [flat paper
fan] or piece of cardboard. Sprinkle
the flavored rice vinegar as you cut,
turn , spread, and waft until all of
the vinegar has been incorporated
and the rice is barely warm and is
shiny but not wet. Spread in the
handai or on a large round serving
platter at least 1'/• inches (3
cm) deep .
Assemble the dish: Starting with
the nori threads, strew the nori,
shiitake, kanJ!Yo, bamboo shoot,
carrot , egg, benishoga, and green
beans . Cover until ready to serve
family-style . Each person should
cut off portions of the sushi using
their chopsticks . Best the same day,
though fine the next if kept at
a
cool ambient temperature.

recipes.title: Salad Sushi Go Han - Rice
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, I hour
Cooking time, 30
minutes
Serves, 6
I lily bulb , brown parts pared off ,
"petals " separated
2 dried
shiitake , soaked in boiling water
for 30 minutes
½ cup (4 fl oz/125 ml) Konbu Dashi
(page 156)
2 tablespoons soy sauce
• I tablespoon mirin
I usuage [deep-fried tofu pouch],
halved lengthwise
• Boiling water
• I tablespoon gold sesame oil
¼ Kyoto - style orange-red carrot
or I small carrot (2 % oz/ 7 5 g) , finely
julienned
• 'I• cup (6 fl oz/r8o ml) sake
• I teaspoon fine sea salt
r'I• oz (50 g) small lotus root , sliced
into thin half-rounds, and soaked in a
small bowl of water with a splash of rice
vinegar
• I'I• oz (50 g) thin burdock root ,
scrubbed and finely julienned,
and
soaked in a small bowl of water with
a splash of vinegar
• 12 ginkgo nuts, shelled and skinned
(see Note, page 202)
3 vacuum-packed,
peeled chestnuts, cut
into slices 1/• inch (6 mm) wide
· Japanese Rice (page 291), aerated and
cooled
to room temperature

toasted in a small, dry frying pan
I handful mitsuba , cut crosswise into
'/•-inch (2 cm) pieces
SALAD SUSHI
This dish takes some time to
prepare, because there are a lot
of ingredients. Nonetheless, the
result is worth the effort. Doubling
or tripling the recipe will not
add much time , except for the
julienning operation. This is a
great dish to bring to a friend's
house as it holds up at room
temperature for several hours.
In a small pan of lightly salted
water boiling water, blanch the
lily "petals " for
I minute . Refresh
under cold , running water
and drain .
Drain the shiitake, remove and
discard the stems, and thinly slice
the caps. In a saucepan, combine
the shiitake, dashi, soy sauce, and mirin
and simmer for about 2 minutes
to absorb flavor. Remove from the
heat and cool in the simmering
liquid.
Place the usuage in a wire-mesh sieve
and pour a steady stream of boiling
water over it for IO seconds. Cut
crosswise into julienne strips and
blot dry in a clean tea towel.
Heat a large frying pan over
medium-high heat. When the
heat starts to rise from the surface
of the pan, add the sesame oil.
Stir-fry the carrot until it starts
to soften, I minute. Splash in
4 tablespoons
of the sake and
½ teaspoon of the salt and stir -
fry for I more minute . Scoop the
carrot out of the simmering liquid
with a wire-mesh sieve and slip into
a medium bowl.
GO HAN - RICE
Add the lotus root to the same
simmering liquid and stir-fry
until glossy and the liquid has
evaporated, I minute . Add
4 tablespoons sake and the
remaining ½ teaspoon of salt and
stir-fry for I more minute. Scoop
out the lotus root with a wire-mesh
sieve and slide into the bowl with
the carrots.
Add the burdock and stir-fry in
the remaining simmering juices
until sizzling and the liquid has
evaporated, I minute. Splash in
the remaining 4 tablespoons
of
sake and stir-fry over high heat for
I more minute until the liquid has
evaporated . Scrape the burdock
into the bowl with the carrots and
lotus root. Toss in the lily "petals ,"
simmered shiitake, usuage, ginkgo
nuts , and chestnut. Cool to room
temperature, about
15 minutes.
In
a large serving bowl, cut the
cooled ingredients in the medium
bowl into the cooled rice with
a rice paddle or a wooden spoon.
Fold in the sesame seeds and mitsuba
and serve .

recipes.title: Sour Plum-Scattered Sushi Fish Sauce-Grilled Rice Balls
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time , 35 minutes
Cooking time, I minute
Serves, 6
½ tablespoon fine sea salt
2% oz (75 g) shungiku [edible
chrysanthemum
greens]
· 4 oz (n5 g) daikon, scrubbed and
finely julienned
•
I large pinch flaky sea salt

pitted and finely chopped
• Japanese
Rice (page 29I) ,
aerated and cooled

warmed in a small dry frying pan , and
slightly smashed in a suribachi [grinding
bowl] or nut grinder
• ½ teaspoon anori
[powdered green nori]
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Makes, 9 rice
balls
2 tablespoons Japanese fish sauce
(preferably anchovy
or mackerel ishiri;
or sandfish shottsuru)
· Japanese Rice (page 29I)

in
a small, dry pan until fragrant

• Gold

SOUR PLUM-SCATTERED SUSHI
Chirashi zushi [scattered sushi] is not
just about the balance of flavors ,
but also about the colors in the dish
and commonly involves vibrant
yellow egg threads and surimi [hot ­
pink imitation crabmeat]. Here
the sushi rice is "vinegarized" by
umeboshi [salted sour plum]-rather
than vinegar, sugar, and salt-giving
the rice a gentle yet puckery base.
The colors of the dish make an
attractive addition to the table .
Fill a medium pot three-quarters
full of water, bring to a boil , add
the fine sea
salt, and hold the
shungiku stems in the boiling water
until they have softened, about
I minute. Push down the greens to
blanch for 30 seconds more. Scoop
out with a wire-mesh sieve and
plunge in a bowl of cold water to
refresh. Pick up the greens by their
stem ends and squeeze down to the
tip of the leaves to remove excess
water. Squeeze again in absorbent
paper towels, then lay on a cutting
board and finely chop.
Place
the julienned daikon in a
medium bowl and massage in the
flaky sea salt. Let sit for
IO minutes , lift out the daikon from
any lingering salt, and squeeze
lightly before laying on absorbent
paper towels to absorb any
remaining moisture.
Cut the chopped umeboshi into the
cooked rice with a rice paddle
or a wooden spoon, until well
incorporated and the rice is evenly
colored. Smooth the rice in a
¾-inch (2 cm) layer onto a large
plate. Strew the surface evenly with
the chopped shungiku. Scatter the
julienned daikon on top , followed by
the sesame seeds, and finally
a dusting of aonori.
To serve, cut down to the bottom
of the plate and use a spatula to
remove sections (to show all the
layers) onto small plates .
[QJ p .295
FISH SAUCE-GRILLED
RICE BALLS
Slow-grilling over charcoal embers
is the key to these warm rice balls
that have just a hint of the fish sauce.
Sprinkle
the fish sauce
across the
surface of the rice and cut in with
a rice paddle or a wooden spoon
to incorporate. Fold in the sesame
seeds and katsuobushi until evenly
distributed .
Form 9 triangular rice balls, Wet
the palms of your hands and scoop
up% cup (3 3/+ oz/no g) rice. Place
the rice in your nondominant hand
and cup your hand to form the
bottom of the rice ball.
294 COHAN - RICE
Cup your dominant
hand crosswise
on top to form the top of the
triangle. Press gently , but firmly ,
taking
care not to over compress
the rice.
Grill over charcoal embers on a
shichirin U apan ese charcoal brazier]
or in a small amount of gold
sesame oil in a cast - iron pan over
low heat , until crisped on all sides,
7-8 minutes.
Eat warm.

recipes.title: Pressed Sushi Rice With Daikon Greens Cohan - Rice
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 30 minutes
Weighting time, 15 minutes
Serves, 4-6
2% oz
(75 g) Japanese cucumber,
julienned
¼ teaspoon fine sea salt
• Sushi Rice (page 291)
• Rice vinegar, for shaping the sushi
½ lb (125 g) fresh crabmeat, picked
over for shells and cartilage
· Egg Threads (page 2 2
2)

finely chopped
fresh chives

2 tablespoons
white sesame seeds
• Soy sauce, for dipping
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 6
3 1/2 oz (100 g) young daikon greens
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
2 tablespoons
white sesame seeds,
warmed in a small, dry frying pan
2 ½ cups (1 lb / 450 g) Japanese Rice
(page 291)
2 tablespoons
finely snipped

PRESSED SUSHI
Pressed sushi is prepared like chirashi
zushi [Scattered Sushi , page 292),
but is then pressed. The rice is
packed in a form, such as a square
pan with a removable bottom, and
after the toppings are scattered
over the rice , a weight is added to
compact. This makes the rice easier
to cut, and thus convenient as part
of a light summer lunch.
Toss the cucumber with the salt and
let sit for 5 minutes. Squeeze gently
and drop into a small bowl.
Line the bottom of an 8-inch
(20 em) square cake pan with a
removable bottom with a piece of
parchment paper. Spoon half of
the rice into the cake pan. Pour a
little rice vinegar into a small howl ,
dip your fingers into the vinegar ,
and gently spread the rice across the
bottom of the pan to make an even
layer . Strew half of the cucumber,
crab, egg threads, chives, ginger,
and sesame seeds evenly over the
rice, taking care not to neglect
the edges and corners. Wetting
your fingers again in the vinegar,
press and spread the remaining
rice into the pan. Strew the
remaining ingredients over the top
layer of rice and spread a layer of
parchment paper across the surface.
Set another 8-inch (20 cm) square
pan or two 8 x
4-inch (20
x IO cm)
loaf pans on top of the rice, weight
with a medium frying pan, and
leave at room temperature for
15 minutes.
Remove the weights, run a sharp
knife dipped in rice vinegar around
the sides , and unmold. Wet the
knife with vinegar again and cut
into 16 pieces. Transfer the pieces
to a pretty platter, leaving the
parchment paper liner behind.
Pour a small pool of soy sauce into
a saucer and serve on the side for
dipping.
RICE WITH DAIKON GREENS
Tender young daikon greens appear
at farmers markets in Japan in
the late spring when the farmers
are thinning their young daikon in
the fields. Folding boiled greens
into rice results in a quick and
healthy one-dish lunch , and the
vibrant colors make for a stunning
presentation. Substitute turnip
greens if you cannot find the
daikon variety.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil
over high heat. Lower the daikon
stem ends into the water (do not
let go) for a count of 20, then
submerge the greens in the boiling
water and cook for 90 seconds
more. (If using tender young
greens, blanch for I minute, until
soft.) Drain and refresh under cold
running water. Align the stem ends
COHAN - RICE
and
squeeze down the length of the
greens, from the ends to the tips
to remove excess water . Lay out on
a cutting board and finely chop.
Squeeze one more time by handfuls
and drop into a medium bowl.
Toss with the salt. (The greens are
intentionally salty to balance against
the white rice, but you could cut
the salt to 3/• teaspoon if you prefer
a slightly less salty palate.)
Fold the salted greens and warmed
sesame seeds into freshly cooked
rice. Mound into 6 small rice
bowls and strew with nori threads.
Serve hot.

ROLLED SARDINE SUSHI
Traditionally, farm wives made sushi
rolls for special occasions, though
fewer and fewer do today. Here a
simple filling of chopped fish with
grated
ginger and scallions (spring
onions) makes for quickly executed
and well-balanced sushi rolls. Horse
mackerel fillets or anchovies can be

Cut or pinch off the heads of the
fish (depending
on size) and tear
down toward the belly and pull out

and pat dry on a tea towel. Pull

crosswise into a fine dice.
Chop

Lay a sheet of nori shiny side down
with the striations horizontally
oriented on a makisu [bamboo
rolling mat]. Set up a bowl with
CURRY RICE
In Japan , the cut of meat used in
curry rice is komagiri-thinly cut pork
from the shoulder area with some
fat on the edges. Ask the butcher
to machine-slice pork shoulder or
butt meat that has some fat on it.
Cut the pork slices crosswise into
1½-inch (4 cm) strips.
In a medium heavy pot, heat the
oils over medium heat until hot
but not smoking. Slide in the pork
and stir - fry for
I-2 minutes, then
add the onion and cook, stirring,
until the pork has browned and the

5 minutes. Stir in the ginger in the
last minute or two before the pork
and onions are done.
GOHAN - RICE
the vinegar. Dip your fingers in
the vinegar and spread a layer
of sushi rice ½ inch (12 mm)
deep
on the surface of the nori ,
starting ½ inch (12 mm)
in from
the top edge of the nori. Spoon
an even line of one-quarter of

the rice
about 3/+ inch (2 cm)
up from the

finger with
rice vinegar and brush

with
the bamboo rolling mat.
Continue rolling and secure with

Rub
rice vinegar on the blade of a

in half, then each half into thirds.
Serve as is or with soy sauce for

Add the broth and deglaze the pan .
Bring to a boil over high heat,

Add the potato starch mixture,

Serve hot on top of a bed of
Japanese rice. The curry rice heats

recipes.title: Seki Han Go Han - Rice
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes , plus
overnight soaking
Cooking time: 55 minutes
Serves, 6
½ cup (3¾ oz/no g) dried azuki beans
• 3¾ cups (2 lb/900 g) mochi gome
[glutinous/sweet rice]
• I tablespoon flaky sea salt
4 tablespoons black sesame seeds
SEKI HAN
Sekihan [sticky rice with red beans) is
a celebratory dish made for special
holidays, though sadly it is prepared
less and less in modern Japan. Most
people buy it ready made, and the
rice has been colored pink with
artificial dye . While it is possible to
come up with some sort of serving
substitute for the traditional
lacquer boxes, it would not seem
quite right.
Start the day before serving. Soak
the beans in a medium saucepan
with plenty of cold water for I hour.
Drain , return to the saucepan, and
add cold water to cover the beans
by 2 inches (5 cm). Bring to a boil
over medium-high heat, adjust to
a gentle simmer, and cook for 15
minutes, until half cooked. Reserve
the simmering liquid, drain the
beans. Store the half - cooked
beans in the refrigerator. Set the
simmering liquid aside to cool.
Scrub the rice to dislodge bran
and wash in several changes of cold
water until the water runs clear.
Drain. Place the rice in a bowl and
add the cooled bean simmering
liquid. Leave overnight to allow
the rice to become infused with the
pink bean liquid.
The following day, drain the rice
and mix in the half-cooked beans.
Line a steamer basket with a large
piece of muslin cloth. Scrape the
rice and beans onto the cloth,
spreading them out evenly. The
rice will be at least
2 inches (5 cm)
deep. Fold the ends of the cloth
into the center, but leave a small
bit of the center of the rice peeking
out. Poke your finger into the
center about I-inch
(2.5 cm) down
to make a guide to check how much
the rice has inflated as it cooks.
GO HAN - RICE
Set up the steamer over a large pot
of water and bring the water to a
boil. Add the steamer basket, cover ,
and steam for 15 minutes. Uncover
and sprinkle a little cold water on
the surface of the rice. Rewrap,
leaving a center steam gap, cover,
and cook for 15 minutes more.
Repeat the water sprinkle step and
cook IO more minutes .
Once cooked , dump the rice into
a handai [wide wooden tub) or large
wooden board, scraping off any
lingering grains of rice from the
cheesecloth. Spread the rice out
to cool.
In a small, dry frying pan, toast
the salt and sesame seeds over low
heat until the sesame is fragrant.
Immediately slide into a small bowl
to stop the cooking process.
Pack the cooled rice into a stacking
lacquer boxes, if you have them.
Serve sprinkled with the sesame
salt. Lasts for
I or 2 days at room
temperature. Do not refrigerate .

BAMBOO RICE
If fresh bamboo shoots are
available, by all means use them.
Otherwise, vacuum-packed bamboo
shoots are a handy substitute. Keeps
for a day or so at room temperature
and leftovers make tasty rice balls
for a quick meal on the go.
Wash the rice according to the
directions in Japanese Rice (page
291) . Drain. Quarter the bamboo

into 1/+-inch (6 mm) quarter­
moons (itchogiri; see page 446). If

Vibrant green peas against snowy

If possible , use small red-skinned

garlic-a June crop-steadily starts
to deteriorate . Take the time to

have artificial additives. This can
accompany any Japanese meal.

until cooked through but not

serve in small rice bowls .

Cook the rice and garlic, rest, and
fluff following the directions for
Japanese Rice (page 291) . Fold in
the salted red or fresh green shiso.
Serve mounded in small rice bowls.

Tiny young sansho leaves appear on
the tips of sansho trees and sansho
bushes in the spring and have a
hauntingly indescribable flavor.
They are starting to become
available inJapanese and upscale
grocery stores outside of Japan, and

Japanese dishes. You can also grow
them in your garden or at home.

SHISO-PERFUMED RICE
Shiso leaves and buds pair well with

warm summer evening.
Position a rack 4 inches (ro cm)

Place the salmon fillets on a rack set

(grill) for 4 minutes

until fully cooked and the oils have

Massage the salt lightly into the

In

The fried daikon cubes add juicy

This homespun one-dish meal

In a medium frying pan, heat the

YUZU RICE WITH MITSUBA
Yuzu and mitsuba (a bright herb ,
ubiquitous to many Japanese dishes
such as chawan mushi and soups) are
both stars on the Japanese flavor
palette. They should be available at
Japanese or upscale grocery stores
now that chefs are using them
regularly in Western-as well as
Japanese-cooking.
Wash, drain, and soak the rice
according to directions for
Japanese Rice (page 291). Add the
konbu and cook as directed.

razor-sharp knife and cut into thin
strips. Then cut crosswise into
fine dice.

the rice has finished cooking,
let

fluffing with a rice paddle or a
wooden spoon. Fold in theyuzu
zest, mitsuba, and salt. Serve hot in
individual rice bowls.
YUZU RICE WITH NANOHANA
This seemingly modern dish
dates back to the Edo period
(1603-1868). In early spring,
as the winter greens go to seed,
flowering nanohana (brassicas similar
to broccoli rabe/rapini) dot the
fields in
our area. At this time the
yuz:u starts to lose its juiciness, but
its zest still remains flavorful. The
black sesame seeds add contrasting
color, so be sure not to skip. Serve
with a simple supper of grilled
fish or
meat and a salad or pickle
side dish.
Wash and soak the rice according
to the directions for Japanese
Rice (page 291), but remove
4 tablespoons of
the soaking water
and replace with the soy sauce and
sake. Cook per the directions.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil
over high heat. Lower the nanohana
stem ends into the water (do not
let go) for a count of 30, then
submerge the greens in the boiling
water and cook until softened, but
not mushy , another 2-3 minutes.

transfer to
a bowl.
Pare off the zest from theyuzu with
a razor sharp knife and slice the zest
into fine slivers.
Juice theyuzu and
strain the juice. Mix theyuzu zest
and juice, and sesame seeds into
the chopped nanohana until all of the
ingredients are well incorporated.
Once the rice has cooked and
rested for 5 minutes, fold in the
nanohana mixture. Serve hot.

Ginger has a long history inJapan
