made from cooked rice (as in this
recipe) , whereas ok'!Jlu is made from
uncooked (see Machi Porridge ,
page 312). You will need to think
ahead and dry daikon leaves in the
sun until completely desiccated­
they are also used in Dried Daikon
Leaf Fried Rice (page 312), so good
to have in the pantry.
Measure 2 cups (16
fl oz/500 ml)
water into
a heavy medium pot and
drop in the konbu. Soak for
30 minutes until softened, then
snip or slice into thin strips.
Stir the konbu strips back into the
soaking water with the usukuchi sh'!)lu
and sake. Rinse the chilled cooked
rice with cold water, shake off,
and dump into a medium heavy
pot. Stir the seasoned konbu water
slowly into the pot, while breaking
up the lumps and stir in the dried
daikon leaves . Bring to a simmer
over medium - low heat and cook ,
stirring, until creamy and risotto­
like, about 20 minutes . Serve
immediately
in individual rice
bowls and sprinkle with salt , if you
feel it needs it.
GINGER-SOY CHICKEN
RICE BOWL
Ju st about any leftovers can be put
on top of rice and called donburi,
but the best candidates are grilled
dishes such as Yakitori (page 266)
or simmered egg dishes such as
Dashi - Flavored Eggwith Garlic
Chives (page 42).
In
a medium bowl , whisk together
the soy sauce , mirin, ginger, and
garlic. Slip in the chicken, making
sure all sides are submerged.
Let marinate for 15 minutes .
Reserving the marinade, remove
the chicken and pat dry with
absorbent paper towels .
In a large frying pan , heat both oils
over medium heat until shimmering
but not smoking. Carefully place
the thighs in the pan , skin side
down, taking care to avoid any
sputters or jumping droplets.
Reduce the heat to medium-low,
and cook for 5 minutes.,
Flip the
thighs , and cook 7 minutes
more
on the other side. Immediately
314 GO HAN - RICE
adjust the heat to low if the chicken
is blackening or browning too
quickly. Transfer to a cutting board
to rest for 5 minutes
before halving
lengthwise and cutting crosswise
into slices 1/3 inch (1 cm) wide.
Meanwhile, in a medium saucepan,
heat the dashi over medium - high
heat. Add the peas and cook
for 1-3 minutes , depending on
freshness. Scoop out with a wire­
mesh sieve and slide into a small
bowl. Add the reserved marinade
to the dashi and bring to a lively
simmer , about 2 minutes, until the
liquid is reduced by half .
To serve , mound the rice into
6 large donburi [deep soup bowls].
Arrange the chicken pieces in two
small rows on top of the rice , strew
in some peas, and ladle over the
seasoned dashi. Scatter with torn
mitsuba leaves, if desired, and serve .

recipes.title: Katsudon Go Han - Rice
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Cooking time: 15 minutes
Serves:
6
I lb 2 oz (550 g) pork cutlets, 3/• inch
(1 cm) thick
3 tablespoons unbleached all-purpose
(plain) flour
6 eggs, at room temperature
• I cup panko (2 ½ oz/75 g)
4 tablespoons canola
(rapeseed) oil
• 2 ½ cups (20 fl oz/600 ml)
Katsuobushi Dashi (page 156)
• 4 tablespoons soy
sauce
• 2 tablespoons mirin
2 medium onions , halved lengthwise
and sliced into ¼-inch (6 mm)
half-rounds
I tablespoon finely slivered fresh ginger
· Japanese Rice (page 291) , for
serving
KATSUDON
Though it is easy injapan to buy
katsu [fried pork cutlets]-which
makes this dish a snap-the quality
of katsu varies greatly, so homemade
is really best.
Lay out two pieces of parchment
paper across your work surface
and sprinkle with a small amount
of water. Arrange the pork cutlets
on one of the pieces of paper and
top with the other, water-side
down. Lightly whack with a meat
tenderizer to soften , but not
flatten. Sift the flour on top of the
pork. Flop the cutlets around a
little to make sure that both sides
are floured and shake off.
Whisk 2 of
the eggs in a shallow
bowl and set it next to the pork .
Pour some of the panko o nto a
medium dinner plate and place that
next to the eggs. Coat each cutlet
with panko by using one hand for
dipping in the egg and the other
for dredging in the panko. Line up
the cutlets on a clean baking sheet
as yo u go.
In a heavy frying pan, heat the oil
over medium heat. Once hot, fry
the cutlets until golden brown
on the outside but still not quite
cooked through in the middle,
about 2 minutes per side . Drain on
severa l thickness of absorbent paper
towels. Cut each cutlet crosswise ,
at a slight diagonal, into 2~inch
(5
cm) slices.
GO HAN - RICE
In a large clean frying pan, bring
the dashi, soy sauce, mirin, onions,
and ginger to a lively simmer over
medium-high heat. Cook until the
liquid has reduced by half, about
7 minutes. Slide a wide kitchen
knife under the sliced cutlets and
place side by side into the frying
pan. The liquid should only come
one-quarter of the way up to the
top of the cutlets.
Whisk the remaining 4 eggs
until
partially emulsified , swir l across
the surface of the cut let s, cover ,
and cook over medium-high heat
until the eggs have set , but remain
runny in spots, about 45 seconds to
I minute.
Scoop rice into 6 large donburi [de ep
soup bowls] and spoon the katsu,
egg , and simmering liquids on top
of the rice.

recipes.title: Shrimp And Pea Rice Oyakodon Gohan - Rice
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 6
2 tablespoons
canola (rapeseed) oil
• I medium onion, diced
I tablespoon finely chopped
fresh ginger
I cup (4½ oz/r25 g) fresh green peas
• 5'/• oz
(150 g) cooked small
bay shrimp (prawns)
• Japanese Rice (page 291)
• I large pinch flaky sea salt
• I tablespoon usukuchi shoyu
• 4 tablespoons
tomato ketchup
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes
Serves, 6
'I• teaspoon flaky sea salt
½ lb (225 g) boneless, skinless chicken
thigh, cut into ½-inch (12 mm)
cubes
• 2 tablespoons
sake
• I tablespoon finely slivered fresh ginger
· 2 ½
cups (20 fl oz/600 ml)
Katsuobushi
Dashi (page 156)
• 4 tablespoons
soy sauce
• 2 tablespoons
mirin
4 3/• oz (135 g) negi or fat scallions
(spring onions) , cut crosswise into
¾-inch (2 cm) lengths
• 4 eggs,
at room temperature
· Japanese Rice (page 291), for serving
lchimi togarashi [powderedjapanese
red chile] , optional
SHRIMP AND PEA RICE
A vehicle to use up leftovers , h<!Jashi
rice is said to have developed in
the southern island of Japan in
the port city of Kita Kyushu . The
owner of a casual eatery needed to
feed his customers quickly before
they boarded the ship , so he put
together this flavorful ketchup­
based rice dish. While chicken is
commonly used in this dish, here
the shrimp reflects the seaside
roots. Feel free to swap out diced
leftover chicken or pork . In the
same vein , any chopped vegetables
such as carrot, green beans, or
turnips can be substituted for the
green peas.
In a large wok, heat ½ tablespoon
of the oil over medium heat. Add
the onion and ginger and stir-fry
until starting to soften. Add the
peas and cook , tossing with two
OYAKODON
Oyakodon inJapanese means
"parent - child rice bowl, " a word
play on a recipe where both the
chicken and the egg are the stars.
This dish-a favorite with Japanese
children-comes together quickly .
Massage the salt into the chicken
and toss with the
sake and ginger .
In a large frying pan , bring the
dashi, soy sauce , and mirin to a
simmer. Cook for about 3 minutes
to concentrate the seasonings and
reduce the liquids by half. Add
the negi and chicken ginger mixture
and simmer, swirling the pan ,
until the chicken and negi are
cooked through to their centers,
3-5 minutes.
GOHAN - RICE
flat wooden spatulas , for 2 minutes.
Scrape into a small bowl, making
sure to get all of the onion and
ginger pieces out or they will
burn. Stir the shrimp (prawns)
into the peas and onion.
Add the remaining r½ tablespoons
oil to the wok and heat over
medium heat. Dump in the rice
and stir-fry until heated through ,
about 5 minutes. Sprinkle in the
salt and drizzle the usukuchi sh'!Yu
over the rice , toss once or twice,
and spoon in the ketchup. Stir-
fry over low heat to distribute the
ketchup until the rice is evenly
colored pink. Toss the shrimp
and pea mixture into the rice and
serve hot.
Whisk the eggs, but leave some of
the whites visible. Swirl the whisked
eggs over the surface of the chicken
and negi, cover, and cook over low
heat until the egg has partially set,
but still has runny portions,
1-2 minutes.
Mound the cooked rice into
6 large donburi [deep soup bowls]
and ladle the cooked chicken and
egg over the rice . Sprinkle with
ichimi togarashi, if desired, and serve
immediately.
Note, This makes great leftovers,
but the dish tastes best if the egg
is freshly cooked. So if you think
you won't eat this in one sitting, set
aside some of the seasoned chicken
and negi, as well as the number of
eggs you'll need, then complete the
dish when you 're ready to enjoy the
leftovers .

recipes.title: Mustard And Vinegar­ Pickled Eggplant Mustard-Pickled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Pickling
time: 8 hours
Makes: r lb (450 g)
17½ oz
(500 g) mediumJapanese
eggplants (aubergines) , stem ends
trimmed
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
I t ablespoon mustard powder
3 tablespoons rice vinegar
· 3 tabl espoons mirin
3 tablespoons
soy sauc e
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time: 30 seconds
Pickling time: 2 hours
Serves : 4
2 large
handfuls seri Uapanese wild
parsley] or mitsuba
I teaspoon mustard powder
• 2 tablespoons
rice vinegar
• I tablespoon mirin
• I tablespoon usukuchi shoyu
MUSTARD AND VINEGAR­
PICKLED EGGPLANT
The addition of vinegar gives
this version of mustard - pickl ed
eggplant (aubergine) a gentle
acidity. Serve as part of a mix ed
pickle plate that includ es pickles
made from several different
pickling methods to create balance
on the plate. Pickles go well with
any Japanese meal or drinks before
dinner.
Slice the eggplants (aubergine s)
crosswise into ¾ - inch (2 cm)
rounds.
Dr op the eggplant into a
medium bowl and sprinkle with the
salt. Stir gently and leave for
IO minutes.
In a small bowl, whisk I teaspoon
water into the mustard , then whisk
in the vinegar , mirin, and soy sauce.
Lift the eggplant out of the bowl ,
leaving any salt crystals behind
and blot the rounds dry in a clean
tea towel. Wipe out the bowl and
return the eggplant pieces to the
bowl or a small ceramic pot. Toss
with the mustard mixture and set
an otoshibuta [drop lid] or plate on
top. Place a I-lb (500 g) weight
on top and leave in a cool place
for
8 hours. (Alternatively, use
a tsukemonoyoki U apanes e pickling
pres s].) Use
within I-2 days , but
keep
refrigerated.
MUSTARD-PICKLED
JAPANESE PARSLEY
The heat of the mustard matches
the brightness of the seri U apanese
wild parsley] and
these spicy pi ckled
greens go well with grilled food.
Hold the seri by the tops with a pair
of tongs and dip the roots into
a pot of boiling salted water for
20 seconds. Plunge
the seri in and
out of the boiling water and refresh
in a large bowl of cold water. Scoop
out with a wire-mesh sieve and
shake off excess water. Blot dry in
a clean tea towel, cut crosswise into
1½ -inch (4 cm) pieces, and drop
into a quart - size resealable food
storage bag.
In a small bowl, blend together the
mustard powder, vinegar , mirin, and
usukuchi sh'!Yu and scrape the mixture
into the bag with the seri. Tip ba ck
and forth to distribute the pickling
solution around the seri. Roll up
the bag , gently squeezing out the
air without squishing the seri itself ,
and store in the refrigerator for
a couple of hours to absorb flavor.
Use within 1-2 days as the pickling
mixture will eventually
overwhelm
the seri.
321 TSUKEMONO - PICKLES

recipes.title: Miso-Pickled Egg Yolk Ac Hara-Style
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Pickling time, 3 days
Makes, 12 egg
yolks
• 4 tablespoons
mirin or sake
Generous I cup (ro½ oz/300
g)
barley miso
• I2 egg
yolks
Preparation time: ~O minutes
Pickling time, IO minutes
Serves, 6
14 oz
(400 g) carrots , scrubbed
· ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
6 tablespoons brown rice vinegar
· 6 tablespoons mirin
I½ tablespoons usukuchi shoyu
I small dried red chile, seeded cut into
fine rings
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time, IO seconds
Pickling time, I
day
Serves, 6
3 ½ oz (roo g) wasabi stems and leav es,
cleaned
Boiling water
2 tablespoons
soy sauce
• 2 tablespoons sake
MISO-PICKLED
Pickling in miso "cooks" raw egg
yolks and transforms them into
creamy, salty , earthy bites. Serve
as an accompanime nt to a cold
beer or a glass of sake.
In a sma ll bowl, stir the mirin into
the miso to loosen the paste. If the
miso is particularly dense, add more
liquid , using half mirin and half sake.
Spread a little over half of the miso
into the bottom of a rectangular
refrigerator container just large
enough to hold the yo lks. Lay a
double layer of cheesecloth on top
of the miso. Make I2 divots in the
miso the size of the egg yolks by
pushing and rocking a wooden
EGG YOLK
spoon into the miso at even
intervals. Slide a raw egg yolk into
each divot. Drape another double
layer of cheesecloth across a cutting
board and smooth the remaining
miso on top of the cloth,
approximating the same surface
area of the first layer . Dislodge the
miso-smeared cheesecloth from the
board by sliding a fine metal spatu la
between the cloth and the board .
Set the cloth on top of the egg yolks
and cover.
Store in the refrigerator for 3 days.
Recycle the miso mixtur e to make
more pickled egg yolks, or miso so up.
AC HARA-STYLE
CARROT PICKLES
Achara-style pickles are said to
have developed from trade with
India. A little of these delicious,
spicy carrot pickles goes a long way.
Intensel y flavored, they 're best in
small amounts as a condime nt or
a savory bite before dinner or with
carbonated beverages as a snack.
Cut the carrots crosswise into
r½-inch (4 cm) lengths. Slice those
pieces lengthwise into slabs
¾ inc h
(2 cm)
thick. Stack the slabs and cut
into thin flat pieces (tanzaku-giri; see
page 446). Massage lightly with the
salt and let sit for IO minutes. Blot
dry in a clean tea towel, and toss
with the vinegar, mirin, usukuchi sh'!)lu,
and chile. Let macerate for
IO minutes b efo re serving. Keeps
for severa l weeks in the refrigerator.
[Qj p.323
SOY-PICKLED WASABI TOPS
Wasabi stems and leaves have
a pleasant amount of heat and
crunch , making them eminently
suitable for quick pickling.
Set up a bowl of ice water, Chop
the wasabi stems and le aves finely
and place in a wire-mesh sieve.
Pour boiling water over them in
a circular stream for a count of 10,
Immediately plunge into the ice
water to cool. Drain, squeeze , and
drop into a he atproof refrigerator
container.
In a small saucepan, bring the soy
sauce and sake to a simmer, then
immediately remove from the heat
and pour over the wasabi tops. Toss
to distribute evenly, cover, and
refrigerate for I day before using.
Keeps well for severa l days.
322 TSUKEMONO - PICKLES

recipes.title: Quick Mustard-Pickled Eggplant Soy Sauce-Pickled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Pickling time, I hour
Makes, r lb (500
g)
I lb (500 g) Japanese eggplants
(aubergines), stem ends trimmed
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
I tablespoon mustard powder
• 3 tablespoons soy
sauce
• I½ tablespoons mirin
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Pickling time, I day
Makes , 2 lb
(900 g)
2 1/+ lb (1 kg) unpeeled Japanese
cucumbers , ends trimmed
• ½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
6-inch (15 cm) piece konbu
• I tablespoon sake
2 small
dried Japanese red chiles
• ½ cup (4 fl oz/ r25 mi) soy sauce
Preparation time: IO minutes
Pickling time, I day
Makes, I cup (7 oz/200 g)
12 medium
myoga, bottoms trimmed,
halved lengthwise
3 tablespoons
rice vinegar
· 3 tablespoons
mirin
3 tablespoons
soy sauce
QUICK MUSTARD-PICKLED
EGGPLANT
Mustard brings out eggplant's
(aubergine) earthy flavor and the
generous amount used here makes
this a potent pickle.
Cut the eggplants (aubergines)
crosswise into ¼-inch (6 mm)
rounds . Massage gently with the salt
and let sit for IO minutes .
In a small bowl , mash together the
mustard powder, soy sauce, and
mirin to form a loose paste.
Pat the eggplant pieces dry on
a clean tea towel. Toss with the
mustard mixture and scrape into
a medium bowl. Place an otoshibuta
[drop lid] or plate on top and
allow to absorb flavor for I hour.
Eggplant tends to darken quickly ,
so eat these fairly soon after they
are ready . Store in the refrigerator
for
I- 2 days.
SOY SAUCE-PICKLED
CUCUMBERS
Matsumae is an area of Hokkaido
where this pickling style originated.
Western or Persian cucumbers
may be substituted; best to peel
at intervals , halve lengthwise , and
scoop out the seeds before using .
Cut the cucumbers crosswise into
r¼-inch (3 cm) lengths. Massage
with salt the and leave for IO
minutes . Brush the konbu with the
sake and let soften . Once softened
enough to cut , snip into thin strips
I 'I• inches (3 cm) long.
Squeeze the cucumbers gently and
place in a large bowl, ceramic pot ,
or tsukemonoyoki [plastic pickle press,
page 445] and add the soy sauce
and chiles. Place an otoshibuta [drop
lid] over the cucumbers and set a
2 lb
(1 kg) weight on top of the
drop lid, or screw down the plate of
the pickle press. Leave for
24 hours in
a cool spot before
eating. These pickles keep for
several days , refrigerated in their
pickling liquid , but will lose crunch
over time .
@ p.325
THREE-WAY VINEGAR­
PICKLED MYOGA
Available only in the summer,
myoga is a pleasantly bitter rhizome
bud in the ginger family bearing
no resemblance to ginger in
appearance or flavor . Serve
alongside grilled fish .
Drop the "!JIOga into a
small ceramic
pickling crock with the vinegar,
mirin, and soy sauce. Place an
otoshibuta [drop lid] on top and set
a IO oz (300 g) weight on top of
the drop lid. (Alternatively use
a tsukemono yoki U apanese pickling
press].) Leave for 24 hours at
room
temperature before using. Keeps
for 2-3 weeks,
if refrigerated in the
pickling liquid.
324 TSUKEMONO
- PICKLES

recipes.title: Quick Shibazuke Fish Sauce-Pickled Eggplant
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Pickling time, 1-2 hours
Makes, 1
lb (450 g)
6 oz (175 g) Japanese eggplants
(aubergines) , cut crosswise into %-inch
(1
cm) rounds
• 7 oz (200 g) Japanese cucumbers, cut
crosswise into %-inch (1
cm) rounds
• I teaspoon flaky sea salt
· 3 myoga , halved
lengthwise
12 red
shiso leaves, rolled and sliced
into fine tendrils
4 tablespoons
umesu
[sour plum "vinegar"]
Preparation time: IO minutes
Pickling time, 3 hours
Makes, 20 pickled
eggplants
2 lb
3 oz (1 kg) whole baby Japanese
eggplants (aubergines), 2-3 inches
(5-7½
cm) long , with stems intact
• Generous 2 cups
(17 fl oz / 500 ml)
squid fish sauce , preferably
Japanese
QUICK SHIBAZUKE
Shibazuke, a well-known salty-sour
Kyoto pickle , uses red shiso and
umesu [sour plum "vinegar"] to
pickle weighted vegetables. Here,
slicing the vegetables thinly, rather
than leaving them in chunks, speeds
up the process.
Massage the eggplants (aubergines)
and cucumber slices lightly with
¾ teaspoon of the salt . Massage the
myoga with the remaining
¼ teaspoon salt. After IO minutes ,
squeeze the eggplant and cucumber
gently, blot off the excess salt and
liquid with an absorbent paper
towel, and place in a medium bowl
or ceramic pot. Squeeze the n,yoga
and drop in with the eggplant
and cucumber . Add the red shiso
and umesu and toss. Set a small
plate on top of the vegetables and
weight with a measuring cup filled
with water or something similar.
(Alternatively, use a tsukemonoyoki
[Japanese pickle press] and screw
down just enough to create pressure
but not crush the vegetables.) The
pickles will be ready to eat in
1-2 hours,
but these pickles will
hold up admirably over the course
of I week.
[Qj p .327
FISH SAUCE-PICKLED
EGGPLANT
Squid fish sauce, dark and pungent
with squid ink , can be a challenge
to use in a dish . However, the sauce
is the perfect medium for pickling
small eggplants (aubergines) , as it
tempers the bitter skin and seeps
into the eggplant flesh. Getting the
timing right is essentiaC so taste
periodically to determine the right
marinating time before serving.
This is great served with a cold beer
on a hot day.
Leaving ½ inch (12 mm) for
aesthetic purposes , snip the stems
off the eggplants (aubergines) .
Place the eggplants in a gallon-size
(4 liter) resealable food storage
bag. Add the fish sauce
and let
marinate at room temperature for
3 hours. Taste. If you feel the flesh
needs a tad more salt , soak for
I more hour. Drain and serve .
326 TSUKEMONO - PICKLES

recipes.title: Salt-Fermented Summer Vegetables Miso-Pickled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minute s
Fermenting time, 3 days
Makes,
3 lb 5 oz (1.5 kg)
2 lb
(900 g) mediumjapanese
cucumbers , unpeeled
r3/+ lb (800 g) mediumjap anese
eggplants (aubergines), unpeeled
IO½ oz (300 g) green beans , topped
• IO½ oz (300 g) small carrots, cut to
the size of the green beans
3 tablespoons
plus I teaspoon flaky
sea salt
Preparation time, 15
minutes, plus
2 days
for air-drying
Pickling time, I week
Makes, ½ lb (225 g)
½ lb (225 g) young ginger, scrubbed
well with a stiff brush
· 2 tablespoons
mirin
½ cup (4 3/+ oz/ 135 g) barley miso
SALT-FERMENTED
SUMMER VEGETABLES
Because of the warm weather , salt ­
pickling progresses quickly in the
summer, so keep your eye on these .
Slice the cu cumbers and eggplants
(aubergines) crosswise into %-inch
(2
cm) rounds . Put each of the
types of vegetable in its own bowl
and massage in proportional
amounts of the salt. Pack in a large
pickling crock or small pickling
barrel in layers , starting with the
green beans and carrots, followed
by the cucumbers and eggplants,
patting down each layer
firmly
before
introducing the next one .
Cover with an otoshibuta [drop lid)
and set a 6% lb (3 kg) weight on
top of the drop lid. Leave in a
cool, shady spot for 3 days
until
fe rmentation takes hold. Once
soured to your personal taste , store
in the refrigerator.
MISO-PICKLED
Finely sliced , this ginger makes for
a tasty bite with beer or a spicy foil
to Curry Rice (page 297).
Air-dry the ginger in a shady
spot for
I-2 days. Cut the ginger
crosswise into ¼-inch (6 mm)
slices . Mash the mirin into the miso
and smooth over the ginger pieces.
Note, In
the winter, substitute
cabbage , carrots , and turnips
for these summer vegetables .
Winter vegetables need less salt
(4 tablespoons)
and should b e left
for at least 5-7 days.
[Q] p.329
GINGER
Pack in a ceramic pot or plastic
container and stor e in a cool dark
place for I week before using . Keeps
for 3 months,
if refrigerated.
TSUKEMONO - PICKLES

recipes.title: Pickled Red Ginger Soy Sauce-Pickled Shiso Buds
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Piclcling time : 3 months
Makes, 2 1/+ lb (1 kg)
2 1/+ lb (1 kg) fresh ginger, peeled
Generous 2 cups
(17 fl oz/500 mi)
umesu
[sour plum "vinegar"]
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time: 5 minutes
Makes: 1/2 cup (r¾ oz/50 g)
I cup (1½ oz/45 g) hojiso [shiso buds]
· Boiling water
½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
% cup (5 fl oz/r50 mi) soy sauce
PICKLED RED GINGER
Organic umesu [sour plum
"vinegar" ] is available online. As a
caveat: umesu is not actually vinegar:
It is the naturally occurring brine
that is part of the production of
umeboshi [salted sour plum] , and that
makes good-quality umesu expensive.
There are o nly two farmers in Jap an
who make organic ume products for
the commercial market, so these
products are precious.
Cut the ginger crosswise into
1/a-inch (3 mm) slices. Place in a
small piclcling crock with the umesu,
cover the surface with a piece of
heavy-duty food grade plastic for
piclcling, an otoshibuta [drop lid].
and a 2 1/+ lb (1 kg) weight. Cover
and set in a cool place for 3 months
to mellow . Store in jars at room
temperature. It keeps for up to
I year.
@ p.331
SOY SAUCE-PICKLED
SHISO BUDS
When shiso flower buds emerge in
the spri ng and seeding bud s in
the autumn, they are plentiful , so
piclcling them makes sense. Often
packed in salt, here the soy sauce
gives a more intense result. Use as
a condiment for white rice. They 're
also excellent with egg dishes,
especially fried eggs or raw egg on
hot rice.
Place the shiso buds in a wire - mesh
sieve and pour a steady stream
of boiling water over them for
IO seconds. Cool. Massage in the
salt. In a small saucepan, simmer
the buds in the soy sauce, until
slightly reduced and you can smell
the soy sauce caramelizing, about
2 minutes. Pack
in a small jar with
the soy sauce and refrigerate. It
keeps well for several months.

recipes.title: Miso-Pickled Shiso Buds And Myoga Soy Sauce-Pickled Garlic
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Pickling time, 5-6 days
Makes, 1% cup (6½ oz/r85 g)
10½
oz (300 g) myoga, quartered
lengthwise
½ teaspoon flaky sea salt
2½ cups
(3½ oz/loo g) hojiso [shiso
buds]
Boiling water
2 tablespoons
sake
I cup (9¾ oz/275 g) brown rice miso
Preparation time, 20 minutes
Cooking
time, 30 seconds
Pickling time, I week
Makes, I cup (5½ oz/r6o g)
8
smallish heads garlic , separated into
cloves and peeled
• Boiling water
I cup (8 fl oz / 250 mi) soy sauce
MISO-PICKLED SHISO BUDS
AND MYOGA
Hojiso (literally "stem shiso") refers
to the flowering and seeding buds
that appear on the stems in spring
(flowers) and autumn (seeds). Both
are used for culinary purposes in
Japan. Serve this tasty pickle as a
condiment to Japanese rice or on
a zensai plate. The shiso buds provide
an earthy, slightly salty foil to the
crunchy lll)IOga.
Massage the myoga with the salt .
Leave for 20 minutes
to soften . Put
the shiso buds in a wire-mesh sieve
and pour boiling
water over them
for IO seconds. Refresh under cold
running water and pat dry in a tea
towel. Tie the myoga and shiso buds
together in a piece of cheesecloth .
Stir the sake into the miso and
pack into a small ceramic pot or
cylindrical covered container. Poke
the cheesecloth bundle down into
the miso, cover, and store in a cool ,
dark place for 5-6 days before
pulling out and using. Good for 2-3
months , if
stored in a cool place.
SOY SAUCE-PICKLED GARLIC
Pickling the garlic in soy sauce
softens its heat and renders it
almost creamy. Make these when
garlic is in season in the beginning
of summer. You will not regret the
time it takes to peel the cloves. If
possible , try to source rose garlic
(pink-purple skinned garlic)
because it is mild.
Drop the garli c cloves into a
wire-mesh sieve and pour a steady
stream of boiling water over them
for IO seconds. Pat dry and pack
into a small jar with the soy sauce
(the soy sauce should cover the
garlic). Leave in a cool , dark
place to pickle for I week before
sampling. The pickles can be left
for several months , and as time
goes by, the garlic will become
milder and milder. Once you
have eaten all of the garlic , use the
pickling solution as a savory soy
sauce for stir-frying.

recipes.title: Salt-Fermented Mustard Greens Green Chile Relish
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes , plus I day
air - drying
Fermenting time: 2-3 weeks
Makes, 3 lb (r.4 kg)
· 9 lb (4 kg)
takana
14 oz
(400 g) flaky sea salt
Preparation time: 25 minutes ,
Cooking
time: 5 minutes
Pickling
time: 8 -12 hours
Makes: I quart (1 liter)
• 3 ½
oz (roo g)
konbu
2 ½ cups (20 fl oz / 600 ml) sake
·
2½ cups (20 fl oz / 600 ml) mirin
2 ½
cups (20 fl oz / 600 ml) soy
sauce
¾ oz (25 g) fresh green japones chiles,
finely diced

piman or small green
peppers. finely diced

freshly shaved

SALT-FERMENTED
MUSTARD GREENS
Takana is a type of Japanese mustard
plant prized for pickling . It grows
up to 2 feet (60 cm) high and
appears only for a short time
in early autumn . Komatsuna, bok
choy, or mustard greens can be
substituted. It can be eaten as is
(in moderation), with ri ce, sauteed
with root vegetables and tofu, or
dropped into miso soup.
Lay the takana out , so the strands
are not touching, on a flat basket
elevated off the ground for good air
circulation . (Alternatively, use a wire
rack lined with cheesecloth.) Air-dry
for a full day in a shady spot.
Pound the stems gently with a
surikogi Uapanese grinding pestle]
or wooden rolling pin to break
down the fibers a little. Working
over a pickling crock, massage
the salt into the leaves and stems
and pack tightly in the crock,
alternating stem ends in each layer.
(You want to use IO percent of the
greens' weight for salt.) Press an
otoshibuta [drop lid] directly on top
of!eaves and set a 13 lb
(6 kg) weight on top of the drop
lid. Leave for 2-3 weeks in a cool
place to ferment.
Once fermented , remove from the
crock and store , tightly wrapped,
in the refrigerator for a few weeks
as you use it up.
If the pickle is too
salty, soak in cold water for 20 - 30
minutes before squeezing and
cutting. Cut crosswise into 1 1/.+­
inch
(3 cm) pieces before using.
GREEN CHILE RELISH
This pickle is made in Iwate
prefecture in northeastjapan . The
chopping takes a little while, but
is worth the time , since this spicy
condiment keeps for an extended
time , if refrigerated.
Soak the konbu in the sake until soft,
about 15 minutes . Pluck out , and
snip into fine threads.
In a medium
saucepan, combine the sake, konbu
threads , mirin, soy sauce , chiles ,
and piman. Bring to a simmer, cool
until just barely warm, and stir in
the rice koji, and katsuobushi. Cover
with a clean tea towel and leave
overnight before using . Pack into
a jar and store in the refrigerator.
This relish keeps for a few weeks.

recipes.title: Green Pepper Relish Miso-Pickled Turnips 334 Tsukemono - Pickles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time, 2-3 hours
Makes,
Generous 2 cups
(17 fl oz/500 ml)
I lb 5 oz (600 g) pimans Qapanese green
peppers] , diced
r'/2 cups (ro'/2 oz/300 g) chuzarato
[coa rs e brown sugar crystals ]
· 1¾ lb (800 g) rice koji
7 1/2 cups (60 fl oz/r.8 liters) soy sauce
· 8 sma ll whole dried red japones chiles
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Pickling time, 4-5 days
Makes,
6 pickled turnips
• 6 small turnips with tops
(r lb I 450 g), scrubbed
I tablespoon gold sesame seeds
J ½ tablespoons finely slivered yuzu or
Meyer lemon zest
6 tablespoons white miso
• I teaspoon gold sesame oil
GREEN PEPPER RELISH
No matter whether fried, raw , or
pickled, there is no better match
for pimanUapanese green pepper],
than miso. The natural bitterness of
the piman somehow softens from the
earthy salty miso. Here, the koji acts
as a fermenting agent and also gives
texture to this condiment.
In a large heavy pot, combine the
piman, chu:,;arato, koji, soy
sauce , and
chiles. Simmer over medium-low
heat , stirring occasionally, until
the liquid has evaporated and the
mixture is jam-like, 2-3 hours.
Scrape into a jar and store in the
refrigerator for 2 to 3 months.
MISO-PICKLED TURNIPS
Turnips benefit from all kinds of Transfer the 2 sets of 3 turnips to
pickling , and theyu,u- and sesame-
separate resealable food storage
miso treatments make for a versatile bags and refrigerate for 4-5 days
pickle
that can be served as a side
dish or appetizer. These turnips
pair particularly well with Achara­
Style Carrot Pickles (page 322).
Leaving% inch (r cm) of the stems,
lop off the turnip tops. (Save the
leaves for another dish.)
In a small, dry frying pan , toast
the sesame seeds over medium heat
until fragrant , shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Slide the seeds
into a suribachi [grinding bowl]
or spice grinder and grind to a
coarse powder.
In a small bowl, mash together
theyuzu zest
and 3 tablespoons
of the miso. In a second bowl ,
mash together the ground sesame
seeds, sesame oil, and remaining
3 tablespoons miso. Smooth the
yu~u-m iso over
all surfaces of 3 of the
turnips and the sesame-miso over
the other 3.
before using. Once fully cured ,
scrape off and discard the miso. Blot
the turnips dry and cut into wedges
for serving. The pickled turnips
will keep well for I week or two , if
stored without the miso.
[variation]
For a quick version: Saute bite­
size triangular chunks (rangiri; Page
446) of turnip in a small amount
of sesame oil and fold in either the
yuzu-miso or the sesame-miso before
serving.

recipes.title: Overnight Pickled Napa Cabbage Spicy Napa Cabbage Pickles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Pickling time, 2 hours salting , plus
overnight macerating
Makes, 14 oz (400 g)
7 oz
(200 g) napa cabbage
( Chinese leaf)
7 oz (200 g) green cabbage
8 oz (225 g)
daikon, scrubbed
I medium carrot, scrubbed
· Flaky sea salt
6 tablespoons rice vinegar
• 3 tablespoons
soy sauce
· 6 tablespoons mirin
• I teaspoon fine sea salt
I (6-inch/r5 cm) piece konbu, brushed
with water to soften
Slivered zest of I yuzu or
½ Meyer lemon
Preparation time: IO minutes
Pickling time, I hour
Serves, 6
II oz (325 g) large napa cabbage
(Chinese leaf) leaves, center
stems
separated from the leaves
• I small carrot, scrubbed
• 1/2 teaspoon flaky sea salt
• I tablespoon rice vinegar
• I tablespoon soy sauce
• I tablespoon mirin
I tablespoon gold sesame oil
I small dried japones red chile,
cut into fine rings
OVERNIGHT PICKLED
NAPA CABBAGE
Overnight salting is probably the
most ingenious of preparations in
ruraljapan, since the philosophy is
based on the lives of busy farmers
and fishermen, Salting is done at
the end of the day when work slows
down, and eaten the following day
when a surfeit of work means few
idle hands .
Cut the napa cabbage (Chinese
leaf) and
green cabbage crosswise
into 11/2-inch (4 cm) pieces.
Quarter the daikon and carrot
lengthwise and slice crosswise into
'/•-inch (6 mm) quarter-rounds.
Halve all of the half rounds
crosswise to make quarters . Toss
the vegetables with the flaky salt.
You want to use enough salt to add
up to 2 percent
of the vegetables'
combined weight; in this case it
should be about 1/2 oz (15 g).
Transfer to a tsukemono yoki
Uapanese pickle press] and screw
down to press until the liquid is
expressed from the vegetables .
(Alternatively, pack in a resealable
food storage bag, squeeze out all
of the air , and place in a large
bowl. Fill another bag with water
and place on top to weight the
vegetables until their natural
liquids are released.) Drain after
2 hours and
discard the brine.
In a small bowl, whisk together the
vinegar, soy sauce, mirin, and fine
salt.
Snip the softened konbu into
thin threads . Layer the vegetables
in a refrigerator container with the
JUsU zest and konbu threads. Pour the
vinegar mixture over the vegetables
and refrigerate overnight to pickle.
These are not long-term pickles,
but nonetheless will hold up for
I week or so.
SPICY NAPA CABBAGE PICKLES
Quick pickles are part of daily life
in Japan with many methods used
to prepare them. Adding a bit of
sesame oil to the brine gives this
pickle some body. Use the best mirin
and soy sauce you can find as their
complex flavors are key. Serve as a
pickle with rice and soup, or a bite
before dinner .
Cut the napa cabbage ( Chinese
leaf) stems and carrot into
% x
2-inch (r x 5 cm) thin sticks. Slice
the leaves crosswise into I½-inch
(4 cm) pieces. Gently massage the
salt into the cabbage and carrot
until ever so slightly fatigued. Put
the vegetables in a large bowl.
In a small saucepan , whisk together
the vinegar , soy sauce, mirin, sesame
oil, and chile. Bring to a simmer
over medium heat, then remove
from the heat and pour over the
vegetables , toss, and place a weight
over the surface . Let macerate for
I hour before eating .

recipes.title: Quick Salt-Pickled Cabbage Rice Bran-Pickled Cabbage
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Pickling time, 2- 3 days
Makes:
1½ lb (650 g)
2 ¼ lb (1 kg) napa cabbage
( Chinese leaf)
2 oz
(60 g) flaky sea salt
I (4-inch/10 cm) piece konbu , brushed
with water to soften, and snipped into
fine threads
2 small dried
red japones chiles , sliced
into fi.ne rounds
Preparation
time: 20 minutes
Pickling time: 3-4 days
Makes:
14 oz (400 g)
8 tablespoons flaky sea salt
I lb 5 oz (600 g) head green cabbage,
cored with whole leaves intact
2 cups (4 1/2 oz/130 g) rice bran
8 small dried red chiles (preferably
Japanese or Thai)
8 teaspoons slivered fresh ginger
QUICK SALT-PICKLED
CABBAGE
Western cabbage can be substituted
for the napa cabbage ( Chinese leaf).
This is a Plain-Jane version of Salt­
Fermented Napa Cabbage (opposite
page) , but good for beginners to
have in their repertoire. Aromatics
such as garlic, ginger ,yu.tu, or dried
red chiles can be added to the
cabbage as it is salted and pa cked in
the crock.
Quarter the cabbage by slicing
through the core about 4-inches
(10 cm) up into the leaf area .
Pull the quarters apart. Rinse off
any dirt or dust particles from
the cabbage and shake dry. Strew
some of the salt in the bottom of a
pickling crock and pack the cabbage
quarters in, cut side down, wedging
them closely together. Strew with
the konbu and chiles and more salt.
If making more than one layer, salt
each layer before adding the next
layer until all of the ingredients
have been used up . Once all of
the cabbage has been placed in
the crock , press down hard on the
surface with the palm of your hand
to eliminate air pockets. Add water
to come about one - quarter of the
way up the cabbage (poke your
fingers down
the side to check). Lay
an otoshibuta [drop lid] on top and
set a 2 lb
(1 kg) weight on top of the
drop lid. Leave for 2-3 days in a
warm room before using. Once the
souring has began (as opposed to
merely being salty), refrigerate and
eat within 4 days.
RICE BRAN-PICKLED CABBAGE
Rice bran pickles have a funky , sour
profile that cannot be duplicated
by other pickling methods . This
quick version allows you to achieve
excellent results without the time­
consuming process of creating a
rice bran pickling bed.
Sprinkle I tablespoon of salt evenly
across the bottom of a pickling
crock. Separate the cabbage leaves
into 8 piles. Working with one pile,
sandwich 2 whole leaves together
at a time and smooth them on top
of the salt until all of the leaves in
the pile have been used . Mix the
remaining salt into the rice bran
and sprinkle in one - quarter of the
mixture in an even layer. Smooth
in another pile ofleaves , 2 leaves at
a time as described above , and strew
with I whole chile and I teaspoon of
the ginger.
Repeat the same order to make 8
layers ending with rice bran , chile,
and ginger. Place an otoshibuta [drop
lid] on top and set a 4 1/2 lb (2 kg)
weight on top of the drop lid.
The cabbage pickles will be ready to
eat in
3-4 days,
depending on the
weather. Once pickled sufficiently ,
transfer to a plastic container and
store in the refrigerator. To serve,
rinse a few leaves in cold water, pat
dry, stack and cut into I½-inch
(2 cm) squares.

recipes.title: Salt-Fermented Napa Cabbage 339 Tsukemono - Pickles
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 15 minutes, plus
4-6 hours
air-drying
Fermenting time, 2 weeks
Makes, 4 lb
(2.5 kg)
6 lb IO oz (3 kg) whole napa cabbage
( Chinese leaf)
6-inch (15 cm) piece konbu
• I tablespoon sake
3 oz (90 g) flaky sea salt (3% of the
cabbage weight)
I small Japanese red chile , sliced into
fine rounds
SALT-FERMENTED
NAPA CABBAGE
The Japanese version of sauerkraut,
this cabbage pickle is an easy one
for novices who want to try their
hand at fermentation. To use the
cabbage , cut crosswise into 2-inch
(5 cm) lengths and serve with
a dribble of soy sauce if a little
additional salt is desired.
Quarter the cabbage ( Chinese leaf)
by slicing through the core about
4 inches (10 cm) up into the leaf
area. Pull the quarters apart from
the core, so you do not cut the
leaves. Cut each quarter in the same
manner. and pull apart to create
8 pieces total.
Spread out a thick layer of
newspaper and arrange the cabbage
wedges on the newspaper. Dry
under indirect sunlight, cut side s
up, for half a day (4-6 hours ,
depending on the weather). The
cabbage should be slightly dried,
but not wilting.
Brush the
konbu with sake and soft en
until it can be snipped into thin
strips 1½ inches (4 cm) long.
Place a large plastic pickling bag
in a pickling crock or small pickle
barrel. (Alternatively , just rinse
the pot or barrel with hot water
and use as is , but keep an eye on
the pickles to make sure no mold
forms .) Massage the salt into the
cabbage wedges and pack into the
pickling container. cut side down,
sprinkling in the
konbu and chile as
you go. Flatten the bag across the
surface of the cabbage, so the edges
are flush to the side of the pot and
drape over the pot.
Place another bag , filled with
water and tightly secured , on top.
(If not using the plastic bag, just
press an otoshibuta [drop lid] firmly
on the cabbage and set a 6 ½ lb
[3 kg] weight on top of the drop
lid .) Leave for 2 weeks in a cool
place to ferment. Remove from
the barrel as needed . This cabbage
keeps for about I month or so while
the weather holds, otherwise store
tightly wrapped in the refrigerator
for a few weeks.

recipes.title: Dried Daikon Pickled In Three-Way Vinegar Miso-Pickled Daikon
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 5 minutes, plus
I hour soaking time
Pickling time : 2 days
Makes:
6½ oz (185 g)
13/+ oz
(50 g) kiriboshi daikon
6 tablespoons rice vinegar
• 6 tablespoons mirin
6 tablespoons soy sauce
I small driedJapanese red chile,
cut into fine rounds
Preparation time : 1½ hours
Pickling time: 9-14 days
initially, then
1½-2 months
Makes,
8 lb 13 oz (4 kg)
II lb (5 kg) daikon, with leaves

sea
salt
11/+ cups (IO fl oz/300 ml) mirin
6½
lb (3 kg) inaka , brown rice , or
barley miso
DRIED DAIKON PICKLED IN
THREE-WAY VINEGAR
Dried daikon comes in two forms:
kiriboshi daikon [fine threads] or
wariboshi daikon [fat strands] . Either
can be used here, though kiriboshi
daikon seems to be easier to find.
Kanl!Yo [gourd strands] could also be
substituted. Use this as a side pickle
for any Japanese meal.
Soak the kiriboshi daikon for I hour
in a medium bowl of cold water to
generously cover. Lift out of the
water and drop into a wire-mesh
sieve. Rinse under cold , running
water, and shake off any excess
drops . Pat dry in a clean tea towel
and cut crosswise into 1½-inch
(4 cm) lengths. Place in a
refrigerator container that just
holds the reconstituted daikon and
add the rice vinegar , mirin, soy
sauce , and chile . Refrigerate for
2 days
before using and store for
up to 2 weeks .
MISO-PICKLED DAIKON
These pickles involve a two-step Drape over the rope again to air-
process, so plan ahead , and be sure dry outside for I more day.
to start when there are still at least
two months of cold weather ahead. Stir the
mirin into the miso and
Scrub the daikon well and halve
lengthwise. If quite thick, quarter.
Tie two daikon halves together at the
base of the leaves and hang over
a rope outdoors in the winter air
for 1 - 3 days until soft and flexible,
but cover at night to ward off frost.
Coil the semi-dried daikon tightly
into the barrel or crock . Mix the
IO½ oz (300g) salt with I cup (8 fl
oz/235 ml) water
and pour over the
daikon. Place an otoshibuta [drop lid]
on top and set an II lb (5 kg) weight
on top of the drop lid . Leave for
7-IO days.
Remove
the salted daikon from the
brine and soak in a bowl of cold
water for 6 hours, but dump the
soaking water each hour and add
fresh cold water.
spread enough miso onto the bottom
of a large pickling crock to make a
2-inch (5
cm) layer . Coil a layer of
daikon into the pot as tightly as you
can . Top with a thin layer of miso.
Keep adding layers of daikon with
miso until all of the daikon has been
wedged into the pot. Smooth the
rest of the miso onto the daikon and
press down to compress. Sprinkle
with the remaining 2 tablespoons
salt,
place an otoshibuta [drop lid)
on top and set a 9 lb (4 kg)
weight
on top of the drop lid. Cover with
a large piece of muslin cloth and
tie twine around the circumference
of the pot to secure. Leave in a
cool, shady spot outside for I ½-2
months
before using.

recipes.title: Quick Rice Bran-Pickled Dai Kon Curry-Pickled Daikon
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Pickling time: 6 hours
Make s : 14 oz
(400 g)
I½ lb (700 g) daikon , with leave s
• 3 tablespoons
flaky sea salt
Generous 1h cup (r oz / 30 g) rice bran
• Shichimi togarashi
[seven - spice powder]
Preparation time: 20 minutes
Pickling time: IO days
Makes, r¾ lb (800 g)
2 lb
3 oz (r kg) daikon , halved
lengthwise
2 tablespoons
(r oz / 30 g) fine sea salt
Generous 2 cups
(17 fl oz / 500 ml) sake
• 4 tablespoons
mirin
2 tablespoons
hot curry powder
QUICK RICE BRAN-PICKLED
DAI KON
Not a true nukazuke [rice bran
pi ckle]-in the sense that it
does not have nukazuke's lovely
sourness-this pickling method
is nonetheless handy when time
is an issue and you don't have a
nukadoko [rice bran pickling bed]
at your disposal. Nukadoko is a bed
of lactic - fermented rice bran that
takes about one week or more to
create , and requires daily attention.
Turnip or whole radishes can be
substituted for the daikon.
Remove the daikon leaves and set
aside. Scrub the daikon and cut it
into ¾-inch (2 cm)
cubes. Massage
I tablespoon of the salt into the
daikon and let sit for IO minutes .
Rinse off the salt under cold
running water and pat dry.
Chop the leaves crosswise into
4-inch (ro
cm) pieces and pack
into the bottom of a small pickling
crock . Strew one-third of the daikon
cubes on top of the leaves in an
even layer and sprinkle with
I tablespoon of salt and
2 tablespoons
of rice bran. Repeat
to make 2 more
layers. Place an
otoshibuta [ drop lid] on top and set
a 2 .2 lb
(r kg) weight on top of the
drop lid. Leave to macerate for
6 hours. Rinse before serving.
Serve sprinkled with shichimi togarashi.
(If the pickle is too salty for your
taste , soak in plenty of cold water
for 30 minutes before using.)
CURRY-PICKLED DAIKON
Japanese love their Curry Rice
(pag e 297) and
curry powder makes
a brilliant addition to pickles ,
especially turnips and daikon.
Cut the daikon crosswise into
manageable pieces that will fit
in a pickling crock. Rub the daikon
pieces with the salt and wedge
tightly into a ceramic or food grade
plastic container . Pour the
sake
and mirin over the daikon, place an
otoshibuta [drop lid] or plate on top
and set a 3 ½ lb (r.6 kg) weight on
top of the drop lid . Cover loosely
with muslin cloth and tie twine
around the circumference of the
pot to secure . Leave for 2 days
in
a cool spot.
After 2 days,
remove the daikon from
the liquid and dry in direct sunlight
for 4-6 hours , depending
on the
weather. The daikon should be dry
and taut- not withered .
Sprinkle the partially dried daikon
with curry powder , pack into a
clean pot, weight, and leave in a
cool spot for I week before using.
To serve, rinse the daikon, pat dry ,
and slice thinly .

recipes.title: Quick Pickled Daikon With Daikon Leaves Miso-Pickled
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 20 minutes, plus
6 hours air-drying time
Pickling time, 2 days
Makes, II oz (325 g)
I lb (450 g) daikon, peeled
• 2 large
handfuls daikon leaves
• Boiling water
I tablespoon slivered fresh ginger
Finely slivered zest of I small sudachi
I small dried japones chile, cut
crosswise into fine rings
½ tablespoon flaky sea salt
Preparation time: IO minutes, plus
I day soaking and 2 days drying
Pickling time, IO days
Makes, 2% lb (1.2 kg)
2% lb (1.2 kg)
slightly
over-the-hill takuan
· Fine sea salt
I cup (9¾ oz/275 g) brown
rice miso
QUICK PICKLED DAIKON
WITH DAIKON LEAVES
Japan is the land of preserving,
but these projects take place at the
times of the year when the fruit
or vegetable (or fish) is
ready to
be harvested and put up . Quick
pickling, on the other hand, is a
daily treatment of fresh vegetables
that goes well with rice. The
vegetables are ready to eat within
minutes or hours , and they often
hold up well for several days.
Halve the daikon lengthwise and slice
crosswise into I 1/+-inch
(3 cm) half-rounds. Cut those
in half to make quarter-moons
(itchogiri; see page 446). Lay the
daikon pieces out on a basket and dry
outdoors for half a day (6 hours)
MISO-PICKLED
Takuan is a rice bran pickle made
from half-dried daikon, which is
prepared in early December and
ready in early January. The pickles
are kept outside or in a pickle
shed and are eaten throughout the
winter. As the weather begins to
warm in March, the winter pickles
start to get slightly funky, and there
are several methods to repurpose
the pickles for a few last uses.
Here, the takuan is soaked to remove
sourness, then pickled in miso
to preserve.
Soak the takuan for I day in lightly
salted water.
Arrange the takuan on a basket or
spread out newspaper and dry
outside for 2 days .
in
a cool, shady spot with good air
circulation. Drop the daikon leaves
into a large wire- mesh sieve and
pour a steady stream of boiling
water over them for IO seconds .
Squeeze to remove water and slice
crosswise into fine chiffonade.
In
a medium bowl, toss the semi­
dried daikon pieces with the daikon
leaves, ginger, sudachi zest, and
chile. Massage in the salt, place an
otoshibuta [drop lid] on top of the
daikon, and weight. Store in the
refrigerator for 2 days
before using.

TAKUAN
Cut the takuan crosswise to fit a
pickling
crock. Smear a layer of
miso 'I+ inch (5 cm) deep in the

layer of miso on top of the takuan,
more takuan followed by miso, until

PACIFIC SAURY SUSHI
Before the edomae zushi [Tokyo­
style sushi] that is still popularly
eaten today , sushi was a type of
fermented rice and vegetable
preparation called narezushi. The
initial preparation steps are
not time-consuming, but the
fermenting process does require
a leap of faith. The deliciously
salty, sour fish that
results after
I or more months makes it worth
venturing into unknown territory.
This is one of those large-scale
fermenting or pickling operations
performed when there is a lot of
one kind vegetable or fish. Feel
free
to make less.
Remove the head and guts from the
fish (leave the scales on). Slice it
down the back to separate into
2 fillets and
peel out the vertebrae.
Rinse well. Sprinkle a layer of the
salt in the bottom of a pickling
container that will hold the fish
flat, and line some
fillets side
by
side across the salt , skin side up .
Sprinkle more salt (eyeballing the
amount of salt and the amount
of fish to
keep the salting process
fairly even), and layer in more fish .
Add
the last layer of fish with the
last of the salt.
Set an otoshibuta [drop lid) on top
of the fish and place a 9 lb (4 kg)
weight
on top of the drop lid . Leave
in a cool, dark place for 2-3 days
until the water and blood rises
above the drop lid. Remove the fish
from the salt, rinse quickly , but do
not soak in water . Discard the salt
and wash the container .
In a medium bowl, combine the
vinegar, mirin , and soy sauce.
Wash, soak and cook the rice in
a large heavy pot, according to
the directions for Japanese Rice
(page 291), but use 4 1/+ cups
(1
liter) of water. Dump out onto
a handai [large wooden tub] or at
lea st two large cutting boards and
sprinkle some of vinegar mixture
over the rice . Cut the vinegar into
the rice with a rice paddle or a
wooden spoon , while fanning the
rice with your other hand. Keep
sprinkling over and cutting in the
vinegar while fanning, until all of
the vinegar has been incorporated
and the rice has cooled until just
barely warm. If not using a handai,
transfer the sushi rice you have
just made to a large bowl. Fold in
the rice koji before the rice cools to
barely warm . Once incorporated,
add the carrots and daikon, and mix
until evenly distributed.
Pack a 3/+-inch (2 cm) layer of
rice in the bottom of the pickling
container used to salt the fish and
arrange
a layer of fillets , side
by
side and skin side up . Spread a
layer of the rice across the layer of
fish and
continue alternating layers
of fish and rice until the last layer
is rice .
Place an otoshibuta [drop lid) on top
of the rice and replace the 9 lb
(4 kg)
weight. Cover with muslin
cloth and tie twine around the
circumference of the container to
secure. Leave to ferment in a cool ,
dark place for 3-4 weeks before
eating. If there is too much liquid
pooling up, tip a little out from
time to time. Lasts for about
2 months following the initial
month of fermentation , if stored
in a cold place .

BEER-PICKLED
These pickles are made in the

Halve the

HORSE MACKEREL SUSHI
Mackerel , sardines, and aji [horse
mackerel] are especially good raw or
cured, rather than cooked , and are
best in the spring to early summer
when the fishes' natural
oils are
high. This sushi is best the first day,
but fine the
next.
Slice off the fish heads
with a sharp
knife and run the knife down the
belly. Pull out the guts, separate the

rinse well in 3 percent
salt water

In a small bowl, whisk together

mackerel fillets over the konbu and
refrigerate for 2 to 3 hours.

Keep at room temperature , but

in which case you should serve it

CHICKEN AND SEAFOOD NABE
This dish comes from the
Matsumae area of Hokkaido, the
northernmost island prefecture
of Japan. Because of the small

sukjyaki-style than brothy nabe.
Bring all the ingredients to the
table and set a cast-iron sukjyaki pan
or skillet on a portable tabletop
burner . Arrange the konbu in the
bottom of the pan and strew the
chicken, negi, prawns , and shiitake
on top. Swirl in the dashi, bring to

heat, and cook for I minute. Add
in the oysters and simmer over
medium-high heat for I minute
longer. Turn the chicken pieces,
prawns, and oysters over with

to a gentle simmer, and cook for
2 minutes more .
Serve in medium soup bowls
splashed with poru:.u and garnished
with the chives and momiji oroshi.

Although today, Hokkaido produces

Nara is the ancient home of dairy
farming in Japan. This milky nabe

OYSTER AND MISO NABE
Dote-style nabe is characterized by
the miso that coats the cooking
vessel before the broth and other
ingredients are added. Here, the
miso is sandwiched with two layers
of negi. The broth in this dish is
densely concentrated and like
Sukiyaki (page 370), the flavorful
ingredients are eaten with a beaten
raw egg. This is a very robust miso­
intense dish.
Break an egg into each of the 4
small miso soup or rice bowls and
beat lightly. Bring to the table along
with a portable tabletop burner.
In a bowl, mash together the
soybean miso, barley miso, mirin, and
sake until well emulsified. Smear
half of the miso mixture across
the bottom and sides of a donabe
[flameproof earthenware casserole]
or Dutch oven (casserole). Strew
with half of the negi. Dollop the
remaining half of the miso on
top of the negi and smooth flat,
as best you can, using a rubber
spatula and small butter knife.
Scatter the remaining negi across
the surface along with the oysters,
tofu, and shungiku.
Place the donabe on the portable
tabletop burner and turn the
burner to medium. Pour in half
of the konbu broth and bring to a
simmer, 3-5 minutes, turning the

heating. Pour in the remaining
dashi in a slow, steady stream. After
the oysters have plumped and are
cooked through, 3-5 minutes
longer (depending on size), ladle
the ingredients into the small bowls
of beaten egg and eat hot.

shrimp (prawns) can substitute for
the oysters.

out all of the ingredients and some
of the soup into the bowls . Each
person should season with
pon{U to
taste-I to 2 teaspoons pon{U for
½ cup (4 fl oz/r25 ml) ofbroth­
and sprinkle in I pinch ofyuzu zest.
Replenish the pot with another
round of the ingredients and
once cooked , another 5 minutes ,
ladle out. Repeat until all of the
ingredients are gone.
[Q] p.357
SHRIMP BALL NABE
Shrimp balls are versatile and can
be served in a simple bowl of Clear
Fish Broth (page 160), rather than
this nabe. Here they add a note of
gorgeousness to the nabe, making
this dish an excellent candidate to
serve company , since often a home­
style nabe consists of ingredients
thrown together on the fly.
Chop the prawns coarsely and
grind to a paste in a suribachi
[grinding bowl) or pulse in a food
processor . Scrape into a medium
bowl and pound in the flour and
salt until well distributed . Beat
in the egg with a wooden spoon
until fluffy.
In a donabe [flameproof earthenware
casserole), combine 5 cups
(40 fl
oz/I. 2 liters)
water and the
konbu. Set on a portable tabletop
burner at the table and bring
almost to a boil over medium-
high heat. Add the soy sauce and
mirin and adjust to a simmer. Drop
tablespoon-size balls of the prawn
mixture into the broth , and once
all of the mixture has been added
to the broth , simmer for 2 minutes
more.
Add the napa cabbage
( Chinese leaf) and shiitake and cook
for 3 minutes. Stir in the mitsuba and
cook for 30 seconds longer . Serve
hot in individual bowls.

CRAB AND MISO NABE
In Japanese the stomach contents
of the crab is called "miso." In
English , there is no good word,
because it is not commonly eaten.
The crab "m iso " is both sweet
and earthy, so it softens the salty
miso, and lends depth to this
flavorful dish.
Tear the kon191aku into walnut - size
pieces, rub with the salt, and place
in a wire-mesh sieve. Pour boiling
water over it for IO seconds and set
the sieve in the sink to drain.
Pull the back off of the crab , but
do not discard. Carefully scrape
into a small bowl, to reserve, any
of the coral or white substance that
is adhering to the back shell or the
crab body. This is crab "miso."
Remove the gills and discard.
Quarter the crab bodies , and
cut the legs and claws in thirds ,
diagonally . Add the brown rice miso
to the residual crab "miso" and
mash
together until well emulsified.
Wash the crab shell and spoon the
crab "miso" into the shell.
Place the crab shell in the bottom
of a donabe [flameproof earthenware
casserole] and set the pot on a
portable tabletop burner over
medium - high heat. Slowly add the
dashi, pouring around the outside
of the shell and inside as well, and
when the crab "miso" starts to melt ,
about 2 minutes, add the sake, mirin,
and soy sauce. Simmer for I minute
before adding the crab, green beans,
kon191aku, tofu , and negi (depending
on the size of your pot . you might
need to cook the ingredients in
two or three batches). Simmer for
5 more minutes, blotting off any
top scum with a folded piece of
absorbent paper towel.
Serve ladled into large ,
donburi
[deep soup bowls]. Sprinkle with
shichimi togarashi, if desired.
@ p.359
PORK AND CABBAGE NABE
There are myriad variations of
cabbage and pork dishes all over
Japan. Despite the simplicity of the
method and ingredients, this nabe is
robust and full of flavor, and could
be doubled or tripled to feed a
hungry crowd.
Place the usuage in a wire-mesh sieve
and pour a steady stream of boiling
water over it for IO seconds . Shake
off excess water and cut crosswise
into strips ½ inch (12 mm) wide.
Cut the carrot crosswise into
1/+-inch (6 mm) half-rounds or
quarter-round s, depending on the
thickness of the diameter.
In a donabe [flameproof earthenware
cassero le] or Dutch oven (casserole),
combine the dashi, soy sauce, mirin,
sake, and salt.
Set a portable tabletop burner on
the table, place the casserole on the
burner, and bring to a simmer.
Bring all of the ingredients to
the table. Add half of the pork ,
cabbage, carrot, usuage, and negi to
the simmering broth and cook until
done, 3-5 minutes.
Ladle
out a scoop of all of the
ingredients, plus soup, into
individual bowls . Sprinkle with
shichimi togarashi, if desired. Repeat
with the remaining ingredients for
a second round.

QUICK MIZUTAKI
While easily made at home, this
dish tends to be eaten more
commonly in restaurants. A small
bowl of Japanese rice will complete
this meal.
In a donabe [flameproof earthenware
cassero le] or Dutch oven (cassero le),
bring the chicken broth to a
boil over high heat. Slip the
chicken , negi, shiitake, tofu, and
napa cabbage ( Chinese leaf) into
the soup.
Set a portable
tabletop burner on
the table, place the casserole on
the burner, and turn the burner
to medium heat. Cook at a lively
simmer until the chicken and
tofu have cooked through and the
vegetable pieces and shiitake have
softened, 7-10 minutes.
Ladle out, little by little, into small
individual soup bowls and season
with a little each of the chive s, momiji
oroshi, and porv;u.
SEAFOOD SUKIYAKI
The tri ck to successfu l seafood
sukjyaki is to keep the seasoning
lighter than when preparing the
traditional meat version, since the
seafood is more delicate and can be
easily overwhelmed.
Give each person a small soup bowl
and a raw egg to break into the
bowl. Each person should beat the
raw egg to use as a dipping sauce.
Set a portable tabletop burner on
the table. Set a cast-iron sukjyaki
pan or skillet on the burner and
measure in the dashi, soy sauce,
and mirin. Bring to a simmer over
medium-high heat.
Core the cabbage and cut crosswise
into 2-inch (5 cm) pieces.
Mound about half of the negi, napa
cabbage ( Chinese leaf), shiitake,
tofu, and shirataki noodles each into
its own area of the pan. Simmer
briskly until half done, about
3 minutes.
Remove the heads from the prawns,
and using a knife , make slits across
the back of the prawns to devein.
Cut the snapper into 2-inch
(5 cm) pieces. Turn the vegetables
and nestle about half of the prawns,
scallops, and snapper into the pan.
Turn the seafood pieces after 2
minutes and simmer until cooked
through , about 3 more minutes.
Serve a ladleful in each bowl of
beaten egg. Replenish the pan and
cook the second batch, using up all
of the ingredients.

Mitutaki [stewed chic ken and

at home, because whole chickens
(and bone - in chicken parts) are
not easy to find in
Japan, making
this more of a dish ordered at
restaurants. This recipe starts with a
whole chicken , which when cooked
makes a broth , but you can make
a shortcut version with prepared
chicken broth (store-bought or
homemade) and boneless, skin less
chunks of chicken. Feel free to
cook and serve from the stovetop.
Japanese would typically eat this
dish with a bowl of rice on the side,
but also might add the rice to the
last bits of soup to make a creamy,
ri so tto-like finish to the meal.
In a donabe [flameproof earthenware

MISO CHICKEN BALLS AND
NAPA SOUP
Once meat began to be consumed
inJapan a few hundred years ago,
it was more of a seasoning than a
main ingredient. But a favorite way
to showcase meat is by using ground
(minced) fish, chicken , and pork to
make
meatballs. These "meatballs "
are sometimes formed into ovals
and fried , but are most often
simmered in soup.
Place the ground (minced) chicken
in a medium bowl and sprinkle the
potato starch over it. Mix in the
miso. Add the mirin , I tablespoon of
the dashi, and the egg and beat all
of the ingredients with a wooden
spoon , until well emulsified.
Set a p o rtable tabletop burner
on the table and place a donabe
[flameproof earthenware cassero le]

mixture into the soup and simmer

MISO ODEN
Convenience stores all over Japan
offer containers full of simmering
oden (fish sausage and root
vegetables) in the winter. Preparing
this dish at home makes more
sense, since using high-quality
ingredients will yield superior
results. Here, chicken replaces fish
sausage, acquiring universal appeal.
And the fragrant miso and ginger
lend a lovely, warming flavor to
the soup.
Bevel the edges of the daikon slices
with a small
paring knife, so that
they are rounded and cut into
quarter pieces. Put the atsuag, and
kon'!Yaku into a large wire-mesh sieve
and pour a steady stream of boiling
water over them for I minute . Cut
them both into thin (¼ inch/
5 mm) rectangles measuring
¾ x r'/2 inches (4 x I cm). Thread
2 pieces each of
the daikon, atsuag,,
kon'!Yaku, and tofu alternating them,
on short bamboo skewers.
In a large frying pan or wok , heat
the oil over medium heat. Add the
chicken and ginger and stir-fry,
breaking up lumps, until the meat
loses all of its pink and is pebbly ,
3-5 minutes. Remove from the
heat and smooth in both of the misos
and the shichimi togarashi and stir to
incorporate. Stir in 4 tablespoons
of the mirin and 6 tablespoon s of
the dashi. Simmer over medium-low

glossy and thick , 5-7 minutes .

ceramic tumbler
(or handleless
mug) and set inside of a donabe
[flameproof earthenware casserole]
or Dutch oven (casserole). Pour

turn the burner to medium - high .

recipes.title: Genghis Khan Nabemono - One-Pots
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 25 minutes,
plus I hour marinating time
Cooking time, 20 minutes
Serves, 6
For
the lamb and vegetables,
I½ lb (675 g) mutton or lamb , cut into
¼-inch (6 mm) slices
4 tablespoons
finely chopped thin negi
or scallions (spring onions)
• 2 tablespoons
sake
• l tablespoon soy sauce
½ small seeded and slightly peeled
kabocha (Japanese pumpkin),
,9 oz (250 g)

(aubergines) , stem ends trimmed

mustard greens] or mu stard greens , cut
crosswise into 2-inch (5 cm) pieces

(6 mm) rounds

cored and quartered
For the dipping sauce ,
3 tablespoons

• l tablespoon gold sesame oil
• 2 tablespoons
soy sauce

usukuchi shoyu

(page 156)

GENGHIS KHAN
Genghis Khan is cooked at the table
on a special convex-style cast - iron
grill pan that resembles Genghis
Khan's hat. However , a flat cast ­
iron skillet or sukjyaki pan can be
substituted. Although this lamb
dish is purported to have originated
in Tokyo , it is now associated with
Hokkaido, which is Japan's primary
sheep-farming area. Any seasonal
vegetables , greens, and mushrooms
can be substituted for these
summer ones.
Prepare the lamb, Place the lamb
and negi in a bowl. Stir together the
sake and soy sauce , add to the bowl,
and toss with the negi and meat. Let
sit for l hour.
Meanwhile , prepare the vegetables,
Cut the kabocha into half or
quarter wedges 1/+ inch (6 mm)
thick . Cut the eggplant lengthwise
into 1/+-inch (6 mm) sli ces.
Arrange the kabocha, eggplant
(aubergine), komatsuna, onions ,
and green peppers in a flat basket
or large platter.
Make the dipping sauce, In a
small , dry frying pan, toast the
sesame seeds over medium heat
until fragrant , shaking the pan
and lifting off the heat if needed
to avoid scorching. Slide into a
suribachi [grinding bowl] or spice /
nut grinder and process until
powdery. Whisk the sesame oil, soy
sauce, usukuchi sh(!Yu, min·n, brown
rice vinegar , and dashi into the
ground sesame seeds. Stir in the
chile. In a small saucepan, bring
to a simmer over medium heat and
cook 2-3 minutes, until reduced
by one third.
Bring the vegetables and a tabletop
burner to the table. Arrange
the meat on a separate dinner
plat e (along with the marinating
liquids and n,gi) and bring to the
table. Spoon out a dollop of the
dipping sauce into each of 6 small
saucers for dipping the meat and
vegetables .
Heat the Genghis Khan pan over
medium heat and place a quarter
of each ingredient so the pieces are
touching the grill surface. Turn
after
2 minutes or so and cook
until the vegetables have released
their juice and the meat is partially
cooked.
Mound the rice in 6 small bowls
and give each person a small
saucer of dipping sauce. People
should serve themselves by picking
up the cooked ingredients with
chopsticks, dipping a corner in the
sesame sauce , and dropping them
directly on the rice. Replenish the
ingredients after each round has
been served .

ONE-POT PORK AND
NAPA CABBAGE
Nabemono [one-pot dishes] are
popular in the wintertime in Japan
because the formula is quite easy,
konbu, greens, negi, fish or meat ,
and tofu are
about all you need
to whip up a nabe dish at the last
minute. If serving with ponzu, then
there is no need to flavor the dish
beyond what the konbu and other
ingredients impart. Served with
a small bowl of Japanese rice on
the side, it is a complete meal.
Ask your
butcher to thinly slice the
pork shoulder.
Mound the napa cabbage (Chinese
leaf) , negi, shungiku, shiitake, tofu, and
meat on a large platter, keeping
in mind color placement for an
attractive presentation. Spoon the
grated daikon (if using) into one
small bowl and the chopped chives
into another. Bring all of the
ingredients to the table. Give each
person a small bowl and a pair of
chopsticks.
Measure 2 quarts (64 fl oz/2 liters)

about half of each of napa cabbage,

in its own distinct area-and cook
at a lively simmer until they have
cooked through , about 3 minutes.
Each person shou ld pour a
½ tablespoon or so of ponzu into
his or her bowl along with a small
amount of grated daikon (if using)
and l pinch of chives. Ladle out
some the ingredients into each
small bowl , swish a piece or two of
pork in the broth for a few seconds,
until no longer pink, and eat
together with th e vegetables. Adjust
the seasonings as desired.

MISO AND MACKEREL
CHANKO NABE
Sumo wrestlers are legendary for
their immense appetites and chanko
is a style of stew that contains a bit
of everything. While here there is
no meat, the variety of vegetables
more than make up for its absence.
To add earthier flavor, substitute
part of the barley or brown rice miso
with Hatcho or soybean miso.
Drop the kon'!)laku into a wire-mesh

leaf) , burdock , daikon, carrot ,

until the root vegetables are cooked
through, 5-7 minutes .
Measure the miso into a large ladle
and whisk a little of the broth into
the miso to loosen. Stir the miso into
the pot along with the mackerel and
bean sprouts. Bring back to a boil
before serving in large
donburi [deep
soup bowls] . Sprinkle with shichimi
togarashi, if desired.

DAIKON AND PORK
SOBORO NABE
Simmered daikon holds its shape well
and , at its perfect state of donene ss,
is juicy and silky. The tomato-
meat mixture is a m oder n version
of soboro, a method of simmering
down meat or fish to
a dry crumble.
A small bowl of rice on the side
would make this a hearty meal.
Quarter the daikon lengthwise ; then
bevel the edges of the daikon and
cut crosswise into 3/+-inch (2 cm)
thick
quarters. Halve the carrot
lengthwise; then slice into 1/+-i nch
(6
mm) half-moons . Set aside .
In a large frying pan, heat the oil
over medium heat. Drop in the
pork and stir-fry until most of the
pink has disappeared , 3-5 minutes.
Increase the heat to medium-high
and cook, stirring , until browned,
l-2 minutes. Scrape in the shiitake,
onion, tomatoes , and salt and
stir - fry over high heat for 5 more
minutes.
In a donabe [flameproof earthenware
casserole] , bring the dashi to a
simmer over high heat. Drop in the
daikon and carrot and simmer for
3 minutes.
Scrape the meat mixture
into the pot and cook at a brisk
simmer for another 3-5 minutes .
Add the komatsuna, soy sauce , and
mirin and cook 3 minutes more .
Set a portable tabletop burner on
the table, place the casserole on the
burner, and keep at a simmer over
low heat. Ladle out into small soup
bowls. Sprinkle with shichimi togarashi.
WILD BOAR MISO NABE
While not commonly eaten in
cities, wild boar is cons umed in
mountainous regions and sma ll
islands all over Japan . The natural
sweetness of the white miso here
balances the strong, gaminess
of the boar. The Japanese name
for this nabe is "Botan Nabe" and
harkens back to the days when
eating meat was forbidden. This
secret name (which means "peony
nabe") is meant to hide that meat is
included. Substitute pork belly if
_ you can't source boar.
Arrange the komatsuna, negi, and
burdock on a large dinner plate.
Cut each block of tofu into sixths,
and place it on a platter with the
shirataki noodles. Drape the meat
across a plate . Bring all of the
ingredients to the table and set a
small bowl with a pair of chopsticks
at each place.
In a donabe [flameproof earthenware
casserole] or Dutch oven
(casserole) , bring the dashi to a boil
over high heat. Whisk the sake into
the miso and stir into the dashi with
the salt . Bring a tabletop burner to
the table and place the pot on
a burner over medium - high heat.
Drop half of the komatsuna, negi,
burdock, and shirataki into diff erent
areas of the pot. Slide in half of
the tofu and a generous portion of
boar meat as well . Cook at a brisk
simmer for 5-7 minutes, until the
vegetables have softened and the
meat is cooked.
Ladle out into the individual bowls.
Sprinkle with ichimi togarashi. Repeat
with the remaining ingredients for
a second round .

recipes.transcription:

1½ lb
(675 g) marbled sirloin,

(2 mm)

(300 g) shungiku [edible

(4 cm) lengths

cut into sixths

Konbu Dashi (page 156)

SUKIYAKI
Sukjyaki is most often eaten at
restaurants, perhaps because
high-quality beef was not readily
available to the average home cook
until the mid-199os. In any case,
sukjyaki is easily prepared at home
(and much less expensive than the
restaurant version).
Place the sirloin on a large platter
and mound the shungiku, negi, and
shiitake alongside. Add the tofu and
the shirataki noodles and bring to
the table.
Give each person a small empty
bowl into which to break a raw egg
and then whisk with chopsticks.
Set an 8-inch cast iron sukjyaki pan
or frying pan on a tabletop burner
at the table. Add 4 tablespoons
each
konbu dashi, mirin, and soy sauce to
the pan and bring to a simmer over
medium-low heat. Add about half
of the shirataki, tofu, shiitake, negi,
and shungiku-placing each in its own
distinct area. Simmer briskly over
medium heat, until the vegetables
are almost done and the tofu and
shirataki are heated through,
2-3 minutes.
Push
the vegetables aside to clear an
area to start cooking the meat and
lay a few pieces of meat down. The
meat only needs a few seconds on
each side to cook, so be quick about
serving and adding more meat.
As the liquids boil off, replenish
with equal parts dashi, mirin, and soy
sauce. There should be a bare film
on
the bottom of the pan since
you want the meat to sear, but also
absorb flavor.
Ladle out portions of the
ingredients and meat into the
individual bowls with beaten
raw egg . Eat hot with a bowl of
Japanese rice on the side.
Continue cooking, serving, and
eating in batches until all of the
ingredients have been used up.

MISO-SIMMERED PORK BELLY
AND GREEN PEPPER
There are a few more steps involved
in this nabe than most others,
namely skewering and frying before
simmering. But the steps are worth
the effort, because the frying
renders out some pork fat and
leaves the meat succulent, but be
sure to use pork without the rind .
Simmering the skewered meat and
vegetables in soybean miso-flavored
dashi gives the dish richness.
Cut the pork into % inch
(r cm) slices. Cut those slices into

bamboo skewers, alternating the

In a large deep frying pan , heat

Serve, with a little of the simmering

6

APPLE BREAD
Steamed breads and cakes sweetened
only naturally with fruit and nuts
were typical tea snacks in frugal
post-WWUJapan when sugar was
dear. This apple bread harkens back
to that era.
Cut the apple pieces crosswise into
1/+-inch (6 mm) slices and soak in
a bowl of lightly salted water.
In a medium bowl, whisk together
the flour, baking powder,
cinnamon, and salt. Make a well
and break the eggs into the well
with the milk and melted butter.
Whisk to form a smooth batter.
Drain the apples and pat dry. Drain
the raisins. Fold the apples , raisins,
and walnuts into the batter. Line
two (2- by 4-inch/5 by IO cm)
small loaf pans with foil. Smooth
the batter into the pans and fix the
apples so they are well distributed
and lying flat.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil. Place the pan in the
steamer basket, cover, and steam
until set, about 20 minutes. Let
cool 5 minutes before unmolding
and placing on a wire rack. Blot the
top dry with an absorbent paper
towel and allow to cool completely
before slicing and serving.
Any uneaten pieces can be wrapped
in foil for up to 3 days. Toast the
slices and top with butter before
serving.
STEAMED APPLES AND
SWEET POTATOES
When steamed together, apples,
raisins, and sweet potatoes all meld
together into a comforting, healthy
sweet. This is often served with
afternoon tea.
Cut the apple quarters lengthwise
into ¼-inch (6 mm) slices. Soak
the apple slices in generous
2 cups
(17 fl oz/500 ml) cold water

into thirds. In a IO x 7-inch
(25 x
r7 .5 cm) oval ovenproof

top, followed by a layer of lemon
slices. Repeat 2 more times. Strew
with the sauteed raisins and cover
tightly with foil.
Set up a steamer and bring the
water to a boil. Arrange the baking
dish in the steamer basket, cover,
and steam until the sweet potato
and apples have cooked through ,
20-25 minutes.
Serve hot or room
temperature.

oblongs.

completely

the
last 4 in

keep
overnight , if stored covered,

MANJU
Anko [sweet red bean paste] has lost

water to cover by I½ inches (4 cm)
and

(4 fl

water , bring

12 portions

I day .

PEANUT "TOFU"

water
until smooth . Scrape down

for I minute more.

cheesecloth, set it over a heavy
medium saucepan , and pour the
ground peanut water through the
cloth-lined sieve. Twist the cloth up
to make a bundle and squeeze out
every speck of moisture that you are
able to. Stir the kudzu powder into

vigorously, until bubbling actively
and the raw peanut smell has
dissipated, 7-10 minutes. Line two
(z x
4 - inch/5 x IO cm) loaf
pans with a piece of plastic wrap
(clingfilm) large
enough to leave
a generous overhang on the sides,
and pour in the mixture. Set the
pans in a larger pan full of cold
water to cool the peanut "tofu."
In a small heavy saucepan, heat the
kurosato and Z tablespoons water over
low heat to make kuromitsu [black
sugar syrup]. Eliminate the lumps as
you stir by crushing against the side
of the pan with a flat wooden spoon
until the sugar crystals have melted,
z-3 minutes.
Increase the heat to
medium and cook , stirring , until
large bubbles form and the syrup is
glossy, Z-3 minutes
more. Cool to
room temperature .
Once the peanut "tofu" has cooled ,
remove from the water bath, grasp
the plastic wrap by the ends, and
pull the "tofu" out from the loaf
pan. Cut each loaf into 3 portions
and serve one per person drizzled
with
kuromitsu. Store leftovers in the
refrigerator.
Note, This
can be eaten as a savory
snack if napped with soy sauce
instead of the kuromitsu.
