GOHEI MOCHI
In Takayama , a popular mountain
town destination in Gifu prefec­
ture, the streets are redolent of the
aroma of charcoal-grilledgohei mochi.
If possible, try to go the extra mile
and grill outside , rather than under
the broiler (grill). This is a salty,
creamy snack that is best served hot
with tea in the afternoon.
Soak 5 small bamboo skewers in
water for 30 minutes. In a small ,
dry frying pan, toast the sesame
seeds over medium heat until
fragrant, shaking the pan and
lifting off the heat if needed to
avoid scorching, about 30 seconds.
Slide into a
suribachi [grinding bowl]
and grind until broken down to a
paste. Mash in the mirin and miso to
combine and set aside.
Wipe off the surikogi [grinding
pestle] used for smashing the
sesame and wash. Dump the cooked
rice into a large bowl and pound
with the surikogi until the rice
adheres together into a sticky mass.
There will still be visible grains of
rice, however.
Prepare a small bowl of water
next to your work surface and wet
your palms and fingers . Divide
the dough into 3 equal
portions.
Working with one portion at a
time, form 5 small
balls (dipping
your palms and fingers in the
water , when needed, to keep the
rice from sticking to your hands),
for a total of 15. Thread 3 balls
on
each skewer.
Light the charcoal in an outdoor
grill (barbecue) and let reduce to
ash-covered embers. (Or position
a rack 4 inches/Io cm
from the
heat source and preheat the broiler
[grill] .) Grill or broil for about
6 minutes, turning every 2 minutes,
until evenly browned all over.
Smooth the miso paste around the
balls and cook for another I½
minutes on each of three "sides ."
SWEET MISO-GLAZED
TOFU BARS
These little tofu bars make a healthy
and delicious afternoon snack.
Slice each tofu horizontally through
the middle to create two layers.
Quarter those layers crosswise to
make 8 bars each, for a total of 16
small bars. Arrange the bars on
a cutting board and prop a small
saucer underneath to angle the
board into the kitchen sink (to
catch drips). Lay another cutting
board on top of the tofu (take care
that it 's not too heavy to avoid
smashing the tofu) to press out
moisture for 20 minutes .
In a small saucepan, stir together
'I• cup (60 ml) water, the mirin , sake,
and miso and cook, stirring , over
low heat , until no longer shiny,
3-4 minutes.
In a large frying pan,
heat
I tablespoon of the oil over medium
heat. Add half of the tofu bars and
fry both sides until golden brown,
I-2 minutes.
Wipe out the pan,
add the remaining I tablespoon oil
and fry the remaining 8 bars.
Smooth the miso on the bars,
sprinkle with ichimi togarashi, and
a few sansho leaves. Serve 2-3 per
person
as is, or threaded on a
teppogushi [bamboo paddle skewer].

Okinawa's cultural heritage is not
considered part of main stream
Japan because it has its roots in
China and the United States (due
to the occupation). There are not
many Okinawan dishes in this
book , but these donuts are iconic .
In a medium bowl , whisk together

suribachi U apanese grinding bowl]

batter.

but still a little warm , stir in the

6 eggs , at room temperature
• 3 tablespoons
sugar

(page
397; see Note)

KARA! DASH!
Stir the kaeshi and dashi together in

SOY MILK GRATIN
Preheat the oven to 395°F (200°C /
Gas Mark 5) .
Cut the mushrooms into
manageable lengths or the
vegetables into bite-size pieces.
In a small frying pan , heat the
sesame oil over medium heat.
Add the flour and cook , stirring
constantly, until paste - like , about
l minute . Reduce the heat to low
and gradually add the soy milk while
slowly stirring so the mixture does
not form a ball.
Once all of the soy milk has been
incorporated and the sauce is
smooth, stir in the salt and karai
dashi and continue stirring until
the consistency is creamy and no
longer loose, but has not become
too thick .
Strew the mushrooms or vegetables
in a 6-inch (15 cm) gratin dish ,
scrape the soy milk sauce over
them, and bake until browned and
bubbling , about 15 minutes.
Note, To get 3 1/2 tablespoons karai
dashi, combine 2 ½ teaspoons kaeshi
with 8 teaspoons dashi.
DASH! MAKI TAMAGO
Break 3 eggs into a small bowl
and the remaining 3 eggs
into
another small bowl and whisk until
emulsified but not frothy .
Measure 1½ tablespoons
sugar into
each of 2 small bowls. Slowly stir
6 tablespoons amadashi into each
bowl until the sugar crystals have
completely dissolved. Whisk one
bowl of the sweetened amadashi into
each bowl of eggs, taking care not
to create foam .
In a small rectangular Japanese
omelet pan , heat l tablespoon of
the sesame oil over medium-low
heat , tipping the pan for even
coverage. Pour the contents of one
of the bowls into the pan and roll
it around so the egg has covered
CHEFS
the entire surface of the pan. While
still soft , starting at the far end of the
pan, roll the egg mixture towards you
to form a log . Add the remaining
l tablespoons oil. Tip the pan
again to distribute the oil, lifting
up the rolled egg to get a little oil
underneath it. Add the contents of
the second bowl and allow the eggs to
evenly cover the surface of the pan ,
including underneath the first egg
roll.
While still soft, roll the formed
egg log away from you , gathering
up the new half - cooked egg layer in
the pan as you go. Turn out onto
a board, cut crosswise into 6 pieces,
and serve .
Note, To get¾ cup (6 fl oz / 180 ml)
amadashi, combine l tablespoon
kaeshi with ½ cup plus 3 tablespoons
(5
½ fl oz/150 ml) dashi.

recipes.title: Shinobu Namae L' Effervescence 2-25-4 Nishi-Azabu
recipes.transcription:

Preparation time, 30 minutes
Cooking time, IO minutes

2 pieces
(12-inch/30 cm) konbu
II oz (320 g) bonito [skipjack tuna],
cut into sixteen 3/+ oz (20 g) slices
• I teaspoon fine sea salt
5 fuki no to [butterbur buds, page 430]

• 4 tablespoons raw sugar

cold-pressed sesame oil
r6 medium or 24 small
green

iso [shiso buds]. buds

SHINOBU NAMAE
L' EFFERVESCENCE
2-25-4 NISHI-AZABU
MINATO-KU,
TOKYO
JAPAN
Seven years after graduating from Keio University with a degree in Political
Science, Shinobu Namae became the sous chef at Michel Bras Toyajapon
in Hokkaido.
In 2008, he spent a year as sous chef and in pastry at
The Fat Duck in London, after which he returned to Tokyo to open
L'Effervescence as executive chef and director. L'Effervescence earned
its first Michelin star in 20II and its second in 2015. L'Effervescence
has consistently ranked high on Asia's 50 Best Restaurant list and in 2017
was ranked number 12. Namae's
food is poetic, soulful, and delicious.
BONITO SASHIMI WITH
BUTTERBUR MISO AND SHISO
Lay a sheet of konbu on a work
surface and arrange the bonito
on top. Press the other sheet of
konbu over the fish and leave for
15 minutes to increase the umami
and eliminate any fish odors. This
technique is called kobujime.
In a medium saucepan, combine
generous 2 cups (17 fl oz/500 ml)
water and the salt to make a 1%
salt solution. Bring to a simmer
over medium heat and drop in
the fuki no to. Blanch for about
IO minutes , until they lose most
of their sharp bitterness. Drain in
a fine - mesh sieve and blot dry in
a clean tea towel.
400 CHEFS
In a
medium bowl , smash together
the miso and sugar. Slowly mash
in the vinegar and oil to form a
smooth paste. Fold in the fuki no
to and mix gently with a rubber
spatula to distribute the fuki no to
evenly into the miso mixture.
Spread I tablespoon of the faki no to
miso on top of 8 of the bonito slices.
Lay 2 medium or 3 small shiso leaves
on top and finish the "sandwich "
with a second slice of bonito. Strew
with 3 hojiso and serve immediately .

recipes.title: Lily Bulb And Shirako Tempura With Matcha Salt 401 1/ I 7 Chefs
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 20 minutes , plus
6 hours chilling time
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Serves, 4
5 teaspoons fine sea salt
2 lily bulbs, root ends cross cut
IO½ oz (300 g) shirako [cod milt]
Neutral oil (such as canola or safflower,
for deep-frying
I egg, at room temperature
'I, cup (13/+ oz/ 50 g) all-purpose
(plain) flour , plus more for dredging
• I teaspoon matcha salt (see Note)
LILY BULB AND SHIRAKO
TEMPURA WITH MATCHA SALT
In a medium saucepan , combine
generous 2 cups (17 fl oz/500 ml)
water and 2 teaspoons of the sea salt
to make a 2% salt solution. Bring to
a brisk simmer over medium-high
heat. Drop in the lily bulbs, reduce
the heat to medium-low , and
simmer gently-otherwise they will
fall apart. Cook until the root end
is soft when pierced with a metal
skewer , several minutes. Remove
from the water and cool on a rack
set over a pan to catch drips.
To clean the shirako, plunge them in
generous 2 cups (17 fl oz/500 ml)
cold water and 2 teaspoons of the
sea salt to make a 2 % salt solution.
Cover and refrigerate for at least
6 hours to leach out any blood.
Drain.
Set up a bowl of ice and water in the
sink. In a medium saucepan, bring
a generous 2 cups (17 fl oz / 500 ml)
water and the remaining I teaspoon
sea salt (1% salt solution) to a
simmer over medium heat and add
the shirako. Cook at a gentle simmer
until the outside skin has a stiff
tension but they are not cooked
through (you will be frying them
later) , about I minute. Drain and
cool in the ice bath. Drain well and
pat dry in a tea towel.
401 1/ I 7 CHEFS
Pour 5 inches (ro cm) oil into
a heavy medium pot and heat over
medium-high heat until hot but
not smoking.
In a small bowl , whisk generous
2 cups (17 fl oz/500 ml) cold water
and the egg lightly into the flour to
form a smooth, but not overmixed,
tempura batter.
Use a soft natural fiber brush
to
dust the shirako with flour .
Dip the lily bulbs and shirako into
the tempura batter, shake off excess
batter , and fry the lily buds for
about I minute and the shirako for
about 2 minutes, until golden
brown. Drain on paper towels for
a couple of seconds , then place
attractively on a plate. Sprinkle
with the matcha salt and serve
immediately.
Note, To make matcha salt, combine
I 2 parts fine sea salt to I part match a
powder.

recipes.title: Daikon Shiokoji "Steak" With Gingered Nori Sauce
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: l hour to l hour 30
minutes, plus 12 hours marinating time
Cooking time: 25 minutes
Serves: 4 as
an appetizer
4 (2-inch / 5
cm) pieces daikon ,
(14 oz/ 400 g)
l tablespoon fine sea salt, ½ teaspoon
for seasoning the dashi
· 4 tablespoons uncooked Japanese
rice
2 tablespoons
cold - pressed sesame oil
• 1/2 teaspoon soy sauce
• Scant 2 teaspoons mirin
· Scant 3 tablespoons
sake
Generous 2 teaspoons grated
fresh ginger
l tablespoon plus l teaspoon well­
crushed kudzu powder
16 sheets
crumbled nori
For the shiokoji:
4 tablespoons
plus 4 teaspoons
rice koji
· l cup (8 fl oz/250 ml) amazake
• l tablespoon plus l teaspoon soy sauce
For the katsuobushi dashi:
· 6-inches (15 cm) konbu
3 small handfuls (15 g) freshly shaved
katsuobushi
DAIKON SHIOKOJI "STEAK"
WITH
GINGERED NORI SAUCE
Bevel the edges of the daikon slices .
In a large saucepan , combine
generous 6 cups (50 fl oz/r.5 liters)
water and l tablespoon of the salt
to make a 1% salt
solution. Add the
rice and bring to a brisk simmer
over medium-high heat. Drop in
the daikon and cook until soft when
pierced with a bamboo skewer,
10-15 minutes. Drain and allow the
daikon to cool to room temperature.
Make the shiokoji: In a small bowl,
mix together½ cup (120ml) water,
the rice koji, amazake, and soy sauce.
Slip in the daikon slices, cover , and
marinate at room temperature for
I2 hours.
Remove
the daikon from the
marinade and wipe any lingering
shiokoji off. Discard the marinade.
In a small frying pan, heat the
oil over high heat and sear the
daikon until warmed to the center ,
I-2 minutes. Adjust the heat if
browning too quickly as shiokoji­
treated foods color easily.
Make the katsuobushi dashi: In
a small saucepan, gently bring
generous 2 cups (17 fl oz /
500 ml) water with the konbu to
1/ .I 7 CHEFS
150°F (65°C)
over medium­
low heat. Remove from the heat
and let stand for 30 minutes
to I hour. Take out the konbu
and discard or use for another
purpose. Set the saucepan over
medium-high heat and bring to
a boil. Remove from the heat and
add the katsuobushi. Once it floats
down to the bottom of the pan,
strain through cheesecloth into a
medium bowl, but do not press on
the cloth or squeeze the katsuobushi
by hand. Season with the soy sauce ,
the remaining ½ teaspoon salt,
mirin, sake, and ginger. Stir scant
2 teaspoons cold water into the
kudzu powder and add to the dashi.
Simmer over low heat for 20-30
seconds until the kudzu becomes
transparent. Add the nori and stir
over low heat for another I-2
minutes, until the nori melts and the
mixture becomes a well-emulsified,
black sauce.
Set the daikon in the center of a salad
plate and drizzle the sauce on top.
Serve as an appetizer.

recipes.title: Matsutake, Burdock, And Kyoto Carrot Kinpira Grilled Shime Saba With
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: IO minutes
Cooking time, 5 minutes
Serves, 4 as
an appetizer
2 tablespoons gold sesame oil
8 oz (240 g) burdock root , finely
julienned
4 oz (120 g) Kyoto or other red-orange
carrot , finely julienned
Scant 2 teaspoons soy sauce
• Scant 2 teaspoons mirin

shredded by hand into
julienne-like strips

warmed in a small , dry frying pan
Finely grated zest of ½ yuzu or 'I•
Meyer lemon

1½ tablespoons fine sea salt

2 teaspoons shiro miso [white mi so]
3/+ cup
(6 fl oz/r8o ml) rice vinegar

l ripe Fu yu persimmon, peeled , pitted ,
and sliced into thin wedges
MATSUTAKE, BURDOCK, AND
KYOTO CARROT KINPIRA
In a small frying pan , heat the
oil over medium heat. Once well
warmed , but not burning hot , add
the burdock and carrot and stir - fry
for l minute to distribute the oil.
Stir in the soy sauce and mirin and
stir-fry until soft , 3-4 minutes.
Add
the matsutake, remove from the
heat , and toss for about 30 seconds
to wilt. Slide into a small bowl,
sprinkle with the sesame seeds ,
and top with the JIL{U zest. Serve
immediately.
GRILLED SHIME SABA WITH
SWEET PERSIMMON MISO SAUCE
In a small bowl , mix together
the salt and sugar . Measure out
a heaping ½ teaspoon (3 g) of
the salt / sugar mixture, 2% of the
weight of the fish , and reserve the
rest for the next time you cure
mackerel.
Rin se the mackerel and pat dry .
Place the fish in a small rectangular
pan and sprinkle both sides with
the measured out salt and sugar
mixture. Refrigerate, uncovered ,
for 2 hours.
In a small bowl, stir together the
miso, a generous 1/2 teaspoon of the
rice vinegar , I teaspoon of the mirin ,
the egg yolk, and oil.
Rins e the mackerel under cold
running water and pat dry. Tn a
small rectangular container, mix
togeth er the remaining rice vin egar
and mirin and slip in the mackerel
so that it is completely submerged.
1/i7 CHEFS
Allow to marinate for 15-20
minutes at room temperature . This
preparation is called shime saba.
Sear all surfaces quickly on a hot
grill or with a culinary blowtorch .
Cool by plunging in ice water to
stop the cooking. Once cool, about
I minute , remove from the ice
water and pat dry. Slice off the belly
bones and pin bones with a razor
sharp thin knife and peel off the
skin slipping your fingers under the
skin and peeling it back. Cut into
¼-inch (6 mm) slices.
Divide the grilled shime saba slices
among 4 salad plates , placing them
in an attractive , overlapping stack
left of center . Place the persimmon
pieces in a similar fashion to the
right of center , next to the shime
saba. Drizzle with the miso sauce and
serve immediately as an appetizer.

recipes.title: Shinichiro Sakamoto Yuyado Sakamoto 15-47 Uedomachi Jisha
recipes.transcription:
•

24 hours marinating time

• Neutral oil, such as canola (rapeseed),
peanut, or safflower, for frying

or whitebait
% cup (roo g) unbleached pastry flour ,

julienned

(page 156)
SHINICHIRO SAKAMOTO
YUYADO SAKAMOTO
15-47 UEDOMACHI JISHA
suzu SHI, ISHIKAWA-KEN
JAPAN
Shinichiro Sakamoto and his wife operate an austerely elegant inn near the
top of the Noto Peninsula. Sakamoto learned his craft from experiencing
the food offered at the best and most interesting restaurants across Japan
and in the countries in which he traveled abroad. Local fish, vegetables,
condiments, herbs, and the full harvest of the sea are his inspiration. Chef
Sakamoto' s food is deceptively spare and deeply considered. These recipes
are from the staff meal at Sakamoto, known as makanai in Japan.
NANBAN-ZUKE MAME AJI
Pour 4 inches (ro cm) oil into
a heavy medium pot and set over
medium-low heat.
Rinse and pat dry the
fish and
toss
with the flour to coat. Shake
off excess flour. Increase the heat
under the oil to medium-high until
the oil is hot but not smoking (test
by dropping a pinch of flour into
the oil-it should float immediately
back up to the top and not sink to
the bottom). Working in batches,
fry the fish until
golden brown,
3-4 minutes per batch, depending
on size. Be careful not to fry too
hot or the stomachs will burst.
Drain on paper towels.
In a rectangular lidded container
just big enough to hold the fish
and
vegetables, make two layers,
1/:,: 7 CHEFS
Place half the fish side by side
across
the bottom of the container
and strew with half of the onions,
piman, and carrot. Sprinkle with
half of the ginger juice and ichimi
togarashi. Repeat with the rest of the
fish, vegetables , ginger
juice , and
ichimi togarashi.
In a bowl, whisk together the
vinegar , mirin1 usukuchi sh'!)'u, and
dashi. Pour over the layered fish and
vegetables.
Cover and refrigerate
for 24 hours, to absorb the
marinade. Since the vegetables
leach out liquid and dilute the
flavor, taste before serving and add
more rice vinegar or usukuchi sh'!)'u,
if needed.

recipes.title: Bozushi Soy-Pickled Dai Kon 1/.I 7 Chefs
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, I hour , plus I-2 hours
weighing time
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Serves,
4-6
2 1/ • cup s (r lb / 450 g) uncooked
Japanese rice
4 - inch (ro cm) square piece konbu
2 1/ . lb (r kg) whole sashimi - grade horse
mackerel or sardines (about 4)
3 ½ teaspoons fine sea
salt , plus more
as needed
½ tablespoon grated fresh ginger
8 ½ tablespoons rice vinegar
· r½ tablespoons sugar
2 tablespoons
finely slivered
young ginger
Preparation time : 15 minutes , plus
2-3 hours pickling time

ro½ oz (300 g) daikon , scrubbed and
halved lengthwise

mirin

sake

BOZUSHI
Measure the rice into a heavy
medium cast-iron pot. Fill with
water to the top of the pot to rinse ,
then drain off the water. Scrub with

drain several times until the water
runs clear . Drain and add 2¼ cups
(r8
fl oz / 540 ml) water. Drop in
the konbu and soak for 30 minutes ,
covered.
Meanwhile , remove the head and
guts of the fish with
a sharp knife
and separate into boneless fillets.
Pull off the skins. Rinse in cold
water, place in a shallow pan , and
sprinkle the fillets with salt on both
sides. Let sit for IO minutes to
cure. Rinse the fillets and the pan
in cold water, and pat both dry.
Return the fillets to the pan, shiny
side down , and spread the grated
ginger across the fish .
In a small bowl, stir together
4 tablespoons
vinegar into
2 teaspoons
salt. Drizzle the vinegar
mixture over the fish and allow to
marinate for IO minutes. Drain,
discard the marinade , and set the
fillets aside on a small plate.
In a small bowl, mix together
the remaining 4½ tablespoons
vinegar, sugar , and I½ teaspoons
salt. Stir occasionally to help the
salt dissolve .
Bring the rice to a boil over high
heat. This will take about
4 minutes.
Reduce the heat to low
and cook for about IO minutes.
Remove from the heat and let rest
for 5 minutes before turning out
onto a
handai [wide wooden tub] or
large wooden board. Sprinkl 7 the
surface evenly with the sweetened

Lay out 4 large pieces
of plastic
wrap (clingfilm) on a work surface

(5 cm)

on top to weight for I to
2 hours
at
room temperature. If the weather
is hot, store in the refrigerator.

cut crosswise (through the plastic
wrap) into sixths, and serve.

Slice the daikon halves into ¼ - inch

and blot off excess moisture (and

1/.I 7 CHEFS
In a small bowl , whisk the soy

and place an otoshibuta [ drop lid]
and weight on top. Leave at room

minutes

to 8

(400 g) shirataki noodles

Place the inaka miso in a small bowl

(4 fl

(at the table) over medium-high
heat. Simmer for I minute before
stirring in the sake-thinned miso,
negi, shirataki, and crab. Bring back
to a simmer, cook for I more
minute, then ladle in theyuba.
Simmer for 3 more minutes,
blotting off any top scum with a
folded piece of paper towel. Ladle
into individual bowls
for serving
and sprinkle with ichimi togarashi,
if desired.

12 hours

Serves, 8
I kinmedai (Japanese golden eye
snapper), about 4½ lb (2 kg),
filleted,
skin on, (see Note)

shiso leaves

AUSTRALIA
Martin Benn, chef/owner of Sepia Restaurant, started his cooking career
in London, working at the Oak Room, the Landmark, and the Criterion.
In 1996 he relocated to Australia, and in 1999 gained a place at Tetsuya' s
working under ChefTetsuya Wakuda, where he became head chef at
twenty-five years old.
KINMEDAI SASHIMI, MYOGA,
AND FRIED SHISO
Remove the pin bones from the
kinmedai fillets. Place the fillets on a
tray skin side up , making sure that
there are no scales on the fillet.
Using
a blowtorch, lightly sear the
skin, then leave to cool and relax.
Soak the konbu in water for
30 minutes, then drain and pat
dry. (The soaking will dou hie the
size of the konbu.)
Place the konbu on a tray. Place the
kinmedai flesh side down onto the
konbu, cover and refrigerate for
12 hours
before use.
Pat dry the shiso leaves to remove the
salt and moisture , and let stand at
room temperature for 2-3 hours ,
until
the leaves are dry .
Halve the "!)'oga lengthwise, then
finely slice on
a mandoline. Soak in
ice water for 30 minutes before use.
Pour the I quart (r liter) oil into
a heavy
pot and heat the oil to
320°F (160°C). One at a time, fry
the shiso leaves until crisp. Drain
on paper towels and set aside in a
warm place.
1/ I 7 CHEFS
In a bowl, mix together the shiro
sh'!)'U and 7 tablespoons sesame oil
and set aside.
Using a sashimi knife, cut the
kinmedai into even thin slices a scant
½ oz (10 g) each (6-8 slices per
person). Lay the slices in a single
layer on a tray and lightly warm
using a blowtorch. Do not heat too
much, just a light sear to warm the
oils in the fish.
Spoon
some of the sh'!)'u and sesame
dre ssing over the kinmedai. Arrange
the fish on
serving plates and lightly
dress again if required. Drain the
"!)'Dga well on paper towels, then
sprinkle evenly over the fish. Break
up the fried shiso leaves and scatter
over the myoga. Finish with fresh
baby shiso leaves.
Note, You should end up with
about I¾ lb (800 g) of fish total.

Make the citrus soy sauce, Pour the

Discard
the konbu and add the yuzu
juice to combine. Store in the
refrigerator until it is time to grill
the shiitake.
Prepare the shiitake, Light the
charcoal in an outdoor grill
(barbecue) and let reduce to ash­
covered embers.
Wipe the shiitake with a cloth and
trim off the woody part of the stem.
Place in a bowl and coat lightly with
some white sesame oil and sea salt.
1/ I 7 CHEFS
Place
the shiitake on the grill
(barbecue) and cook until tender
and golden, about 5 minutes.
Transfer
to the bowl of citrus soy
sauce. Let marinate for I minute,
then scoop out of the sauce.
To serve, stack about 5 shiitake in
each of 8 warm serving bowls.
Drizzle with more citrus soy sauce
and grateyuzu zest on top. Finish
with shiso or oba chiffonade.

recipes.title: Kabu, Awase Miso Broth, Chrysanthemum, And Nori 4,Io Chefs
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 30 minutes
Cooking time, 30 minutes
Serves, 8
3 - inch (8 cm) piece konbu
IO kabu [Tokyo turnips] , golf ball size ,
greens attached
Scant I oz (25 g) katsuobushi
7 oz
(200 g) awase miso (a mixture of
dark and light miso)
• Tosa soy sauce [soy sauce infused with
bonito flakes , optional]
Neutral oil, such as white sesame or
canola (rapeseed)
To serve:
3 scallions (spring onions)
3 sheets nori, cut into fine julienne

flowers ,
petals picked
KABU, AWASE MISO BROTH,
CHRYSANTHEMUM, AND NORI
In a saucepan , combine the konbu
and 2 quarts (2 liters) water and
bring to 144°F (62°C).
Either
maintain the water temperature or
remove from the heat and let steep
for 30 minutes.
Meanwhile , remove the green stems
and leaves from the kabu and set
aside the nice tender ones (discard
the rest). Rinse the leaves and stems
under cold running water, then pat
dry and set aside.
Trim the kabu and use a r½-inch
(4 cm)
round cutter to cut cylinders
around the middle of the kabu.
Repeat for a total of IO cylinders.
Rinse under running water , then
slice crosswise into disks 1/ , inch
(r cm) thick.
Remove the konbu from the water.
Add the kabu disks , bring to a
simmer , and cook gently until just
tender, about 4 minutes. Remove
from the heat but leave in the dashi
stock.
Measure out I quar t (r liter) of the
kabu cooking liquid and transfer to
another pot. Bring to a simmer ,
add the katsuobushi, and remove from
the heat. Cover with a lid and let
infuse for 15 minutes.
4,IO CHEFS
Strain the dashi into a clean pan and
bring back to a simmer. Remove
the pan from the heat and place a
sieve over the
dashi. Add the miso and
push through the sieve into the dashi
stock. Stir to combine . Season with
a little soy sauce, if desired. Keep
the awase miso broth warm.
To serve, Cut the scallions (spring
onions) into fine julienne
and
placed in ice water for 30 minutes
before serving.
Cut the kabu stems in half so that
they are more manageable. Heat
a frying pan over medium to high
heat and add a little white sesame
oil.
Saute the kabu stems and leaves
until just wilted but still crisp and
remove from the pan .
Place the kabu stems and leaves into
the bottom of 8 warmed serving
bowls. Arrange the disks of warm
kabu over the stems. Warm the awase
miso broth and pour around and
over the kabu. Drain the scallions
(spring onions) and place on top
of the kabu. Finish with the nori and
chrysanthemum petals.

recipes.title: Crab And Egg Yolk Rice Bowl With Aonori Salt And Kinome
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time: 15 minutes
Cooking time, 15 minutes
Serves,
8
For the aonori salt,
3 g
coarse sea salt crystals
1/, oz (12 g) aonori [powdered green
nori] , toasted
For the crab and egg yolk rice,
• 14 tablespoons
(7 oz/200 g)
unsalted butter
14 oz
(400 g) raw spanner crabmeat,
picked over for shells and cartilage
% cup (5 fl oz/r50 ml) ichiban dashi
• Scant 3 tablespoons
mirin
Scant 3 tablespoons
light soy sauce
· 2 % cups (17 oz/ 480 g) steamed
Koshihikari rice
16 Taiyouran egg yolks or good
quality egg yolks
• 16 sprigs kinome
[leaves of sansho plant]
CRAB AND EGG YOLK RICE BOWL
WITH AONORI SALT AND KINOME
Make the aonori salt, Place the sea
salt in a mortar and pestle and
grind. Add the toasted aonori and
grind together to a fine powder.
Set
aside .
Make the crab and egg yolk rice,
In
each of 2 large saute pans,
melt
7 tablespoons (105 g) butter over
medium
heat until it bubbles .
(This recipe is best done in two
larger pans for a more even
cooking.) Dividing evenly, spread
the crabmeat over the bottom of
the pans. Cook over medium heat
until about two-thirds cooked (the
crabmeat it still a little opaque) ,
2-3 minutes.
4n 1/ .I 7 CHEFS
In a small bowl, stir together the
dashi, min·n, and soy sauce. Divide the
mixture between the pans. Reduce
the heat to medium - low and add
half the cooked rice to each pan.
Stir to separate the grains slightly.
Lightly whisk the egg yolks, then
divide between the pans, gently
stirring with a spatula . Increase
the heat slightly to cook the eggs,
but do not overcook. Once the
rice mixture is thickened and
unctuous from the eggs, spoon
into serving bowls.
Sprinkle with the
aonori salt and
sprigs of kinome. Serve hot.

recipes.title: Shuko Oda Koya Bar 50 Frith Street
recipes.transcription:
•
Preparation time: 5 minutes , plus
overnight pickling
Cooldng time:
35 minutes
Serves: 2
I handful ramsons (wild garlic)
• Soy sauce
I oz (25 g) freshly shaved katsuobushi
(see Note)
5 g
dried konbu (see Note)
· 3½ tablespoons mirin
· Vegetable oil, for deep-frying
2 pieces
tofu, about 2¾ x 2 x
¾ inch
(7 x 5 x 2 cm)
Potato starch, for dredging
2 teaspoons
grated fresh ginger
SHUKO ODA
KOYA BAR
50 FRITH STREET
LONDON W1D 4SQ
UNITED
KIN GD OM
Raised in the United Kingdom in a Japanese household , Chef Shuko Oda
worked in the kitchen of Claska hotel in Tokyo before joining the Koya
family, She also studied udon-maldng at
Kunitoraya in Paris.
AGEDASHI TOFU WITH
PICKLED AND FRESH RAMSON
Take one-third of the ramsons and
place them in an upright container.
Add enough soy sauce to cover them
(ramsons shrink as they pickle so
you don't need a lot of soy sauce).
Lay a sheet of plastic wrap (cling
film) on
top and a light weight
on top of that to make sure the
ramsons soak well. Leave them
to pickle overnight before using.
Soak the katsuobushi and konbu (wipe
with damp cloth before using) for
a couple of minutes in 2 cups
(r6 fl oz/ 500 ml) water heated
to 185 °F (85°C). Reserving the
broth, strain through cheesecloth
into a small saucepan. Add a scant
½ cup (3 1/2 fl oz/roo ml) soy sauce
and the mirin and bring to a boil.
Keep hot while you fry the tofu.
Pour 4 inches
(ro cm) oil into
a heavy medium pot and heat to
320°F (r6o°C).
Drain the tofu pieces on paper
towels for 5 minutes to get rid of
excess liquid. Dredge the tofu in
the potato starch and brush off any
excess so the tofu is covered in a
thin layer of the starch.
1/ :r. 7 CHEFS
Add the tofu to the hot oil and fry
until all surfaces of the tofu are
crispy , about 6 minutes.
Plate the tofu in individual bowls or
plates with depth. Lay fresh whole
pieces of ramson on top, neatly one
after another. Pour in the hot dashi
slowly from the top, enough to half
cover the tofu; the heat of the
dashi
will also cook the ramson slightly.
Roughly chop the pickled ramsons
and place a little mountain of them
on top of the tofu, along with the
grated ginger.
Note: To make a vegan
dashi, omit
the katsuobushi and increase the
amount of konbu to I oz (25 g). Steep
the konbu for r5 minutes in 2 cups
(r6 fl oz/500 ml) water heated to
r40°F (6o°C).
Reserving the broth,
strain through cheesecloth.

recipes.title: Clams, Fava Beans, And Capers Steamed In Dashi Butter Grilled Hake With Spiced
recipes.transcription:
Preparation time, 4 hours
Cooking time, 30
minutes
Serves, 2
I4 oz
(400 g) Manila (palourde) clams
or surf clams
I oz (25 g) dried konbu
Scant½ cup (3 1/2 fl oz/roo ml)
soy sauce
3 1/2 tablespoons mirin
• 2 knobs unsalted butter
2 teaspoons
salted capers, rinsed

peeled if desired
½ handful sea aster, samphire,
or sea purslane
Scant ½ cup (3 ½ fl oz/roo ml) sake
Preparation time, Overnight
for konbu
water and however long it takes to
dehydrate tangerine peel and cook rice

% oz
(20 g) dried konbu

2 tablespoons sesame seeds
I tablespoon ground sansho pepper
I tablespoon ground dried tangerine
peel (see Note)

5 '/• oz
(150 g) Japanese short
grain rice, cooked
7 oz
(200 g) watercress, roughly
chopped
2 teaspoons soy sauce
I teaspoon mirin
• l pinch of salt
For the fish,
2
pieces hake (3½-5 oz/roo-150 g
each), boned and skinned
2 tablespoons mirin
· 2 lemon wedges
CLAMS, FAVA BEANS, AND CAPERS
STEAMED IN DASHI BUTTER
Place the clams in a single layer in
a container. Make a solution of
3% salt water by weight and add
enough to the clams to just cover
them. Refrigerate overnight.
Steep the konbu for r5 minutes in
2 cups
(16 fl oz/500 ml) water
heated to r40°F (6o°C). Reserving
the broth, strain through a
cheesecloth into a small saucepan.
Add the soy sauce and mirin, bring to
a boil, and remove from the heat.
In a deep frying pan, melt the
butter with the capers over medium
heat. Add the fava (broad) beans
and cook for about 3 minutes until
the beans are half -coo ked.
Quickly rinse the clams and add
them to the pan along with the
sea aster. Measure out a generous
¾ cup (7 fl oz/200 ml) dashi
and add to the pan along with the
sake. Cover and cook until the
clams open.
Serve in a bowl with the broth .
GRILLED HAKE WITH SPICED
SKIN AND GREEN SURINAGASHI
Soak the konbu overnight in 1% cups
(13 fl oz/ 400 ml) cold water to
make konbu water.
Make the spice mixture, In a bowl,
stir together the sesame seeds, sansho
pepper, and tangerine peel.
Make the green surinagashi,
(A traditional surinagashi is a thick
sauce made with ground fish, tofu,
vegetables, and dashi. The version
we use at the restaurant is green.
(It could be any seasonal green leafy
vegetable, but I use watercress and
rice here.) Start the surinagashi by
grinding and mixing the rice with
drops of konbu water with a mortar
and pestle. When all the rice is
mashed, transfer to a blender along
with the rest of the konbu water, the
watercress, soy sauce, mirin, and salt.
Blend until smooth and transfer to
a saucepan. Heat gently while you
cook the fish.
CHEFS
Make the fish, Preheat
the broiler
(grill). Broil (grill) the hake for
10-15 minutes and when almost
cooked, brush with the mirin and
cover the skin side with the spice
mixture and continue broiling
until the fish is cooked and the
spices are crusty, 3-5 minutes.
To serve, pour a small ladle of
the surinagashi onto a plate and place
the hake in the middle along with
a wedge of lemon.
Note, Tangerine
peel can be
dehydrated in a low -te mperature
oven, a dehydrator , or under
the sun, then ground in a spice
grinder. It can also be purchased
in many Asian grocery stores.

skewers
3 large

BRETT REDMAN
JIDORI
89 KINGSLAND HIGH STREET

UNITED KINGDOM
In 2006, after training at Sydney, Australia's top restaurants and when
he was only twenty-six, Chef Brett Redman opened Elliot's-his first
restaurant,
named for the street he grew up on in Australia. Serving dishes
made with locally sourced, seasonal ingredients before the farm-to-table
trend took off , Elliot's was an overnight success. Since then, Redman
opened several more restaurants, includingJidori, which servesyakitori.
TSUKUNE
Finely chop the shiso and scallions
(spring onions) greens. In a large
bowl, using your hands, thoroughly
mix the chicken, panko, scallion
greens , shiso leaves , and salt. Beat
the mixture with your hand until
the mixture is sticky and paste-like.
(The mixing part is very important
to get a soft texture after cooking.)
Form the mixture into 8 even size
balls and refrigerate until firm,
about I hour.
Lightly oil your hand with sesame
oil so the meat mixture won't stick
to them.
GRILLED CORN
Prepare an outdoor grill
(barbecue). On a medium hot part
of the grill, cook the corn in the
husks for about 30 minutes. The
husks will start to go black and look
burned, but no need to worry.
Once the corn is cooked through,
place on a serving platter and
peel the husks away from the top
1/ :r:. 7 CHEFS
Form each ball around a skewer,
molding it into an oval shape
around 1/, inch (r cm) from the tip
and 2½ inches (6 cm) long.
Light the charcoal in an outdoor
grill (barbecue) and let reduce to
ash-covered embers. Cook the
chicken skewers until they register
167°F (75°C)
in the thickest part.
Serve the skewers with tare.
revealing the corn kernels. Smother
this with the butter, sea salt, shichimi
togarashi, lime juice, and zest.
Note, When
grilling (barbecuing)
it 's best to keep the husks on as it
helps to steam the corn and keep
it moist , while still taking on the
smoky flavor of the grill.

piece of chicken , some of the

a fine-mesh sieve , pushing every

Kewpie mayonnaise

sea salt and sansho pepper

(caster) sugar and 3 1/, cups
(6 fl oz / 800 ml) water and bring

scrape with a fork . Continue doing

you let it go too far and end up with

a nice flaky but icy granita.
1/ I. 7 CHEFS

chunks .
Place the silken tofu and powdered

To serve , place a few spoons of
the whipped tofu in the bottom
of a bowl or sundae glass. Top with
some melon and then a nice big
pile of the
flaky sake granita.

recipes.title: Sesame Rings
recipes.transcription:
SİMİT
SESAME RINGS
What pretzels are to New Yorkers,
simit
 are to Istanbulians, who buy them from street stalls all day
long and munch them between appointments.
They are at least 600 years old—Topkapı Palace documents from 1593 include bulk orders for
simid-i halka
 (round simits). They have entered the language of metaphor. A Turk who hates his job
will say: ‘I’d be better off selling
simit
’. Protesters trying to dissuade police from breaking up a
demonstration will shout: ‘Sell
simit
 and leave with honour.’
There are bakeries that cook nothing but
simit
—in wood-fire ovens, of course, at 300°C (570°F/
Gas 10+). And there are cafés, usually with titles such as ‘Palace of Simit’, that serve them with
melted cheese, tomato and other unnecessary additions. Personally, I would never sit down to eat
simit
, and I would never cook them at home if I was in Istanbul. But outside my homeland, you need a
recipe.

combine.

oil and thickened cream. Knead the dough for 5 minutes to make a soft and stretchy dough, adding
more flour if the dough is sticky. Cover the bowl with a damp cloth and rest for 1 hour. It should
expand.
Preheat the oven to 230°C (450°F/Gas 8).
Add the salt to the dough and knead for 3 minutes. Sprinkle some flour on your work surface. Divide

recipes.title: Bazlama Pan-Fried Bread
recipes.transcription:
BAZLAMA
PAN-FRIED BREAD
Bazlama
 is the simplest form of bread in the world—it doesn’t even require an oven. The technique is
probably at least 3000 years old. In Turkish villages, lumps of dough are spread on a
sac
(pronounced ‘sazh’), which is like an upturned wok resting over hot coals. You could try that, or use
a frying pan instead.
Unlike most breads,
bazlama
 involves little preparation time. You could leave it to rise overnight,
or you could wake up on a Sunday morning, decide ‘Lets do a
bazlama
 brunch’, invite your friends,
leave the dough to rise while you’re showering and tidying up, and fry your bread while your guests
are sitting down.
Because it contains
yoğurt
 it has a rich flavour and an interesting texture—soft inside and crunchy
outside. You’d serve it with jams or cheeses (which you would need to make earlier).
SERVES 4
2 teaspoons dry yeast
1 teaspoon sugar
600 g (1 lb 5 oz /4 cups) plain (all-purpose) flour, plus extra for dusting
1 teaspoon salt
125 g (4½ oz/½ cup) plain
yoğurt
vegetable oil, for frying
butter, jam or cheese, to serve
Put the yeast and sugar in a bowl with 250 ml (9 fl oz/1 cup) of lukewarm water, then set aside for 5
minutes. It should start to form bubbles.
Sift the flour into a mixing bowl, make a well in the middle, and pour in the yeast mixture. Knead the
dough for 1 minute, then add the
yoğurt
. Knead for a further 10 minutes or until the dough has reached,
as we say in Turkey, ‘the softness of an earlobe’. Cover the bowl with a damp cloth and rest in a
warm place for 2 hours. The ball of dough should double in size.
Add the salt to the dough and knead for 3 minutes. Sprinkle some flour on your work surface and
divide the dough into four balls. Return the dough to the bowl, cover with a damp cloth and rest for
10 minutes.
Place one ball of dough on the work surface and, using floured hands or a rolling pin, flatten into a
round about 10 cm (4 in) wide and 1 cm (½ in) thick. Repeat with the remaining dough balls.

recipes.title: Poğaça Balkan-Style Brioche Stuffed With Potato And Chilli
recipes.transcription:
POĞAÇA
BALKAN-STYLE BRIOCHE STUFFED WITH
POTATO AND CHILLI
The Turkish word
poğaça
 (pronounced ‘poe-uchah’) comes from the same root as the Italian word
focaccia
: the Latin
panis focacius
, which means bread cooked in the hearth. That suggests it must have
been a favourite of the Romans during their time in Constantinople. In the mid-seventeenth century, the
travel writer Evliya Çelebi reported in his memoir
Seyahatname
 (Tales of the Journey) that a sweet
version of
poğaça
 had been popular in the sultan’s palace 100 years earlier but was introduced as
street food by Balkan immigrants, who would heap hot ashes over the dough, let it bake, then scrape
the bread clean and serve it with cheese or lamb mince. (The description sounds rather like damper, a
favourite of Australian bushies in the nineteenth century.)
My version of this recipe could not have been eaten by the Emperor Constantine, since potatoes
only reached Turkey from South America in the eighteenth century. I think
poğaça
 tastes even better
when the mash melts into the dough.
SERVES 4
1 teaspoon dry yeast
2 teaspoons sugar
70 g (2½ oz) butter
1 egg
125 g (4½ oz/½ cup) plain
yoğurt
300 g (10½ oz/2 cups) plain (all-purpose) flour, plus extra for dusting
3 boiling potatoes (such as desiree)
2 teaspoons salt, plus extra for boiling the potatoes
1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
2 teaspoons chilli flakes
1 heaped tablespoon shredded
kaşar
 (or mozzarella)
1 tablespoon vegetable oil
1 egg yolk
1 tablespoon nigella seeds
1 tablespoon sesame seeds
Mix the yeast and the sugar in a bowl with 125 ml (4 fl oz/½ cup) of lukewarm water and set aside
for 5 minutes. It should start to form bubbles.
Whisk the butter, egg and
yoğurt
 together in a bowl. Sift the flour into a mixing bowl, make a well in

recipes.title: Balikli Ekmek Black Sea Cornbread With Leeks And Whitebait
recipes.transcription:
BALIKLI EKMEK
BLACK SEA CORNBREAD WITH LEEKS
AND WHITEBAIT
When I led my first gourmet tour of Turkey in 2013, we visited the tranquil Istanbul suburb of
Anadolu Kavaği—the last stop for the Bosphorus ferries—lined with casual seaside restaurants
looking out to the Black Sea and up to Yoros Castle. We sat down to a fish feast.
Walking back to the ferry, we passed an unassuming bakery, and one of my guests noted a snack I’d
never seen before—cornbread that seemed to be stuffed with sardines and leeks. He bought some for
everyone and they declared it the highlight of the day. So I researched it and recreated it for this book.
Hamsi
 is the most prized fish of the Black Sea—somewhere between an anchovy and a sardine. I
decided to substitute baby whitebait, because
hamsi
 don’t swim far beyond the Bosphorus and
sardines might be too strong for breakfast.
SERVES 8
½ bunch silverbeet (Swiss chard)
½ bunch dill
½ bunch flat-leaf (Italian) parsley
2 leeks
2 onions
2 tablespoons butter
2 tablespoons dried mint
500 g (1 lb 2 oz) whitebait
2 teaspoons baking powder
1 kg (2 lb 4 oz) maize flour
250 ml (9 fl oz/1 cup) olive oil, plus extra for brushing
1 egg
1 tablespoon salt
Wash the silverbeet and remove the stalks. Finely chop the leaves. Remove the stalks from the dill.
Pick the leaves from the parsley. Remove the roots and green outer layer from the leeks, then rinse to
remove any dirt. Finely chop the leeks, parsley and onions separately.
Melt the butter in a frying pan over high heat. Add the onions and cook for 3 minutes or until soft. Add
the leeks and cook for 3 minutes, then add the silverbeet and cook for a further 5 minutes. Remove
from the heat, turn into a bowl and leave to cool.

recipes.title: Yalanci Kaymak Clotted Cream With Rose Jam Kaymak
recipes.transcription:
YALANCI KAYMAK
CLOTTED CREAM WITH ROSE JAM
The Turkish name for this dish translates as ‘Liar’s
kaymak
’, because our recipe will not end up
tasting the same as the
kaymak
 that has been served for 100 years in my favourite breakfast café in
Istanbul—Pando in Beşiktaş markets. There the
kaymak
 is made with water buffalo milk that has been
slowly simmered until it’s thick and luscious.
In this recipe, I’ve included cornflour as a thickener, on the assumption that you will be using
pasteurised milk. If you have access to creamy unpasteurised milk, lucky you, because you can
eliminate the cornflour and come closer to the
Pando
 experience.
SERVES 4
KAYMAK
60 g (2¼ oz/½ cup) cornflour (cornstarch)
250 ml (9 fl oz/1 cup) full-cream (whole) milk (preferably high-fat such as Jersey or buffalo)
500 ml (17 fl oz /2 cups) thickened (whipping) cream
50 g (1¾ oz) butter
ROSE JAM
50 pink rose petals
500 g (1 lb 2 oz) sugar
1 teaspoon citric acid powder
pide bread
, to serve
First make the
kaymak
. Whisk the cornflour, milk and cream together to dissolve the starch. Transfer
to a baking tray, preferably a stainless steel ¼ gastronorm tray (26.5 x 16.3 x 2 cm/10
1
/
3
 x 6½ x ¾ in).
Place the tray over very low heat and whisk for 5 minutes—being careful not to let the mixture stick.
Add the butter and continue to whisk for 15 minutes or until it thickens to a pudding consistency.
Remove from the heat and leave to rest for 30 minutes, then transfer to the fridge.
To make the jam, first peel the petals from the pink roses. If using organic (non-sprayed) roses, wash
under cold running water. If using commercial roses, blanche in boiling water for 15 seconds, soak in
cold water in the fridge for 12 hours, and then strain and wash under cold running water. Discard any
brown or spotty petals. Cut the white patch off the bottom of each petal and slice any large petals in
half. Pat the petals dry with paper towel. Place a layer of petals in a bowl, sprinkle with sugar, add
another layer and repeat the process until all the petals are coated with the sugar. Cover with plastic
wrap and refrigerate overnight.

recipes.title: Ispanakli Kol Böreği Rolled Pastry With Spinach And Feta
recipes.transcription:
ISPANAKLI KOL BÖREĞI
ROLLED PASTRY WITH SPINACH AND
FETA
The Turkish word
kol
 means ‘arm’, and presumably gets into the Turkish name for this
börek
 because
each roll of pastry is bent to look like an arm coming round to hug you. It would make more sense to
call this a spiral or a labyrinth, since that is how it looks when all the arms are linked together.
My maternal grandma, who came from Yugoslavia, was a master of the ‘arm
börek
’, and she made
giant spirals to feed a large family. In later life, she used an electric
börek
 cooker, called a drum
oven, which was a cylinder with doors on the side and shelves onto which you could place multiple
layers of
börek
.
Spinach is the traditional filling, but you can use kale, silverbeet or even minced lamb.
SERVES 8
250 g (9 oz) English spinach
1 onion
4 spring onions (scallions)
120 ml (4 fl oz) sunflower or vegetable oil
1 tablespoon chilli flakes
1 tablespoon salt
1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon dried mint
150 g (5½ oz) feta
80 ml (2½ fl oz/
1
/
3
 cup) milk
1 egg
1 tablespoon plain
yoğurt
2 sheets
yufka
 (if you cannot buy
yufka
)
Wash the spinach thoroughly. Remove the stalks, then finely chop the leaves. Finely slice the onion.
Wash the spring onions, then remove the roots and green outer layer. Finely chop.
Put 2 tablespoons of oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Add the onions and cook for 3 minutes.
Add the spring onions and cook for 3 minutes more. Add the spinach and cook for a further 3 minutes,
then remove from the heat. Mix in all the herbs and spices and leave in the frying pan to cool. Grate
the feta into the cooled spinach mixture.
Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F/Gas 4).

recipes.title: Kürt Böreği Kurdish-Style Rolled Pastry With Hazelnuts
recipes.transcription:
KÜRT BÖREĞI
KURDISH-STYLE ROLLED PASTRY WITH
HAZELNUTS
The Turkish name for this pastry—
kürt böreği
—suggests it is a Kurdish speciality, but you should not
expect to find it in eastern Anatolia, where the Kurds live. The name seems to have arisen because
it’s the kind of dish Istanbul chefs imagine Kurds might eat. To confuse the issue further, I’ve boosted
it with hazelnuts and crème pâtissière, which makes it more like the kind of rich pastry they love on
the Black Sea.
SERVES 4
ROLLED PASTRY
120 g (4½ oz/1 cup) hazelnuts
1 kg (2 lb 4 oz) plain (all-purpose) flour (plus extra for dusting), or 3 sheets frozen puff pastry
2 eggs
1 tablespoon baking powder
125 ml (4 fl oz/½ cup) vegetable oil
125 g (4½ oz/½ cup) plain
yoğurt
150 g (5½ oz) butter, plus extra for greasing
1 tablespoon cinnamon powder
3 tablespoons icing (confectioners’) sugar
CRÈME PÂTISSIÈRE
310 ml (10¾ fl oz fl oz/1¼ cups) milk
3 egg yolks
3 tablespoons cornflour (cornstarch)
2 tablespoons plain (all-purpose) flour
30 g (1 oz/¼ cup) icing (confectioners’) sugar
1 vanilla bean, or 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F/Gas 4).
Place the hazelnuts on a baking tray and bake for 5 minutes. Remove from the oven and leave to cool.
When the nuts are cool enough to handle, remove the skin, transfer to a food processor and grind
coarsely.
To make the crème pâtissière, warm the milk in a saucepan over low heat for about 10 minutes until it

recipes.title: Kuymak Black Sea Fondue
recipes.transcription:
KUYMAK
BLACK SEA FONDUE
This is a speciality of the Laz people who live along the Black Sea in northern Anatolia. People from
other parts of Turkey say two things about the Laz people: the women are very beautiful and the men
are very smart before midday. The Laz are famous for creating hundreds of recipes from a fish similar
to a sardine called
hamsi
, but this is one of the few sardine-free recipes. It’s a kind of fondue into
which you dip bread, but the maize flour gives it more of a hearty porridge consistency than a Swiss
fondue. It prepares you to face the harsh climate along that windy coast.
SERVES 4
2 tablespoons butter
½ teaspoon salt
½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
100 g (3½ oz) maize flour
115 g (4 oz/¾ cup) shredded mozzarella
1 tablespoon grated parmesan
½ teaspoon smoked paprika
pide bread
, to serve
Combine the butter, salt, pepper and 500 ml (17 fl oz/2 cups) of water in a saucepan over high heat
and bring to the boil. Reduce the heat and add the maize flour. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring
constantly. Add the cheeses and stir in to melt.
Top with paprika and serve hot in the pot, with pide for dipping.

recipes.title: Katmer Pistachio Pancakes With Clotted Cream
recipes.transcription:
KATMER
PISTACHIO PANCAKES WITH CLOTTED
CREAM
When the suffix -
ci
 (pronounced ‘zhee’) is added to a Turkish noun it means ‘a maker of’ that thing.
Thus a
katmerci
 is a maker of
katmer
, the crunchy pancake that is a speciality of Gaziantep, in
southeastern Anatolia. The supreme
katmerci
 in that foodie city is a man named Mehmet Özsimitci,
whose surname translates as ‘maker of genuine simits’. That tells you that one of his ancestors was a
specialist in the pretzel/bagels that every Turk consumes as a street snack.
Somewhere along the line, Mehmet’s family swapped from making
simits
 to making
katmers
,
adding greatly to the happiness of the world. Outside his shop, at the end of an arcade in the modern
part of the city, Mehmet displays a slogan that translates as ‘
Katmer
 is not a product of a pastry shop
but a culture of master Zekeriya’. Zekeriya is Mehmet’s father, who these days sits at the cash register
while Mehmet supervises his team of young pastry rollers and dances around the outside tables,
taking orders and chatting to customers.
He’ll tell you that
katmer
 is best consumed with tea rather than coffee (and he’ll order you a tea
from the shop next door); that
katmer
 is traditionally the first meal eaten by a bride and groom after
their wedding night (to restore their energy); and that half his daily production goes to home delivery
—transported by moped across Gaziantep and by mail to homesick Turks all over Europe.
I hope my recipe does him justice.
SERVES 4
2 sheets chilled filo pastry, about 40 x 27 cm (16 x 10¾ in) each
2 tablespoons
ghee
2 tablespoons thick (double) cream, or
kaymak
2 heaped tablespoons ground pistachios
1 tablespoon sugar
Take the filo sheets out of the fridge and leave to warm to room temperature for 1 hour. Spread one
sheet out on a large work surface and overlap with another sheet to create a 40 x 40 cm (16 x 16 in)
square of filo. Paint a little ghee where the sheets overlap, and join them together.
Leaving a margin of about 10 cm (4 in) around the edges, dot nine dobs of cream onto the filo to make
a square about 20 cm (8 in) wide. Sprinkle the pistachios and sugar over the cream, and then fold the
four edges of pastry over to make a square parcel about 20 cm (8 in) wide.
Pour 1 tablespoons of ghee into a frying pan and swirl to coat. Place the pan over medium heat and let

recipes.title: Cartlak Kebabi Liver Kebaps Kebaps
recipes.transcription:
CARTLAK KEBABI
LIVER KEBAPS
You’ve got to get up pretty early in the morning to catch Ali Haydar. Around 6 am should do it. If you
wait till 8, you might find he has sold out of his speciality and gone home. This speciality is lamb
liver
kebaps
—another breakfast tradition of southeastern Anatolia that baffles visitors from Istanbul.
Ali opens his little
kebap
 shop, just down the hill from Gaziantep Castle, immediately after the
dawn prayer, which means around 5 am in the summer and around 6 am in the winter. Gradually the
customers arrive to sit on the tiny stools outside the shop. Some sit at an angle that suggests they are
on the way home from a night of drinking. Others are straight-backed and alert, suggesting they are
just out of the nearby mosque and on their way to work.
Inside the shop, Ali, in a light-blue butcher’s jacket, risks setting fire to his moustache as he uses a
sheet of cardboard to fan the coals of his charcoal grill. He closely watches his skewers and, at the
moment the exterior turns crunchy while the inside stays pink, he lifts them away from the coals and
wipes them into a mitten of flatbread. When all his livers (and his hearts, lungs and kidneys) have
been cooked and consumed by customers, he heads home. In the afternoon he visits the offal market
(distinguished by a large sign announcing ‘Cleaned Heads’) and collects the ingredients to be
prepared overnight for the next morning’s feast.
SERVES 4
KEBAPS
2 lamb livers, about 300 g (10½ oz)
250 ml (9 fl oz/1 cup) milk
4 mild green or red chillies
1 teaspoon cumin
1 teaspoon hot paprika
1 teaspoon chilli flakes
1 teaspoon salt
250 g (9 oz) butter, softened
PARSLEY SALAD
1 bunch flat-leaf (Italian) parsley
1 red onion
1 tablespoon sumac
1 teaspoon chilli flakes
2 teaspoons
pomegranate molasses
1 tablespoon olive oil

recipes.title: İnci̇r Uyutmasi̇ The Sleeping Figs
recipes.transcription:
İNCİR UYUTMASİ
THE SLEEPING FIGS
‘
While shepherds watched their flocks by night, all seated on the ground, they also soaked their figs in
milk, and then some sleep they found.
’
 That’s essentially the back story of this dish. I love its name—
the Sleeping Figs—because it suggests the gentle process of warming the milk and resting the pudding
overnight.
A version of this dessert, called
teleme
, has been a typical goat herder’s snack popular for
thousands of years in northwestern Anatolia. They’d milk their goats, add a few drops of sap from
fresh figs to the milk, mix it for a few minutes and let it set into
yoğurt
. Then they would slice fresh
figs through it. Of course, that restricted the pleasure to early autumn, when figs are at their best. Our
version uses cow’s milk, walnuts and dried figs to make a healthy breakfast for all seasons.
SERVES 4
10 dried figs
500 ml (17 fl oz/2 cups) milk
2 fresh figs
2 tablespoons grape molasses
60 g (2¼ oz/½ cup) walnuts
Put the figs in a bowl, cover with hot water and leave to soak for 15 minutes. Transfer the figs to
paper towel, leave to drain for 10 minutes, then remove the stalks. Roughly chop each fig into about
six pieces and then set aside.
Warm the milk in a saucepan over low heat until it reaches a low simmer, preferably using a simmer
mat. Try to keep the temperature around 70°C (160°F) if you have a food thermometer, being careful
not to let the milk start to boil.
Add the chopped figs and, using a hand-held blender, mix to a purée. Simmer for a further 5 minutes.
(If you don’t have a stick blender, pour the mixture into a blender and pulse until smooth, then pour it
back into the saucepan and warm for a further 7 minutes).
Half fill four small bowls with the fig purée. Put the bowls in a cool spot, cover with a tea towel
(dish towel) and rest for 2 hours. Cover the bowls with plastic wrap and place in the fridge
overnight.
When you’re nearly ready to serve, preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F/Gas 4).

recipes.title: Menemen Smashed Eggs With Bullhorn Peppers And Tomato
recipes.transcription:
MENEMEN
SMASHED EGGS WITH BULLHORN
PEPPERS AND TOMATO
Menemen
 is a famous breakfast dish in Turkey—the nearest thing we do to scrambled eggs—but
nobody can agree on the perfect version. It varies from village to village and from house to house—
even in the Aegean town called Menemen, which is not necessarily its place of origin. There is
constant debate among chefs and domestic cooks on whether to use butter or oil, whether to include
onions or garlic, whether to include peppers or tomatoes, and whether to leave the eggs whole for the
eater to smash, or scramble them as part of the cooking process.
I prefer to use oil, because I want to cook the onions and peppers without burning the butter. I add
the tomatoes at the last minute so they taste fresh. And I prefer my eggs stirred not scrambled. You can
join the debate and vary the dish to your taste.
SERVES 4
4 ripe tomatoes
2 green bullhorn peppers (or 1 large green capsicum/pepper)
1 red onion (optional)
2 tablespoons olive oil
4 eggs
1 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon chopped flat-leaf (Italian) parsley
Score a shallow cross in the base of each tomato. Put the tomatoes in a heatproof bowl and cover
with boiling water. Leave for 30 seconds, then transfer to a bowl of cold water and peel the skin
away from the cross. To seed, cut the tomato in half and scoop out the seeds with a teaspoon. Chop
the tomatoes into 1 cm (½ in) dice.
Cut the peppers in half and discard the stems and seeds. Chop the peppers into 1 cm (½ in) pieces. If
you are using an onion, finely slice it.
Heat the olive oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Add a drop of water to the oil. If it sizzles, the oil
is ready. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes. Add the chopped peppers and cook for a further 5
minutes, or until soft. Break the eggs into the pan and cook for 30 seconds. Add the tomatoes, salt and
pepper. Stir two or three times to mix in the eggs, but don’t blend. Cook over medium heat for a
further 3 minutes until the egg whites are set.

recipes.title: Sucuklu Yumurta Spicy Sausage With Eggs Sucuk*
recipes.transcription:
SUCUKLU YUMURTA
SPICY SAUSAGE WITH EGGS
There is nothing sophisticated about this recipe, but I had to include it because it’s one of the most
common breakfasts all over my land. It’s our answer to Britain’s bacon and eggs. A wife might say of
her husband: ‘He’s so hopeless, he can’t even cook
sucuk
 and eggs’.
You can buy
sucuk
 everywhere in Turkey, so nobody would bother to make it at home. But if you
can’t find it near you, you could use the recipe we offer here (or substitute chorizo). Bear in mind that
this won’t taste exactly like a professional
sucuk
, since that is stuffed into intestine casings, then hung
and dried for a month. But it will be tasty.
SERVES 4
SUCUK*
2 garlic cloves, crushed
250 g (9 oz) minced (ground) veal or beef
150 g (5½ oz) minced (ground) lamb
1 teaspoon cumin
1 teaspoon dried oregano
2 teaspoons chilli flakes
2 teaspoons smoked paprika
1 tablespoon
capsicum (pepper) paste
1 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 teaspoon butter
1 teaspoon salt
4 eggs
pide bread
, to serve
To make your own
sucuk
, crush the garlic into a fine paste. Put the garlic into a mixing bowl, add the
ground meat and spices, and knead for 10 minutes.
Using a rolling pin, flatten the meat mixture into a strip about 1 cm (½ in) thick and then roll it into a
log about 4 cm (1½ in) wide. Wrap tightly with plastic wrap, squeezing all the air out, then freeze for
1 hour.
Remove the
sucuk
 from the freezer, remove the plastic wrap, and slice off twenty thin slices (about 5
mm/¼ in thick). Put the remaining
sucuk
 in the fridge where it will keep, wrapped in plastic, for 2
weeks.

recipes.title: Poached Eggs In Garlic Yoğurt And Paprika
recipes.transcription:
ÇİLBİU
POACHED EGGS IN GARLIC YOĞURT AND
PAPRIKA
In Ottoman times,
çılbır
 was the generic term for poached eggs, done all sorts of ways. Palace
records from the fifteenth century show that a version of
çılbır
 containing poached eggs and onion
was cooked for the mighty sultan Mehmet II. The imperial cooks kept improving on it over the years.
This recipe, with garlic
yoğurt
, was a favourite of the second-last sultan in the empire, Abdulhamid
II, in the early twentieth century, and became the gold standard for
çılbır
 in homes and restaurants
across Anatolia.
SERVES 4
1 garlic clove (or chopped garlic shoots)
500 g (1 lb 2 oz/2 cups) plain
yoğurt
½ small red capsicum (pepper)
125 ml (4 fl oz/½ cup) white vinegar
8 eggs
2 tablespoons butter
½ tablespoon aleppo red pepper flakes (or chilli flakes)
4 teaspoons smoked paprika
pide bread
, to serve
Crush the garlic and mix it with the
yoğurt
 (if the taste of raw garlic in the morning is too strong for
you, you could leave out this step, and instead fry a little garlic or chopped garlic shoots later with
the capsicum). Set aside at room temperature.
Remove the seeds from the capsicum and finely chop.
Divide the
yoğurt
 mixture into four bowls.
Put 1 litre (35 fl oz/4 cups) of water and the vinegar in a deep frying pan over high heat. Bring to the
boil, then reduce the heat to a gentle simmer. Carefully break in the eggs, one at a time, with a
maximum of three eggs poaching at a time. Cook for 2–3 minutes, or until the whites are set and the
yolks are still soft and runny.
While the eggs are poaching, melt the butter in a saucepan, add the red pepper flakes, paprika and
capsicum (and garlic, if you’ve saved it for this step) and cook for 3 minutes.

recipes.title: Kaygana Cretan Eggs With Wild Weeds
recipes.transcription:
KAYGANA
CRETAN EGGS WITH WILD WEEDS
There’s a joke about a salad farmer who is having a tea in the village café. A neighbour comes in and
says: ‘There’s a goat in your field.’ The farmer says: ‘Don’t worry, he won’t eat much’. Shortly
afterward, the neighbour returns and says: ‘There’s a cow in your field.’ The farmer keeps sipping his
tea and says: ‘Don’t worry about it.’ Then the neighbour returns and says: ‘There’s a man from Crete
in your field.’ The farmer leaps up and rushes back to save his field before everything green has been
stripped.
People of Cretan background are famous for eating the dark-green weeds that grow wild along the
Aegean coast and that were ignored for centuries by Turkish cooks. This egg dish uses the kind of
wild (and tame) greens the Cretans have taught the Turks to love.
SERVES 4
1 cup of any or all of these, mixed: nettles, curly endives, chicory, dandelion greens, round radicchio,
beetroot (beet) leaves, wild rocket (but not witlof)
3 spring onions (scallions)
1 onion
80 ml (2½ fl oz/
1
/
3
 cup) olive oil
1 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 teaspoon hot paprika
4 eggs
pide bread
, to serve
If you are using nettles, use gloves to handle them. To remove the sting, put in a heatproof bowl and
cover with boiling water for 30 seconds. Transfer to cold water for 30 seconds. Pick the green leaves
and discard the stems.
Clean and finely chop the endives and the chicory, discarding the woody stems. Wash the spring
onions, then remove the roots and green outer layer. Finely chop the onion.
Heat the olive oil in a non-stick frying pan over medium heat, then add the onion and brown for 5
minutes. Add the spring onions and cook for another 3 minutes, then add the wild leaves in this order
(from toughest to softest): endives, chicory, radicchio, nettle, dandelion, beetroot leaves, wild rocket.
Lightly fry for about 5 minutes to let any excess water evaporate. Add the spices and stir. Make four
wells in the mixture and break an egg into each well. Continue to cook until the whites are set but the
yolks are still runny.

recipes.title: Beyran Fiery Lamb And Rice Soup
recipes.transcription:
BEYRAN
FIERY LAMB AND RICE SOUP
Take a whole sheep, skin it and gut it. Boil it for 12 hours. Shred all the meat. Boil the same weight of
rice. Put some rice, a handful of meat and a hell of a lot of garlic and chilli into a bowl. Put it over an
open flame so the fat on the surface catches fire. Serve.
That’s not the recipe we’re suggesting for
beyran
, but it’s what Mustafa Hasırcı and his team do
every day at Metanet, just behind the central spice market in Gaziantep, southeastern Turkey. The
restaurant’s name means ‘endurance’ or ‘fortitude’, which is presumably what you need to eat this
spicy soup every day for breakfast as many citizens of Gaziantep do (only tourists think of having
beyran
 for lunch).
Mustafa certainly has endurance. For the past forty years he’s been getting up every day at 4 am to
make his soup—following in the footsteps of his father, the founder of Metanet. Mustafa has earned
the title
usta
, which means ‘master of your craft’. He has no equal in Gaziantep.
Our soup is a modified version of Mustafa’s masterwork, and we won’t tell anybody if you decide
to have it for lunch or dinner.
SERVES 4
1 lamb neck, about 1 kg (2 lb 4 oz)
220 g (7¾ oz/1 cup) medium-grain rice
2 teaspoons salt
4 garlic cloves, crushed
1 tablespoon chilli flakes
Put the lamb neck in a large saucepan with 1 litre (35 fl oz/4 cups) of water, then cover, and bring to
the boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for about 1½ hours.
Lift out the neck and place on a rack or plate to cool. Do not discard the cooking water. When the
lamb is cool enough to handle, strip off the meat and discard the bones. Shred the lamb into small
strips and set aside.
Pour the rice into the pot of lamb-flavoured water and bring it back to the boil over medium heat.
Cook the rice for 15 minutes, then add the salt, garlic, shredded lamb and chilli flakes. Increase the
heat to very high and boil rapidly for 1 minute to spread the red-chilli colour through the liquid. Serve
immediately, while very hot.

recipes.title: Pi̇rpi̇ri̇m Aşi Purslane And Ancient Grains Stew
recipes.transcription:
PİRPİRİM AŞI
PURSLANE AND ANCIENT GRAINS STEW
Vegetarians are always surprised by how many interesting dishes the land of lamb lovers can offer. In
season, this stew appears regularly on the famous ‘Fifty Bowl’ display table at Çiya restaurant in
Istanbul’s Kadıköy market, using the kind of grains humans have been boiling for millennia. While it
is likely that lentils and chickpeas originated in Anatolia, black-eyed peas are recent arrivals—
brought from Africa in the fifteenth century for palace chefs eager to surprise the sultan.
The sour-salty green purslane, which contains more omega-3 than any other leafy vegetable, is
Turkey’s favourite weed, usually consumed fresh in summer and dried in winter. In the first great
work on botany, written in the fourth century BC, the Greek philosopher Theophrastus advises sowing
purslane in mid-spring so you can enjoy it in summer. If you can’t find purslane, the best substitute is
baby rocket (arugula).
SERVES 4
95 g (3¼ oz/½ cup) dried chickpeas

pide bread

recipes.title: Anali Ki̇zli ‘Mother And Daughter’ (Dumpling And Chickpea Stew)
recipes.transcription:
ANALI KİZLI
‘MOTHER AND DAUGHTER’ (DUMPLING
AND CHICKPEA STEW)
This complex combination of large and small dumplings in a lamb and chickpea stew comes from
Malatya in eastern Anatolia, an area best known for apricots. The mothers are a mixture of beef and
bulgur stuffed with minced lamb. The daughters are not big enough to have stuffing. You won’t find
this dish in many restaurants—only home cooks (and my friend Musa) have the time to do it properly.
For the mums’ outer coating it’s important to choose beef with a low fat content and to knead it
thoroughly so it dissolves into the bulgur.
SERVES 4
BASE
50 g (1¾ oz/¼ cup) dried chickpeas

recipes.title: Summer Vegetable Casserole
recipes.transcription:
TÜRLÜ
SUMMER VEGETABLE CASSEROLE
The Turkish word
türlü
 means ‘with variety’, and implies that you can use any kind of vegetable
that’s available in summer. This is sometimes called the Turkish ratatouille, but
türlü
 has many more
ingredients than the French dish, and you can even include lamb or beef and still call it türlü.
You need to layer the ingredients in a deep pot (traditionally clay), with the slowest-cooking
vegetables at the bottom, and simmer it for a long time. So yes, it’s a casserole, which is normally
thought of as a winter warmer. But this version, which includes green beans and okra, is perfect
served cold on the hottest day, with a side of rice pilav and yoğurt. It tastes even better the next day.
SERVES 4
1 long eggplant (aubergine)
1 zucchini (courgette)

2 onions
